📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We can all agree that the universe is more or less 13.8 billion years old, right?
  • What would happen if we tried to figure out the age of the universe with only tangible matter and energy?
  • “In this framework, only quantities with explicit length dimensionality covary through a universal scaling function, while dimensionless constants and dimensionless ratios remain invariant,” the researchers wrote in a study recently published in Universe, also adding that their model ensures “[Massive Bang nucleosynthesis] predictions are preserved.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We can all agree that the universe is more or less 13.8 billion years old, right? That figure comes largely from the European Space Agency’s Planck satellite, which mapped the cosmic microwave background (the leftover glow of the Big Bang), with results released in 2013 and finalized in 2018. Ground-based observations from the Atacama Cosmology Telescope (ACT) in Chile later arrived at nearly the same number. Both fit the standard model of cosmology, known as lambda cold dark matter (ΛCDM). There’s just one problem: That age depends on the existence of dark matter and dark energy, neither of which has ever been directly detected.

What would happen if we tried to figure out the age of the universe with only tangible matter and energy? Physicists Rajendra Gupta and Nikolaos Samaras of the University of Ottawa are asking this exact question. Frustrated by theories built on invisible matter and on an expansion driven by energy no one has detected, Gupta and Samaras developed their own cosmological framework, called covarying coupling constants plus tired light (CCC+TL). In this model, only quantities measured in units of length change together over cosmic time, while dimensionless constants stay fixed. The researchers tested whether CCC+TL could reproduce Significant Bang nucleosynthesis, the process that forged the universe’s first light elements in its earliest minutes. It could. The same model puts the age of the universe at 26.7 billion years, nearly twice the standard estimate.

“In this framework, only quantities with explicit length dimensionality covary through a universal scaling function, while dimensionless constants and dimensionless ratios remain invariant,” the researchers wrote in a study recently published in Universe, also adding that their model ensures “[Massive Bang nucleosynthesis] predictions are preserved.”.

In 1929, astronomer Edwin Hubble (namesake of the Hubble Space Telescope) found that the farther away a galaxy is, the more its light is shifted toward the red end of the spectrum. Most astronomers came to read this redshift as evidence that the universe is expanding. That same year, astronomer Fritz Zwicky proposed a different explanation, known as “tired light”: Light gradually loses energy as it crosses vast distances, so light from more distant galaxies arrives redder simply because it has traveled farther. Most cosmologists set tired light aside decades ago, but Gupta has revived a version of it as part of CCC+TL.

In a recent development, gupta and Samaras are challenging the prevailing view. In ΛCDM, the hot plasma of the newborn universe expanded and cooled, and ordinary (baryonic) matter then gathered inside vast haloes of dark matter to form galaxies. Dark energy, meanwhile, is thought to be driving the universe’s accelerating expansion. CCC+TL abandons both of those hypotheses. Instead, the upcoming theory modifies the standard equations for gravity and expansion, yet still reproduces the observed expansion of the universe and the amounts of hydrogen, helium, and other light elements formed in its first minutes. It can also reproduce galactic rotation curves, which measure how fast stars and gas orbit at different distances from a galaxy’s center.

In a recent development, gupta has also argued, in earlier papers, that CCC+TL gets around the objections that sank tired light the first time, including time dilation. In an expanding universe, light from distant supernovae is stretched out in time, so the supernovae seem to brighten and fade more slowly than nearby ones. Simple tired-light models don’t provide an explanation for that phenomenon. Time dilation itself comes from Einstein: Because light always travels at the same speed, observers moving at different speeds experience time differently, and time passes more slowly for someone moving very fast. That’s why astronauts aboard the International Space Station, which circles Earth at about 17,500 mph (28,000 kph), age very slightly more slowly than people on the ground. Gupta claims his new theory works better because the tired-light effect runs alongside cosmic expansion, instead of replacing it.

It has been revealed that dark matter and dark energy have been used to explain phenomena that would otherwise make no sense. CCC+TL tries to explain the same phenomena with modified gravitational effects instead. It also changes the cosmic timeline. In a 2023 paper, Gupta used CCC+TL to put the age of the universe at 26.7 billion years. That would give the first galaxies billions of years longer to form, which could explain surprisingly mature galaxies in the early universe and the Methuselah star, which some age estimates make older than the universe itself.

Recent findings suggest that “A central requirement for any alternative cosmology is that it preserves the key empirical successes of standard Big Bang nucleosynthesis,” Samaras and Gupta wrote. They concluded that “the CCC+TL model is consistent with the [Big Bang]-predicted primordial helium and other light-element observations.”.

It has been revealed that the idea remains well outside the mainstream. Most cosmologists still see ΛCDM, for all its unknowns, as the best fit to a wide range of observations, from the cosmic microwave background to how galaxies are spread across the sky. CCC+TL will have to pass many more tests to win them over.

She lurks right outside Latest York City with her parrot, Lestat. When not writing, she can be found drawing, playing the piano or shapeshifting.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the best black bags are, above all else, wardrobe necessities. Just like a good pair of jeans or a crisp white T-shirt, they’re the kind of accessories that never feel out of place, seamlessly working just about anything in your closet. Having a few different styles to rotate depending on the occasion just makes sense.

Sources indicate that tote bags and roomy bucket bags are ideal for office days, when carrying your laptop and other commuter essentials is a must, while shoulder bags offer a streamlined option for when you want to travel a little lighter. Crossbody bags offer a hands-free approach, while top handles give instant polish on the go, tapping into ladylike sensibilities that can make even the simplest outfit feel a little more pulled together. And for evenings out, party bags bring just the right amount of occasion-worthy appeal, with playful accents and embellishments that make getting dressed feel a little more fun.

If you’re in the market for a black handbag, consider this your guide to the very best styles available. From iconic shapes like Bottega Veneta’s Andiamo woven bag to Gucci’s reimagined Jackie shoulder bag, these are a few of the investment-worthy luxury designs that will earn their keep in your wardrobe for years to come. But you also don’t have to spend a fortune to find a great option: Coach’s offerings strike the perfect balance between timeless design, quality, and affordability.

Ahead, browse Vogue’s edit of the best black handbags to buy and cherish.

It has been revealed that ideal for office days, when carrying your laptop and other commuter essentials is a must, tote bags are the hardest-working styles in any handbag lineup. Choose one with staying power that can go the distance. From Bottega Veneta’s woven leather Andiamo and Dragon Diffusion’s large Santa Croce style to The Row’s Clement and Coach’s roomy Brooklyn shopper (a favorite of Bella Hadid), these carryalls make a case for investing in a black work bag you’ll reach for day after day.

In a recent development, when traveling a little lighter, black shoulder bags offer a streamlined option that still leaves room for the essentials—and looks great while doing it. Whether you’re drawn to Gucci’s reimagined Jackie shoulder bag (a celebrity favorite), Staud’s minimalist-friendly Strada, or Alaïa’s sculptural Click, think of these as silhouettes that can take you from daytime meetings to evenings out with ease.

Reach for a top-handle bag for instant polish on the go. With their ladylike sensibilities, these classic styles make even the simplest outfit feel a little more pulled together, especially in timeless black. Prada’s Passage shot straight to the top of our wish lists for its sleek silhouette, while Savette’s Symmetry is the editor-approved ‘IYKYK’ choice, each one of these luxury bags striking the sweet spot between timeless appeal and modern design.

Recent findings suggest that for a hands-free approach, crossbody bags do the job and then some. Whether you’re commuting, traveling, running weekend errands, or tackling everything in between, what can’t these black bags do? Some of our favorites include Khaite’s Blake, Toteme’s T-lock (it’s convertible!), and Demellier’s Vancouver—all versatile options that offer plenty of styling mileage.

It has been revealed that party bags are the category where you can experiment a little more. Although still versatile because of their color, they’ll bring something playful to the table that your everyday handbag cannot. Sleek satin clutches, embellished pouches, and velvet wristlets (even something in suede!) all add an instant dose of personality to even the simplest going-out look, thanks to a new wave of contemporary designs from Liffner, Sophie Buhai, and Valesque.

Cocktail hour was drawing to a close; the traditional pre-party dinner for the 31st edition of GQ’s legendary Men of the Year event, presented by Johnnie Walker Blue Label, was about to kick off. GQ’s Designer of the Year, Celine’s Michael Rider, and our Director of the Year, Denis Villeneuve, were already posted up inside the Chateau Marmont’s lobby lounge; the guests lingering just past the entrance included Odysseus himself, Matt Damon, building with his Ocean’s partner-in-crime Don Cheadle before pivoting to greet Chris Rock—like Damon, one of GQ’s three Men of the Year concern cover stars. (Andrew Garfield, subject of that third cover, had rolled in a few minutes earlier, resplendently coiffed, immediately gathering his After the Hunt co-star Ayo Edebiri and director Luca Guadagnino into a reunion hug.).

It has been revealed that but among the Men of the Year veterans in attendance—like Rock, who scored his first MOTY cover in 1999, circa Bigger and Blacker—there were also plenty of first-timers from the newly introduced class of news-makers and paradigm-shakers celebrated in GQ’s 2026 Breakouts portfolio. And that varied mix—of longtime icons and undeniable up-and-comers, from Owen Thiele and Inde Navarette to I Play Rocky’s Anthony Ippolito and electro-rock duo Fcukers—made for a veritable particle accelerator of improbable collisions.

Chicken Shop Date’s Amelia Dimoldenberg in deep confab with Tinashe. Tony’s Stavros Halkias in an across-the-table comedy summit with Chris Rock. Journalist Pablo Torre, whose reporting on Kawhi Leonard and the LA Clippers salary-cap shenanigans shook the NBA, engrossed in conversation with GQ’s own Zach Baron and Villeneuve, who’d just signed off on the prints—for real this time—for his third and final Dune movie, soon to shake the walls of nearly every IMAX theater on Earth.

And Villeneuve wasn’t the only auteur on hand: Between the Dune mastermind, Misty Green writer/director/star Rock, Club Kid’s similarly slashed Jordan Firstman, the La Bola Negra writer-directors jointly known as Los Javis (Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrosi) and Guadagnino, who upon arriving had almost immediately located a cinematically moody lamplit corner to hold court in, the Chateau’s lobby was, quipped GQ Global Editorial Director Adam Baidawi, “an incredible room to be an out-of-work actor in.”.

Because journalism doesn’t take a night off—not even GQ’s biggest night—Baidawi also tried, during his opening remarks, to pry some info regarding the identity of the newly introduced James Bond (off the record, just between us) out of Villeneuve.

In a recent development, as the director politely demurred—hey, we had to try—another guest piped up from across the table. “Wait,” said Matt Damon, as Baidawi passed the former superspy the mic. “I have a question. Just a thought experiment. What if James Bond were older? And American?” (In the unlikely event that Damon just booked a second iconic-superspy role, you heard it here first.).

Toast time was upon us: Rosalind Eleazar, raising a glass to Chris Rock, recalled her Zoom audition with Rock for Misty Green, which was followed in short order by a missed call from an American number and the two-word text message that would change her life: “Chris Rock.” (That’s right—when Chris Rock calls you from an unknown number and gets your voice mail, he follows up with a text that just indicates “Chris Rock,” an absolute power-move that is, unfortunately, hard to replicate by the rest of us.).

“Thinking I was being rather witty, I replied, ‘Rosalind Eleazar,’” Eleazar said. “I waited eagerly for his response and—not so much as a laughing emoji. And I rapidly realized that I am communicating with one of the funniest people on the planet and I should probably just leave the funny to him.”.

Sources indicate that eleazar recalled Rock telling her on set, My movie—your character, giving her the freedom to discover Misty on her own. “And that’s a rare gift,” she said, “and one that I will always be grateful for.”.

Recent findings suggest that “Thank you, Rosalind,” Rock said. “The check will be there in the morning.”.

Ayo Edebiri began by saluting “my dear friend, one of my favorite people in the world, one of the best actors ever, and a little bit of a role model to me if I’m being honest: Robert Pattinson.” She paused as the crowd fell out laughing. “Andrew! Andrew Garfield. I’m so sorry. This is a different speech for a different guy.”.

“You never know what you’re going to get when you work with somebody,” Edebiri noted, but said the resolutely “normal” Garfield had put her immediately at ease on After the Hunt, making it “safe to be unsafe” in difficult scenes. “And, on that movie especially, we had tough stuff to do,” she said. “We were not nice to each other. Some of the boys these days, on Method, you never know.”.

“If you ever see him in public,” Edebiri continued, “don't try any small talk with this man. Just don't do it. He's medically allergic to small talk. You get very deep, very fast. You will end up talking about esoteric poetry or the nature of masculinity in the modern world or just water, like the power and the mystery of water.” (This we can confirm.).

“I just love you so, so dearly,” Garfield responded, “and I hope we can be in each other's lives forever.”.

And with that moment of open-hearted sincerity out of the way, it was time for Damon to hear from frenemy Jimmy Kimmel, who fired off weapons-grade roast jokes. “I fought for the First Amendment this year,” Kimmel remarked. “You fought a puppet cyclops.”.

Industry observers note that damon, in response, mostly took the high road, offering up praise (for Edebiri’s speech) before getting the last word. “In closing, I would just like to repeat that I did not invite Jimmy Kimmel to this place. I’ve never invited him anywhere, and I never will. He is a horrible human being. And I thank you all for being here.” ✦.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that of all the incredible dips we’ve created over the years, our cranberry whipped feta dip is an internet and personal favorite—so much so that I just had to come back with an equally luxurious variation: this cranberry-topped whipped cream cheese spread. With the holiday party season just around the corner, this spread is begging to be included in your party spread. Plus, it's as easy to make as it is delicious—a tangy, sweet cranberry sauce gets finished with brandy, then is spooned atop a lemony whipped cream cheese for a guaranteed winning combo.

Fresh Or Frozen Cranberries? I used both while testing, and they both work interchangeably. I found the fresh cranberries broke down a little more than frozen, so it depends on whether or not you’re looking for more or less texture in your sauce.

What temperature should the cream cheese be? Make sure the cream cheese is chilled and softened but not super cold. It should be somewhat pliable when whipping to avoid lumps; this will ensure the mixture is light and airy. A little heavy cream will loosen the mixture if it's too thick.

The lemon zest: I found that the cream cheese layer needed a little more oomph. If you get a bite of cream cheese on a cracker, it shouldn’t be one-dimensional. Adding a touch of lemon zest makes it more palatable.

Storage:Store the cream cheese spread, with or without cranberry sauce, in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days.

#7414. The 8 Best Home Generators Are a Major Investment. These Deliver Reliable Power During an Outage.

The 8 Best Home Generators Are a Major Investment. These Deliver Reliable Power During an Outage.

📅 07 Nov 2018 | ⏱️ 25 min read (4938 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~25 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Stronger and more frequent severe weather events are making a compelling argument for investing in a home generator.
  • Industry observers note that the term “home generator” can be confusing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Stronger and more frequent severe weather events are making a compelling argument for investing in a home generator. A large portable generator or a permanently installed standby generator can keep your entire home powered and operational for several days, or at least keep a few critical appliances such as a refrigerator running until the power comes back on. The cost of emergency power is never a small investment, though it is an increasingly notable one.

Industry observers note that the term “home generator” can be confusing. It’s an unofficial category that includes larger portable generators capable of powering several appliances or a few critical circuits using a transfer switch (not all portable generators are built for this task). It also includes permanently installed standby generators that can automatically switch to whole-home backup power when the lights go out. Choosing the right size generator primarily comes down to how much power you think you’ll need in an emergency.

There are many reliable home generators that deliver a great deal of power. Some offer you the choice of running on multiple different fuels, while other models use an inverter that can give you quieter and “cleaner” operation. There is a nice range of prices available, too, so you can easily find a generator below that fits your needs as well as your budget.

For the generators on this list that we tested, we considered the difficulty of unboxing, assembling, and starting each generator for the first time, because few things are as frustrating as buying a tool that turns out to be unnecessarily complicated from the get-go.

In a recent development, once set up, the generators we reviewed were subjected to different load conditions, including things such as power tools, home appliances, and even recharging large power stations. We assessed the features that distinguish these generators from each other, including safety features, app connectivity, and portability, among other things.

A few picks on our list have not been tested, but we included them here after considerable research, taking into account the brand’s reputation, our knowledge of its product lines, various outside reviews, and our own experience testing similar models from those same brands.

It has been revealed that the DuroMax XP11000iH is a powerful midsize dual-fuel inverter generator, capable of keeping most homes up and running for an extended period of time. Inverter generators are a step above traditional generators because they convert alternating current (AC) to direct current (DC) and then back again to AC. This process creates cleaner, more efficient power and enables the generator to run more quietly and fuel efficiently.

It has been revealed that having two fuel options—gas and propane—provides a massive boost of convenience by allowing you to use whatever’s handy. No gasoline? You can use the same tank of propane you use for your gas grill. It’s also parallel-capable, so you can daisy-chain it with another generator if you need extra power.

According to recent reports, the generator is enclosed in a large, sturdy plastic casing, which makes it durable and provides a fair amount of sound dampening. Of the many gas generators I’ve tested, it may be the quietest model that’s capable of backing up a whole home, especially when it’s running on propane, which trims it down by another few decibels. At 61 decibels on a 20 percent load, it’s about as loud as a dishwasher. Most comparably sized generators go up to around 80 decibels—about the same volume as a police siren.

In addition to a full suite of essential modern safety features such as a carbon monoxide shutoff and low-oil shutoff, it goes the extra mile with lots of little touches, like remote start. The integrated battery tender keeps it ready to start, no matter how long it’s been sitting, which can be a lifesaver, too. When you do run out to check it, an onboard display reveals you key stats such as hours run, current load, and voltage output.

The only downside I could find was its weight. At upward of 200 pounds, it isn’t easy to carry. It does have wheels and sturdy handles, though, so it isn’t hard to wheel around on flat, paved ground—if you can push a loaded wheelbarrow, you can push this. Not that you’ll need to move it much; it’s a very sturdy generator, and it comes assembled with the wheels and handles attached (not all generators come with those pre-attached). —Reviewed by Nick Hilden.

According to recent reports, technically, there are cheaper generators out there, but the Generac GP9500E offers an outstanding blend of capability, quality, and durability at a very reasonable price. As such, this is where I’d steer you if you’re trying to shave down your spend.

Sources indicate that its 9,500-watt running capacity is slightly higher than the DuroMax’s, and it’s capable of powering all but the largest of homes. It can get a little noisy under a heavy load, but that’s common with units this size. It let out a relatively moderate purr when it was just powering the lights and a few appliances, but it became more of a roar when the heat kicked on.

With three fuel options—gas, propane, and natural gas—you get about as much versatility as you could possibly expect from a generator. A relatively large 7.5-gallon gas tank delivers a long runtime between fill-ups. And, while I was initially skeptical as to the necessity of the third fuel option, having natural gas support demonstrated its value when a storm knocked out the power, and I didn’t have gas or propane on hand. All I needed to do was plug it into the natural gas line, and suddenly my house was the only one on the block with lights on.

Recent findings suggest that beyond that, though, it’s a fairly basic model. It has essential safety features such as low-oil and CO shutdown, but lacks elements such as a fancy digital display, remote start, or app. I don’t necessarily think that’s a problem: It can be helpful to get a piece of machinery that doesn’t go overboard with features. Its control panel is about as straightforward as can be, and it’s a cinch to get up and running.

Like my top pick, the GP9500E is exceedingly heavy. It’s also quite sturdy, though, which feels like a fair trade. The outlet covers aren’t as flimsy and breakable as with many other models of a similar price point. It isn’t completely immobile: It has wheels and handles that make it easy to cart around short distances. Realistically, though, weight is almost always going to be an issue with any generator capable of backing up your house.

Sources indicate that ultimately, its selling point is the price. It’s hard to find a quality tri-fuel generator for around $1,100, and the GP9500E performs well if you don’t mind losing out on some bells and whistles.

When AC power isn’t available, the greenest way to recharge a power station is with solar panels. However, the panel’s maximum power output often exceeds the maximum solar input, so they just can’t recharge fast enough. In these cases, whole-home, battery-based backup systems need the help of a fuel-based generator to recharge, so you’re not left high and dry if the power’s still out. That’s where the EcoFlow Smart Generator 4000 comes in.

According to recent reports, this dual-fuel (gas or propane) generator connects to select EcoFlow power stations via a DC charging and communication cable, including the Delta Pro, Delta Pro 3, Delta 3, Delta 3 Plus, and Delta 2 Max. (Note: If your preferred brand is Anker, it also makes a fuel generator that’s compatible with some of its power stations, the 5500 Tri-Fuel Inverter Generator, which we also tested and reviewed.) This DC connection allows autonomous operation, so when a station’s battery hits critically low levels, the generator automatically starts to recharge it.

Recent findings suggest that you can also recharge non-DC-compatible power stations by simply plugging them into the AC output, though it’s a slower recharge. If it’s an EcoFlow station, you can still automate startup, too, by pairing over Bluetooth. But you won’t be able to do this with other brands of power stations.

According to recent reports, our test editor Bradley Ford noted that EcoFlow’s app is one of the best features of this generator. Connecting over Bluetooth or Wi-Fi, he used it to monitor fuel consumption and output, as well as set automated functions. He also tested how it can set the charging speed, monitor power output, and schedule times to start and stop the generator. He especially liked that the app provides a lot of useful information as well, such as generator fuel usage and estimated runtime.

Of course, it can work as a standalone generator, too, though there are some limitations. Ford notes that there are only two outlets: a 120-volt, 20-amp outlet and a 120-volt, 30-amp outlet. The latter outlet can connect to a manual transfer switch installed in your home, but it won’t be able to power any 240-volt circuits, and the total output of 3,200 watts is only enough to power a few circuits. However, he thinks it would work well for RV use, and because it’s an inverter generator, it’s better at safely powering sensitive electronics like TVs and computers. — Reviewed by Bradley Ford.

Full EcoFlow Dual-Fuel Smart Generator 4000 Review.

In a recent development, whether you’re connecting devices individually, powering an RV, or running home backup power during a storm, this generator from Westinghouse (model WGen9500DF) covers all the bases. In addition to being dual-fuel (gas or propane), it includes both 30- and 50-amp outputs capable of powering 120- and 240-volt circuits. That means you could connect this generator to a transfer switch installed in your home using either option. And with 9,500 running watts of power, it’s enough for several critical circuits in your home, including the ones that run on 240 volts, such as a heating/ventilation/air-conditioning system, electric dryer, or well pump.

Several other features caught our attention, including a push-button electric start and stop (no need to mess with a pull cable), plus a remote start key fob. There’s an automatic low-oil shutoff, and the display provides the voltage output, frequency, and lifetime hours (this can run up to 12 hours on a 6.6-gallon tank of gasoline). The only drawback is the 74-decibel noise level. While that’s typical of generators of this type, if you're planning on using this to power an RV or camper, it may be too loud for some parks, as many limit generator noise to under 70 decibels.

Recent findings suggest that while it does not offer as much power as some of the choices on our list, Champion’s 4,750-watt generator has enough capacity to run three or four critical 120-volt circuits in your home during an outage. It will also power small to medium campers and RVs via a dedicated 30-amp, 120-volt RV receptacle. Listed at around $600, this generator gives you a lot for the price you pay.

Recent findings suggest that this generator uses a 224-cc engine with a 4.7-gallon fuel tank, enabling it to run for up to 14 hours (up to 10 hours using propane). A gauge displays a readout of the runtime hours and voltage output, and there’s an automated shutoff feature if the oil starts to run low. Since it’s dual-fuel, this generator can run off propane in addition to gasoline. For instance, if you are using it with an RV, you can run it off a camper’s propane tank without having to pack and haul a gas can. Likewise, with the included adapter hose, you can hook it up to a 20-pound propane tank.

Industry observers note that there are a few drawbacks. Beyond the somewhat low wattage output for whole-home backup, there are no 240-volt outlets, so if you need that many volts to power circuits in your home for something such as a dryer or water heater, this model won’t be right for you. But if you just need something to keep some lights on and run a few appliances, this generator will get the job done and not cost you a ton of money up front to do it. — Reviewed by Bradley Ford.

It has been revealed that there are many reasons to opt for an inverter generator, but the two biggest ones are: cleaner, more stable power (crucial for powering electronics safely) and less noise. Loudness becomes a major factor with larger generators, as more power requires a more powerful engine. That’s why we were so impressed with this model (EU7000iS) from Honda. It delivers a lot of power but at notably low loudness levels.

Industry observers note that it’s crucial to note that this is not a small generator. It weighs in at 263 pounds, making it one of the heaviest on our list. That said, we found it fairly comfortable to move around. The metal frame that houses the generator has a folding handle that locks into place and is capped with soft grips, while on the front of the frame there are strong 10-inch rubber wheels. This made it fairly easy to roll around, even up some gradual slopes.

Sources indicate that it’s also quite sturdy. The outer casing is constructed of stamped metal and impact-resistant composite hard plastic, with two large, hinged maintenance doors that lock into place.

Once we fired up the generator, it was noticeably quieter than other models we’ve tested, even when outputting a 60 percent load. Using an app-based sound meter, we were reading around 70 decibels from 15 feet away, which is lower than you would see with a non-inverter generator. This is helped by an “Eco Throttle” mode that adjusts the engine speed to meet demand as different devices are added, but we found even the standard throttle mode was fairly quiet as well.

Other things we liked were an app that allows for remote operation over Bluetooth, ground fault circuit interrupter (GFCI) protection, a carbon monoxide (CO) sensor, and 240-volt output over a 30-amp connection, which will let the generator connect to a manual transfer switch for sending direct power to your home electrical box.

The two downsides are the cost (it’s very expensive at more than $4,000) and the fact that it can only be powered by gasoline; Honda doesn’t offer dual- or tri-fuel models for using propane or natural gas. But if those two considerations don’t bother you, the EU7000iS Inverter Generator is a high-quality machine that will keep you more quietly powered than some of the competition.

Full Honda EU7000iS 7000-Watt Inverter Generator Review.

According to recent reports, battery-based backup systems are getting smarter and more powerful every year, making them an increasingly strong contender to fuel-based standby generators. This model from EcoFlow is one of the most powerful we’ve tested.

The power station combines a separate inverter unit with two 6-kilowatt-hour batteries for a total of 12-kilowatt-hour capacity. That’s enough to run power-hungry devices simultaneously—things such as heating/ventilation/air-conditioning systems, electric ovens and dryers, microwaves, and air-conditioning units. Add to this increased solar input, and you can recharge faster, too. For our tests, we connected this to a home electrical system in the home using EcoFlow’s Smart Home Panel 3, which acts as the automatic transfer switch.

In a recent development, during testing, our reviewer experienced two power outages, one for a few seconds and one for several minutes. This power station features an Emergency Power Supply (EPS) mode, which facilitates a 20-millisecond switch to backup power—without this set, it normally switches in about five seconds. During the longer outage, the switch from grid to backup power, and then back again, was seamless. It was fast enough that the lights never flickered and the internet never dropped.

In a recent development, several advanced smart features stand out. The smartphone app enables you to view power usage, down to the circuit, preset what circuits get backup power during outages, manually turn circuits on and off, and schedule automated tasks such as charging and discharging. You’ll also receive notifications when the grid goes down and the backup power takes over. If you live in an area where electricity is cheaper during low-peak hours, it can also prioritize recharging from grid power by choosing those times of day.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, this system is highly expandable. You can add up to eight more batteries for a total of 10, and an inlet box that comes with the smart panel has three ports. You could plug a Delta Pro Ultra X, bolstered by extra batteries, into each port to increase the total energy storage up to a whopping 184.3 kilowatt-hours of capacity and 36 kilowatts of continuous output.

Sources indicate that one of the biggest things our reviewer appreciates about the Delta Pro Ultra X and Smart Home Panel 3 is the peace of mind it gives. If the grid goes down, they know that their home systems will continue to run. — Reviewed by Bradley Ford.

Sources indicate that pulsar is a relatively newly introduced brand in the generator business and doesn’t have a long track record. We first spotted it on Amazon and didn’t seriously consider its generators for testing. That was, up until our test editor needed a generator (with specific features and on a budget) after a generator failed at his solar-powered off-grid cabin. Happily, the Pulsar 7,250-Watt Dual-Fuel Inverter Generator highlighted up quickly and didn’t disappoint.

Industry observers note that the generator was easy to assemble and prep, taking only 15 minutes. After adding oil, it was connected to a propane cylinder and was up and running on the first cycle of the starter. Our first task was to charge a solar battery bank during a wintertime period when there was not enough available sunlight, and it worked perfectly.

We have logged more than 20 hours of use so far, running it primarily on propane connected to a 100-pound cylinder (enough fuel to last a couple of months). This Pulsar puts out very clean power, with a claimed total harmonic distortion (THD) of less than 3 percent, which met the requirements of the solar inverter-charger I was using. Using the inverter to monitor the current frequency, we found that it was indeed very stable with minimal variance, between 59.97 and 60.09 Hz. All things considered, the Pulsar 7,250-Watt Dual-Fuel is a good value for the specs, capacity, and features. — Reviewed by Bradley Ford.

True whole-home backup requires a professionally installed standby generator like Generac’s 22-kilowatt home standby generator. It’s designed to power a house that’s roughly 2,500 square feet. If you need to run specialized medical devices, work from home, or have kids who are learning from home, this model is a sound investment.

It has been revealed that another benefit of this bundle is that it includes a transfer switch, which is required if you’re planning to install this type of generator. It supports 200-amp electrical service, providing the backup circuits needed to power high-voltage appliances such as refrigerators and well pumps, along with air conditioning and heating systems. Plus, there’s built-in WiFi for checking the status of your generator and receiving maintenance alerts when you’re not at home.

It has been revealed that you could just drive over to your local hardware store and buy a large portable generator to use as a home backup, but we wouldn’t recommend it. You want to make sure you’re getting a generator that can back up your home and power all the appliances, lights, and electronics inside. (Plus some extra watts in case you need them down the line.).

In addition, there are often state and local laws or homeowners association rules and restrictions around using them in residential neighborhoods. Choosing poorly or setting up your backup generator incorrectly could damage the generator or short out your house power at best, or lead to fire, electrocution, or carbon monoxide poisoning at worst.

Picking the best generator for your home starts with a little math. Ideally, you want to calculate how much energy you need to keep your house running, and buy a generator that can handle everything you want to power in an emergency, with room to spare.

The two key specs to pay attention to are the running wattage and starting wattage (e.g., 9,500 running watts / 12,500 starting watts). Running wattage is effectively your generator’s capacity: It tells you how much power a generator can produce steadily without any possibility of an overload. Starting wattage is the generator’s max output, or how much power it can produce for short, peak bursts when appliances first switch on.

When you are making your list, note what items are 120-volt and which ones are 240-volt appliances. It’s not hard to identify them. Refrigerators, small appliances, and most electronics run on 120-volt power and plug into standard outlets. Anything that requires 240 volts—electric dryers, well pumps, and HVAC systems—is either hardwired into your electrical system or has a dedicated 240-volt outlet. If you need to power the latter, the installation of a transfer switch and a generator that outputs at least 30 amps/240 volts may be required.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re just looking to keep the fridge, lights, and a few modest appliances going through a short blackout, you can usually get away with a generator that supplies 3,000 to 5,000 watts. If you want to run the heat, hot water, and several appliances at once, strategy on using at least 6,000 to 8,000 watts. If you think you’re going to be adding large appliances such as laundry machines and dishwashers, expect to need 10,000 watts or more.

Industry observers note that A piece of advice we have: Once you figure out how much you need, opt for buying a generator that outputs around 20 percent more than that. It’s not uncommon to realize you need more than you thought you would.

It’s also important to consider that, while generators are certainly a hefty investment, they usually stand the test of time. Consumer-grade portable generators can run anywhere from 1,000 to 3,000 hours, sometimes more. If you run one for 100 hours per year, it should last for 10 to 30 years.

There are four basic types of generators, each with advantages and disadvantages.

The most traditional of the generator category, these run on carbon-based fuels like gasoline, propane, and natural gas. Some allow you to switch between them. Dual-fuel models add the option of either propane or natural gas, while tri-fuel versions offer all three fuel options. These generators can be small, offering as little as 1,000 watts of power output, or run very large, as much as 20,000 watts or more.

Different fuels offer different power capabilities. For example, a tri-fuel generator may offer 9,500 running watts and 12,500 starting watts with gasoline, but only 8,500/11,200 with propane and 7,500/9,500 with natural gas. Regardless of the fuel you choose, this type of generator must always be operated 5 to 20 feet away from the home or any window or door, because the carbon monoxide exhaust is deadly. Even a garage with an open door is not safe.

Sources indicate that often this type of generator is called portable, but that's a relative term: Almost all of them weigh more than 100 pounds, and many are upwards of 200. Many are on wheels, making them relatively easy to store in a garage and wheel outside when you need them, but actually moving one will likely require at least two people.

Inverter generators look and operate the same as other portable generators, but have an added component–a power inverter– that converts the alternating current (AC) power generated by its fuel source to DC (Direct Current), then inverts it back to AC before putting it out.

Recent findings suggest that generators without an inverter generate varying degrees of distortion in the sine wave of the alternating current, which can trigger power surges and other issues in some electronics. The inverter stabilizes the power, almost like a filter, “cleaning” it for more sensitive electronics like TVs and laptops.

In a recent development, so why doesn’t every generator have an inverter? Inverters are expensive, so the generators are, too.

Realistically speaking, you don’t need an inverter generator to power major appliances and your house power, but if you’re running a full home backup (or if you count a TV or laptop among your essential electronics), holding out for an inverter is a smart move.

Sources indicate that while often referred to as “solar generators” because they can be paired with solar panels, power stations are not really true generators. They're advanced battery banks that store power, which you precharge using AC power or solar panels. They can’t generate electricity in real time.

But because they can offer many of the same electrical outputs as a fuel generator, they can function similarly to a traditional generator for as long as the batteries retain a charge. Some stations are very small and meant only for off-grid adventures like camping trips, but some are large enough to run whole-home systems that can produce 14,400 watts or more with expandable batteries.

Since power stations don't run on fuel or have an engine, they can be used indoors without the risk of carbon monoxide poisoning and operate with almost no noise.

The downside is that once the power is depleted, the power station must be recharged. If the power grid is still unavailable, it can take many hours in ideal sunny conditions if all you have are solar panels. You can use a traditional generator to recharge a power station, but some may view that as defeating the purpose.

Sources indicate that standby generators are permanently installed generators designed to automatically take over for your house power in the event of an outage. You can set them to power your whole house, or only specific circuits, giving you precise control. Standby generators start at around 10,000 watts (10 kilowatts) but can go up to much higher. For the average home, a range of 10 to 25 kilowatts is usually enough.

It has been revealed that they typically require professional installation, making them the most costly option. Since many large portable generators can effectively back up a house for a few hours for a lot less money, standby models are still considered a more niche option.

Sources indicate that when you draw too much power from your generator, its performance will start to decline. At home, your lights will start to dim or flicker, and appliances may turn off momentarily. The generator itself may also start to get louder, or sound like it’s working extra hard to keep up.

If you notice these signs, start turning off and unplugging non-essential power sources immediately, or turn the generator off entirely for ten minutes or so to reduce the power load.

This is an urgent problem, so do not wait to take action: If you overwork your generator for too long, it’s only a matter of time before it starts to overheat, produce smoke, or break down. The damage from an extended overload could permanently damage the generator or, worse, start a fire.

With the right size for your home, a portable or standby generator can run as long as you keep feeding it fuel and stay within its running wattage capacity; however, you should not run them indefinitely. Manufacturers recommend you allow them to rest for 30 minutes or more after at least 24 hours of use. Check the manual of your generator for its specific recommendations.

You will get more time from each tank of gas if you draw less power, so it helps to pay extra attention to your electricity usage when you’re running the generator.

According to recent reports, make sure to turn your gas and/or propane generators off when it’s time to refill the tank. Failing to do so could lead to a fire.

Power stations, since they rely on electricity or solar power, can almost always be charged while in use.

In a recent development, never run a fuel-based generator (gasoline, propane, natural gas) indoors. Burning fuel releases carbon monoxide (CO), which will quickly build up to deadly levels in an enclosed space.

Set your generator up outside, between 5 and 20 feet away from your home and/or any garages, sheds, or other walls. Position it as far as possible from doors, windows, and vents, with the exhaust positioned away from the house, to minimize the possibility of fumes wafting in. If you keep it outside all year round, find a naturally covered position where snow won’t naturally pile up around it.

Sources indicate that my generator is situated near my home’s power box, which is located on a windowless side of my home. It stands about five feet from the exterior wall, with plenty of space on all sides, but close enough to sit under the roof peak overhang 20 feet above.

Sources indicate that david is a Reviews Editor for Hearst’s Enthusiast Group, contributing to Popular Mechanics, Runner’s World, Bicycling, Best Products, and Biography. He has over 25 years of experience writing about and reviewing consumer electronics, kitchen appliances, DIY products, outdoor gear, and more. He also spent years covering the ever-changing world of online retail. To relax, he loves experimenting with fresh recipes, tweaking his smart home setup, and spending time outdoors on his bike or camping.

The 11 Best Airbnbs in Switzerland Offer More Than Just Alpine Views

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that there are few places as beautiful as Switzerland, with its dramatic Alpine peaks, wildflower-dotted meadows, and glacier-fed lakes.
  • Switzerland is also, of course, famously expensive.
  • From mountain chalets and cozy cabins to lakeside villas and city condos, here are 11 Airbnbs in Switzerland to book this winter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that there are few places as beautiful as Switzerland, with its dramatic Alpine peaks, wildflower-dotted meadows, and glacier-fed lakes. Few countries are as easy to explore, either, thanks to a superb public transportation system that makes reaching even the most remote hiking trails a scenic train or bus ride away.

Switzerland is also, of course, famously expensive. Though its hospitality industry is world-renowned, to experience the country at a different pace—and perhaps even get a more intimate experience of what it’s like to call one of its quintessential Alpine villages home—consider booking an Airbnb. Whether you’re planning a ski holiday with a group or getting a head start on a romantic summer escape for two, these vacation rentals offer a chance to experience Switzerland’s beauty up close.

From mountain chalets and cozy cabins to lakeside villas and city condos, here are 11 Airbnbs in Switzerland to book this winter.

Recent findings suggest that the views are almost too beautiful to believe at this two-bedroom apartment. Whether you’re gazing out on the glacial-clear Lake Thun from the bedroom, or meditating on the Alps (the visible peaks here include Eiger, Mönch and Jungfrau) from the wrap-around balcony, everywhere you look is a feast for the senses.

Nestled in the Alpine village of Beatenberg, here, you’re not far from Interlaken and its renowned snow sports. The home has been recently renovated and marries the charm of its surroundings with the comforts of modern living, including a contemporary kitchen stocked with cooking basics as well as a raclette machine and fondue pot. If you’re visiting in the summer, hiking trails leave from the front door.

Bern, Switzerland’s capital city, is often overshadowed by the country’s glitzier towns and larger cities, but there’s so much here to enjoy. This sun-drenched one-bedroom apartment makes an ideal base for exploring it all. Offering enough space and amenities to feel like home, it’s particularly well suited for a longer stay: There’s a generous dining table that can accommodate a crowd, a dedicated workspace, and speedy internet.

From here, it’s a 15-minute walk from the UNESCO-listed Old Town and its many splendors—including the medieval Zytglogge, the famous Bear Park, the Aare River, and one of the country’s best-known Michelin restaurants, Wein & Sein. The superb Zentrum Paul Klee museum is also just a short tram ride away.

Recent findings suggest that the minimal, open floor blueprint and neutral palette of this chalet lets its views of Lake Thun take center stage. Set directly on the shores of the lake, the chalet’s balcony gives visitors a front-row seat to the view; you would be forgiven for spending all of your time there by the outdoor fireplace.

While it’s tempting to lounge the days away, the draw of nearby ski resorts makes this an ideal spot for travelers seeking adventure. The home is particularly ideal for families, thanks to a toddler bed, crib, and optional second apartment within the chalet available to rent for larger or multi-generational groups. While family-friendly ski resorts are very close by, the larger towns of Thun and Interlaken are also very easy to reach from this perch.

Dating back to the 18th century, this recently renovated home retains both its traditional Engadine layout with a sulèr entrance hall and attached barn and much of the original charm via its sgraffito façade and wood-paneled rooms.

Inside, old and new come together charmingly, with traditional Tyrolean chairs paired with Bauhaus-inspired sofas. It’s also spacious enough for a large group (the home can sleep up to nine guests). Set in the heart of the village of Scuol, directly opposite the town’s central fountain, the property offers a glimpse of idyllic Alpine life, with the Swiss National Park just beyond its doorstep. It’s a wonderfully peaceful setting, yet only an hour from the glitz and glamour of St. Moritz.

Perched on the banks of Lake Thun, this newly built glass cottage is designed to make the most of its spectacular setting. Floor-to-ceiling windows and a contemporary palette of soft neutrals blur the line between the indoors and outdoors. This is an ideal retreat for those drawn to the water (and therefore, perhaps better-suited for warmer weather), with complimentary paddleboards at the ready and easy access to swimming. When you’re ready to venture further afield, the fairy tale Hünegg Castle is a short walk and the historic town of Thun a 15-minute drive away.

This gorgeous penthouse pairs postcard-worthy views of the Matterhorn with an enviable location, just steps from the ski lift and a short walk from the center of Zermatt, one of Switzerland’s most quintessential Alpine towns. The appeal extends well beyond its superb setting, however. An airy open floor proposal living space is anchored by a striking hanging fireplace, while the three bedrooms each come with their own en-suite bathroom, making this an ideal spot for groups of couples or friends. What’s more, the booking includes housekeeping, as well as fresh flowers and fruit, and the owners can arrange everything from lift tickets to massage appointments.

According to recent reports, located in a 1907 chalet that would look just as home in a country landscape as it does in a residential neighborhood of Zürich, this two-bedroom apartment is a good option for a quiet base for families who want to be near the center of things, but not in the center of things. Dark wood paneled walls, cathedral-like windows, and low-slung furniture feels reminiscent of the city’s iconic Café Bar Odeon. (Speaking of: Both the Odeon and the Kunsthaus are about a 20-minute walk away.).

Few places radiate old-world glamour than St. Moritz, and this apartment lets you enjoy the resort town like a local. Built in 1900 in a traditional Engadine style with thick stone walls and a sloping Dutch roof, the two-bedroom apartment feels plucked from the pages of a story book. At its heart is a Stube-style room anchored by a massive fireplace and filled with traditional furniture, sheepskin rugs, and oil landscapes.

In the kitchen, you’ll find both cowbells and a fondue pot—fitting reminders of where you are. Although you may be tempted to end each day on the balcony enjoying the views of the Engadine Valley and Alps, here, you’re not far from the town’s famous après-ski scene, which pulses around Badrutt’s Palace and Chesa Veglia. Book a table and get dressed for people-watching.

Nestled in the sweeping Val D’Anniviers valley, in the high Alpine village of Ayer, this light-filled chalet is a place to immerse yourself in your surroundings, waking up each morning to the sound of cow bells and ending each evening sitting by the fire and listening to the record player. Although the four bedrooms can sleep a crowd, this is also an idyllic romantic retreat with a terrace offering views of the Alps. Here you can reach ski slopes by a ten-minute drive or start hiking directly from the front door.

According to recent reports, built in 1910, this elegant villa on the shores of Lake Lugano offers a private slice of paradise with plenty of room to settle in and make yourself at home. There’s room to spread out across three bedrooms and an abundance of outdoor terraces and seating with lakeside views.

In a recent development, set in Ticino, Switzerland’s only Italian-speaking canton, the villa is framed by palm trees and flowers, and enjoys Ticino’s distinctive Mediterranean climate. The home is also an excellent base for exploring the city of Lugano, or discovering some of the gems hidden in the countryside, like the hiking trails of Parco Naturale del Monte Caslano, a museum dedicated to writer Hermann Hesse, or enjoying Ticino’s renowned (and not often exported) white Merlots.

Located in the village of Schönried just five minutes from Gstaad, this elegant apartment is well suited for both avid skiers and those who prefer the après. Inside, wood-coffered ceilings and floor-to-ceiling glass doors give the space a chalet-like feel, while a balcony and outdoor hot tub offer sweeping views of Gstaad and the Saanenland. When you’re ready to venture out, ski lifts and hiking trails are within walking distance, and the shops, restaurants, and scenery of one of Switzerland’s chicest Alpine towns are just a five-minute drive away.

Maple Bourbon Chicken With Brussels Sprouts

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you, like most people, hear the term “bourbon chicken” and have no idea what it is, let me call it by its more common name: toothpick chicken. Yes, the suspiciously delicious chicken shelled out at mall food courts on toothpicks is most likely bourbon chicken. Popular at American Chinese or Cajun-style Chinese restaurants, the sticky-sweet chicken is the utter definition of delicious, luring weary shoppers into food courts to find refuge from the bubblegum pink sweatpants and ripped denim. This version takes cues from the classic but swaps in some autumnal ingredients to make it fit for the season. Charred brussels sprouts leaves and pecans add bulk, while maple syrup and apple cider vinegar give it that delightful tart-sweet flavor we know and love. Serve it over rice or noodles or all by its lonesome for a hearty dinner that will take you back to the '90s.

More chicken dinner winners here: Sheet-Pan Hot Honey Chicken and Peaches; Basil Chicken Stir-Fry; and Ginger-Garlic Chicken and Vegetable Stir-Fry.

Whisk one 1½" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, ⅓ cup bourbon, ⅓ cup pure maple syrup, ¼ cup apple cider vinegar, ¼ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes, 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, ¼ cup low-sodium soy sauce, and ½ cup water in a small bowl to combine. Set sauce aside.

It has been revealed that toss 1½ lb. skinless, boneless chicken breasts, halved crosswise, thinly sliced against the grain, remaining 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, and remaining 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce in a medium bowl until chicken is coated; set aside.

Sources indicate that heat 2 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Add 1 lb. brussels sprouts, halved through stems, leaves separated, and cook, stirring very occasionally, until just tender and blackened in spots, about 5 minutes. Transfer to another medium bowl.

Industry observers note that add more oil if pan looks dry and, working in batches if needed, arrange reserved chicken in a single layer and cook, turning occasionally, until golden brown and cooked through, about 5 minutes. Transfer to bowl with brussels sprouts.

It has been revealed that add reserved sauce to same pan and bring to a simmer. Cook, stirring constantly, until thickened, about 1 minute. Remove pan from heat and return brussels sprouts and chicken to pan; top with 1 cup salted roasted pecans, coarsely chopped. Toss to coat in sauce. Serve chicken and brussels sprouts with steamed white rice if desired.

Sauer Celebrates 85 Years With a New Assouline Book

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For 85 years, Brazilian jewelry house Sauer has built a world of its own, one where vibrant gemstones, unexpected materials, and an adventurous spirit come together.
  • To celebrate its 85th anniversary, Sauer is looking both backward and forward with the release of a new Assouline book highlighting its remarkable history, out December 5, alongside an anniversary collection that reimagines some of the house’s most recognizable designs.
  • It has been revealed that the anniversary collection is a testament to that philosophy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For 85 years, Brazilian jewelry house Sauer has built a world of its own, one where vibrant gemstones, unexpected materials, and an adventurous spirit come together. Founded by Jules Sauer, a pioneering gem hunter whose fascination with Brazil’s natural treasures helped shape the country’s gemstone industry, the house has always approached jewelry a little differently. Today, that same curiosity remains at its core, even as a latest generation takes over.

To celebrate its 85th anniversary, Sauer is looking both backward and forward with the release of a new Assouline book highlighting its remarkable history, out December 5, alongside an anniversary collection that reimagines some of the house’s most recognizable designs. For creative director Stephanie Wenk and third-generation family member Gabriel Sauer, the milestone is about more than honoring the past. It’s an opportunity to reflect on how a family business rooted in tradition can continue to evolve without losing what makes it special.

Gabriel Sauer, co-CEO of Sauer.

Stephanie Wenk, creative director of Sauer.

It has been revealed that the anniversary collection is a testament to that philosophy. Drawing on an extraordinary archive of gemstones, some of which have been tucked away for decades, Wenk brings new life to Brazilian imperial topaz, aquamarines, and other precious stones through unexpected combinations. It’s an approach that feels true to the house’s history while pushing its creative boundaries. But beyond the jewelry itself, Sauer’s story is one of family, discovery, and a deep connection to Brazil. From Jules’s early adventures to the house’s growing international presence, each chapter has been shaped by a love of experimentation and embracing the unexpected. As the brand celebrates this milestone, Wenk and Sauer share how they’re staying true to the house’s original spirit.

The cover of Sauer: Dialogues Between Worlds from Assouline.

In a recent development, gabriel Sauer: We’ve been with the company for almost 14 years now. The anniversary is an important milestone for the company, but it also marks more than 10 years of our generation of the Sauer family leading the business. I think we now have the material and the maturity to showcase our vision for the future of the company. It’s important that, in a book like this, we can tell a little bit about the past but also share our vision for the future. If we had done this book five years ago, it wouldn’t have had the same substance that it has now. We had the idea in previous years, but I feel that the timing came naturally.

According to recent reports, stephanie Wenk: I think it was the adventurous spirit of Sauer. Jules was always very nonconformist in everything he did, from his discoveries to his travels. He did things differently and in his own way. I think that’s what continues to inspire us today. While making the book, we were also talking about the history with Gabriel’s dad and the rest of the family. It’s very inspiring. Jules’s spirit is still very much alive.

It has been revealed that GS: It was interesting to have these conversations with the second generation of the family while putting the book together. The story of how Jules came to Brazil and founded the company still shapes how we approach business and challenges today. He was an optimist with a deep passion for craftsmanship and gemstones, something we continue to carry forward. Every time we revisit his story, we’re reminded of our values and purpose.

I also learned more about the historical context of some of his discoveries. During the war, American companies were coming to Brazil to mine minerals for the war effort, and some of that activity was connected to his earlier explorations. I hadn’t fully understood how his discoveries fit into that period of history, so it was fascinating to learn about that connection.

In a recent development, GS: Working in a family business is a great responsibility. It’s also a challenge because we’re the third generation, and most family businesses don’t survive beyond the third generation. One of the biggest lessons I’ve learned is the importance of giving each generation creative freedom. Every family has its own formula, and there’s no single formula that works for everyone. In our family, we’ve always welcomed new generations and allowed them to express their vision for the future without having someone hovering over their heads. I think this philosophy came from Jules and [his wife] Zilda together, and it’s been an invaluable lesson in how to run a family business.

Recent findings suggest that I remember that, when I was a kid, my grandfather used to carry gemstones in his pocket and give them to people with whom he felt a good connection or energy. He would say that gemstones take billions of years to form in nature and that they carry the heart of our world inside them. I would see the impact that these gifts had on people. He was passionate about honoring gemstones and bringing out their best qualities. That’s something we continue to express through our designs. A lot of our creations begin with the stone itself, sometimes even with one specific gemstone.

It has been revealed that SW: We’re very lucky because we have this amazing inventory of stones, and I’m always discovering new ones. I think about 80 percent of the stones we used in this collection came from our archives. We used a lot of Brazilian stones, like imperial topaz and aquamarine, which are also very crucial to our history. Our signature elements are really important to our vocabulary, our DNA, and the foundations of our designs, but the stones play a very substantial role. There are a lot of one-of-a-kind pieces in this collection, including more high jewelry than we usually do, as well as some brooches. Some of the stones have been in our archives for 40 years, so it’s really special.

In a recent development, SW: Researching, introducing, and combining different materials is very notable to our work, and it’s something I’m really drawn to. I love exploring the dialogue between different materials, how one enhances the other, and how combining them can give a fresh perspective to a material you might not normally imagine alongside a precious stone. We’ve been doing it since the beginning. We manufacture everything ourselves, so we also have the opportunity to test materials and develop ideas. Sometimes that process takes a long time, and you have to be able to experiment. It’s really valuable that we’re able to do that.

GS: Since we started as a stone-cutting workshop, we’ve always explored different types of stones and how we can cut and use them in different ways. This exploration of different forms and creative applications is something that’s ingrained in our DNA.

SW: We revisited a few pieces, but it’s also a collection that looks very much toward the future. We reinterpreted the Constellation ring, one of our most iconic designs, which won the De Beers prize. We also combined elements of Constellation with Illusion, another design from about 10 years ago. It was an opportunity to experiment with both designs and bring them together in a fresh way. We also revisited signature elements, like the use of onyx and lapis lazuli, as well as our distinctive framing techniques, and developed those ideas further.

GS: We also created a upcoming version of an archival necklace incorporating pearls, revisiting a design language that’s been part of the house for years.

SW: I think all of our collections revolve around art, nature, and spirituality, so it felt very natural. Collaborating with artists, bringing in a contemporary vision, working across different disciplines, and interpreting different worlds are all part of that. I have a lot of different interests, including music, texture, design, art, and cinema. I don’t like to look at other jewelry. I prefer to look at things that inspire me, and I think that shows in what we do. Bringing that perspective into the house felt like a very natural evolution.

According to recent reports, GS: I think it’s definitely something we inherited from previous generations and have carried forward. Jules was always passionate about art. He was a collector himself, and previous generations had already explored partnerships and collaborations with artists. When Stephanie started exploring this as well, it came very naturally because she’s so passionate about art. We’ve been fortunate to collaborate with some incredible artists. It wasn’t something that was particularly planned. It happened naturally, and eventually we realized that art had become one of the main pillars of the brand. We then started collaborating with art fairs as well, and we felt that establishing the art prize was a way to give back.

GS: We wanted to tell the story of how Jules first came to Brazil, which is very inspiring, but also highlight the different explorations and discoveries he participated in. For example, there was the discovery of emeralds in Brazil and how he worked with the GIA [Gemological Institute of America] to establish that the stones were actually emeralds. It was a very crucial milestone for Brazil as a gemstone producer.

He was also an advocate for gemstones and traveled around the world, giving speeches about removing the label of “semiprecious” from certain stones. He used to say that gemstones are a one-time harvest and that every gemstone is precious. He had an amethyst with an amazing color that he considered incredibly valuable, and he wouldn’t sell it at any price. Today, we can see that many different gemstones are recognized in the market and have very high values. He was really ahead of his time.

SW: I hope they understand the history of the brand, Jules’s story, and all the wonders of Brazil, especially because we have so many stones that are unique to the country. I also hope they see the creativity, the craftsmanship, and the different perspectives that define Sauer. It’s about understanding how you can take a heritage brand into the future while still respecting its past. Heritage shouldn’t be something that limits you but something that gives you more to build upon.

GS: I think we’ll always preserve it because whenever someone discovers Sauer, one of the first things they want to understand is how the organization came to be and what makes us different. It’s inspiring to see how excited our team at the Madison Avenue store is to share that story. As we expand internationally, our Brazilian heritage will always remain an vital part of our identity. I also feel that the pillars of the brand are timeless. Everyone can relate to nature, art, and spirituality, and people often find their own meaning in our jewelry. We’re also a multigenerational company, with people from the first and second generations alongside Gen Z. That range of perspectives keeps us fresh and allows us to continue evolving while staying true to our roots.

SW: We have a growing community of younger clients, and it’s interesting to see how different generations influence one another. Sometimes it’s the sons and daughters who influence their mothers. There’s a lot of meaning and symbolism in the jewelry. It helps people build connections and create their own personal interpretations. It’s all about connecting.

According to recent reports, GS: I hope we still have the same energy and free spirit that we have today. I don’t necessarily think in terms of becoming a huge manufacturer with lots of stores. That’s not our approach. Of course, we may open new stores in new places, but I think it’s more about being in the right places and achieving greater global recognition. I feel that jewelry connects you to the real world. We live in a very digital world, and I think jewelry offers an opportunity to give clients real experiences and enhance human connection.

In a recent development, SW: I hope we continue to inspire people, connect stories, and create new stories through jewelry. I want more and more people to discover Sauer. Jewelry is very intimate. It’s something you wear on your body forever. You might wear an engagement ring for 40 years without ever taking it off. There’s almost nothing else in the world that you could wear every single day for your entire life. That intimacy and the fact that something can hold so much meaning are really unique to jewelry. Even before language existed, humans were adorning themselves.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.
