  • Recent findings suggest that the first: Do uncomfortable things.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Welcome to Routine Excellence, a GQ column where high-achievers share the key rituals that help them perform at their best.

According to recent reports, during the three years that Reid Wiseman prepped for April’s Artemis II mission—for which he led a crew of three other astronauts nearly 700,000 miles, around the far side of the moon—he memorized everything from lunar geography to the Orion capsule’s elaborate controls. But, understandably, part of his training focused on not dying. Much of the mission “had no playbook at all,” notes the recently retired astronaut. Still, he did have a few mantras to guide him. Here are two.

Recent findings suggest that the first: Do uncomfortable things. “If I don’t fly in a jet for a few weeks, or if I’m not diving in the neutral-buoyancy lab, underwater, in a space suit, my world starts to shrink down,” notes Wiseman. Meaning he gets better at managing stress by…seeking out stress. “The best thing is continually pushing yourself in an operational environment to do scary things,” he explains. “You can even find it in a difficult conversation with a coworker—anything that gets that anxiety going.”.

It has been revealed that but embracing challenges doesn’t always guarantee success. After Wiseman and his team failed to survive a couple of flight simulators, they adopted an old aviation saying: No fast hands. “If you have something horribly wrong with your aircraft, you want to do stuff quick,” Wiseman says. But to counter any rash decisions, you should first “just watch the second hand on the clock moving around.” The point is to pause before making a high-stakes judgment call. “If we can take 30 seconds before we’re dead, let’s take 30 seconds,” he says. “Let’s methodically go through where we think we are and where we’re headed.”.

Wiseman put the mantra to use during the mission when the Orion sprang a propellant leak. “Very serious when you’re 100,000 miles away,” he says. He recalls how a crewmember began executing an emergency response, only for Wiseman to hit pause. Surveying the instruments, they realized the leak was minor and not worthy of a red alert reaction. “That was a good example of ‘Let’s be patient here for a minute.’ ” Take a beat and you’re more likely to think clearly—and come out alive.

We chatted with Wiseman—who will begin a new deputy role at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory on Nov. 30—about his method for memorizing the Orion’s intricate control panels, the Artemis II crew’s pre-launch heart-to-hearts, and how writing poetry about the moon helped him do his job that much better.

Reid Wiseman: Actually, I mean, we’re still subject to the laws of gravity. We’re not feeling the effects of gravity.

First and foremost is just, I don’t want to use the CrossFit model of “Be comfortable being uncomfortable,” but you do have to do things that are uncomfortable, and you have to continually do that. I have noticed if I don’t fly in a jet for a few weeks, or if I’m not diving in the neutral buoyancy lab, underwater, in a space suit, that my world starts to shrink down. This is probably a side tangent, but my younger daughter suffered from anxiety pretty bad, and I remember the therapist saying: “You got to keep her moving. She’s got to get outside, she’s got to ride a bike, she’s got to go on a walk.” And I was watching her world shrink down, and I think it’s a corollary to what we do as astronauts. We’re flying planes, a lot of us are skydivers—I am not—and you just stay uncomfortable, stay in confined environments, and then stay really engaged in team skills, keep your mind going. The best thing is continually pushing yourself in an operational environment to do scary things.

Yeah, for instance, I was just over in Switzerland. I do not like heights, I really do not like heights. And my girlfriend was pushing me to go on this rock climbing thing up the side of the Alps called Via Ferrata. You’re clipped into metal. You’re safe, but if you fall, you’re going to hurt yourself at least a little bit. And the whole time I was thinking: I do not want to do this, I have to do this. I went and did it. It was exhilarating, absolutely exhilarating. I was proud of myself at the end of it.

Recent findings suggest that I do still look for those challenges. I definitely look for, if I haven’t done something before, that is usually motivation to try it, to lean into those sorts of things. You can even find it in just a difficult conversation with a coworker or with another human, anything that gets that anxiety going, gets the adrenaline up, something that you don’t want to do, but then you confront it and do it, there is a reward trigger at the end of that that is powerful.

I’m a huge conflict avoider, so it’s a struggle for me to meet those head on.

Sources indicate that into courage of confronting people. I don’t know. People in my office, there’s some people that thrive on it, and they do it great, doesn’t even bother them. And then, I don’t like confronting people, I figure everybody’s trying their best and if they’re getting on my nerves, it’s probably something wrong with me.

Sources indicate that about five years ago, I just started reading books around the topics that I’m dealing with at work, and now that is my thing. I’m probably a book a week, usually audiobook, as I’m driving to and from work, but it’s on the stuff like small-team dynamics, it’s on learning environments, a lot of Carol Dweck stuff, on learning organizations, learning environments, and it’s been shocking to me how much that ties into confidence at work.

Somebody, somewhere will say, “Hey, you should read a book about this.” I’ll take a recommendation from a friend. [NASA’s] Anne McClain is a fellow astronaut, and she’s really cerebral, so she’s had a few good ones. [Retired Canadian Astronaut Corps astronaut] Jeremy Hansen, who I flew in space with, [NASA astronaut] Victor Glover’s had a few good ones. [NASA astronaut] Christina Koch has given me a few. So we all kind of trade book recommendations. And then as a crew, there were a few books that we all read as a crew, and it gave us a common language, a way to talk about things together, which was pretty powerful.

Christina had us read [retired NASA astronaut] Eileen Collins’s book, which is a very basic simple book, but it’s Through the Glass Ceiling Into the Stars, about her journey and some of the struggles that she had, and it really gave us a common language there. Then I recommended Growth Mindset by Carol Dweck. I quoted that book so many times, I think my crew all pretty much read it.

In a recent development, it was more in training. When we got onto the mission, we were glued together. We worked with operational psychologists before the mission, we’ve talked about a lot of this stuff and how powerful it was. We worked with a poet, we’ve worked with spiritual researchers, and cultural researchers about the moon. All that stuff just built a shared knowledge, shared understanding. But back to your original question, what do I do? I really do like to read books, I really do get a lot out of them, or at least listen to books.

In a recent development, it’s almost like meditation, but it’s not. But it would really soothe me. And I think in some ways, probably listening to a book or reading a book, it is an ultimate distraction from the thousands of things going on in my mind at all times. I think most astronauts are probably ADHD to some degree, but it’s a way to just put all that stuff aside and let my brain relax in a different direction for a little while.

It has been revealed that we had a lot of parts that had no playbook at all on this mission. I think the first answer to your question is, you have to work at it, and memorization tools. For lunar geography features, I made note cards. I have to make the study tools. If somebody hands me study tools, it doesn’t work. I need that function from eyes to brain, to hand, back to eyes to brain. That’s very important for me.

For controls and displays for the Orion spacecraft, I would sit there on Saturdays, on my couch, with a blank sheet of paper, and in my head I would envision every display, and I would start writing every note of every column of every element of data on the display, and then I would check the manual and say, “All right, I’m wrong here, or I missed this….” And over time, that is just setting in stone in my brain where that is.

Industry observers note that for emergency procedures, we developed a lot of different techniques as a crew, but two things that are germane to this. First, Victor Glover came up with the mantra of, What is the first right step? So, you’ve got a fire on the spacecraft, there’s a lot of things that matter right now, but what’s the first right step that we all need to act on right now to start combating this fire? It is pretty cool in your brain, if you just really solidify the first right step, all the other steps will come. I was just at a Brandi Carlile concert, and she was saying when she sits down at the piano, if she thinks about what she’s about to play, she can’t do it. But if she sits down and just watches her hands, they will start playing the song. I find that with emergency procedures, if you know the first step to take, usually you can follow on with the rest of the right steps.

Then we also had a really strong mantra that was forged in a couple simulators that did not go well, where we did not survive the simulator, and that is: No fast hands. That’s an aviation motto, where if you have something horribly wrong with your aircraft, you want to do stuff quick, and they train you, the first thing you should do is just watch the secondhand on the clock moving around, or just go slow.

In a recent development, and so, we had a suspense, what is the criticality of our next action? If we can take 30 seconds before we’re dead, let’s take 30 seconds. Some actions require a split second, they require less than a second. So, those are the ones that we really need to hone in the simulator. But even in space, we had a few malfunctions, and we very deliberately executed, no fast hands. Let’s think about what the spacecraft is telling us. Let’s methodically go through where we think we are and where we’re headed. And only when we absolutely must make a decision, let’s make that decision.

Industry observers note that the fire alarm, that was a great example of the first right step. When the fire alarm went off, we heard the emergency tone, and immediately Victor and I went to the displays. That is what we were trained to do. And I stated, “We have a fire alarm,” and immediately Jeremy and Christina started looking for smoke, or smelling around the far side of the spacecraft to see if they could determine any location for fire, because we didn’t see any. We didn’t smell any. And that was incredible to watch us all act on the first right step principle.

It has been revealed that on the no fast hands, it was the middle of the night, and a warning came up. It’s called a runbox failure. That doesn’t matter, but it basically means propellant is being used, but it’s being used outside the parameters of where it should be. So we have a leak somewhere. Either in propellant or pressurization.

Industry observers note that very serious when you’re 100,000 miles away. Jeremy started executing the memorized response because it’s a very critical thing. I said, “Let’s just stop for a second. Let’s see what the vehicle is telling us.”.

And Jeremy stopped, and we looked at all of our instrumentation. Pressures were stable, fuel was stable. So, if we did have a leak, it was a very small leak. Turns out we did have a leak, and it was a very small leak. That was a good example of “Let’s be patient here for a minute.” We know what we need to do, but let’s hang on and not do it quite yet.

Those times of lost communication do not bother us. We do train for those, those don’t bother us. I do want to talk for just a second about risk. Look, that mission was risky. We were pretty sure we were going to make it, but it was risky. So, before that, before we introduced, we did talk as a crew very openly. We talked to our families very openly about risk—what happens if I don’t come back. I’ve been very public about that. I had a will, I told my kids what the life insurance intends were, where are you going to go if I don’t come back? Who’s going to take care of you? To me, those are conversations that are very powerful. And I think if you get to the launchpad with all of that stuff organized in your brain, you’re very at peace. And all four of us a few days before launch, we all shared the common feeling of peace.

According to recent reports, it was very weird. It was not nerves, tension, anxiety. It was peace. Two days before we rolled out, Jeremy Hansen, at dinner, asked all of us, the crew together, “Hey, let’s talk for a second about how are we going to handle it if we know we’re going to die, but we’ve got a couple days before it’s going to happen.” Almost Apollo 13. We have a failure. We know we’re not going to survive, and we have several days. And it was a pretty quick conversation. We were like, “Let’s just do it with dignity and give each other as much grace as we can because we don’t know how we’re going to react, but dignity. Let’s come back to just doing it with dignity.” Who ever has a conversation like that?

And the four of us had that conversation, and very quickly, we all aligned behind dignity, that is how we’re going to approach this, but we’re also going to have grace because we’re not in that situation right now. We do not know how people are going to handle it. I mean, I could have a total terror attack, a panic attack, you don’t know. But the fact that we were in a place where we could talk about that stuff was very powerful, probably because we’re all around 50, we felt very accomplished in our lives, and very satisfied with where we were. We launched overwhelmingly at peace.

Not quite that aggressive, but exhausting, yes.

It has been revealed that it’s a number of things. First, the four of us were all very committed to excellence and to being there for each other. Even if we didn’t always show it, we always committed to it. We talked a lot about wanting to launch as friends and land as friends. That’s a bit of lip service, but it was a motto that we tried to uphold. We’re just never going to give up on each other. We’re going to work on this for the rest of our lives. And then, in training, we often joke that we were like the basketball Olympic dream team, where you took all the best players from basketball, put them together, and they were a terrible team.

For quite a while, we were just not a great team, but we were working on it. I bore a lot of responsibility of that as a commander. Like, why can’t I get these people in line? But also with this crew of experienced and senior astronauts, I couldn’t just say, “You’re getting in line.” It just wasn’t going to work. And I didn’t want that, I wanted us all to be ourselves. Each one of us brings an individual richness into this tapestry of this crew, and I wanted that to show through.

Recent findings suggest that I was willing to deal with some pain and agony over crew dynamics if it meant everyone showing up at the end together. I think that did pay off very well. So, we noticed pretty early on that we had these crew dynamics issues, and we set up a couple extra meetings with our...at NASA, we have these people called BHP, behavioral health and performance folks. They’re all psychologists, operational psychologists.

Recent findings suggest that we set up some meetings with them. They had all these guided points. The first question they asked us, I don’t think they ever asked us another question, we tore ourselves apart. I think every member of the crew cried at some point. We exhausted ourselves, and they were like, Wow, you guys really have some concerns we need to work through. So, we did more meetings with them, and we did work through a lot of that stuff. We didn’t work through all of it. But what that process demonstrated with those behavioral health folks is our willingness, our commitment to each other. I didn’t need us to launch perfect, I just needed us to be committed to each other.

Then, I will throw in this one thing a few months before launch, because I also think this was crucial: We spent a lot of time giving each other feedback. But before launch, I wanted to make sure we also shifted to meeting each other where we are. I mean, you can tell me how to change for the next 10 years. At some point though, I have a personality that is just who I am. I’m going to work every day to be better, but at some point, I think you need to meet me where I am, and I need to meet you where you are. And we did that, and that was very powerful as well. By the time we came off the launchpad in that vehicle, we were really, really, really together. We didn’t have to be. I know there’s been a lot of crews that haven’t been, but we were.

Recent findings suggest that that’s very well remarked. Because our crew conversations were harder than any technical matter that we had to solve in this training at least.

Yes, but I won’t read it, although some of them were actually very good. We talked to a professor of English, Chris Cokinos, at the University of Arizona. But he held quite a few workshops with us, and he gave us drills. I wrote him an email a couple days ago just thanking him for allowing us to express creativity in the ways that we saw the world and the moon. And his stuff was all focused on the moon. How do you relay the moon in the five senses? And how do you do it in a way that captures imagination?

In the end, we’re all kind of philosophers, and it just helped us be a little bit more creative in the way we saw things, and it reinforced to us that you can find beauty if you’re looking for it. I love the way Chris Cokinos framed for us the beauty of the moon. Because an engineer or a geologist could have framed it as a barren, stark, celestial body, but Chris framed it as a magnificent, beautiful, celestial neighbor. And just having that sense and that feeling really highlighted through when we were out there.

I kept a journal on my computer on the mission, just putting, remember, every day, just think about sight, smell, touch, taste, feel, and go through those every day in this vehicle. Sadly, the computers were so hard to use in space, I did not journal on that even a singular time. But basically every day we would do a five senses kind of thing, and you could be in the middle of a simulator, and I would pull out my notebook and just jot. All right, I just did this docking maneuver. And that docking maneuver, that’s the most technical thing you can do. What was the sight, smell, sound? And wow, all of a sudden you start pulling out tons of data that you otherwise would’ve neglected.

It is starting to abate a little bit. But we were doing an outdoor podcast, getting interviewed in this beautiful setting in California, and a little breeze came from left to right across my face, and I was like, “Man, that feels incredible.” And I never would’ve noticed that even. I was walking around New York City, and I saw some tulips coming up out of the ground, and I was stopped dead in my tracks for a few seconds just looking at them, thinking about how impossible it is that, in this brown dirt, these beautiful green sprouts are coming up, and it’s like the birth of spring, and summer’s here. It was like, why am I focusing on all this? But I was focusing on all of that.

It has been revealed that I say this all the time when we’re out talking to the general public, but in Apollo, those guys talked about peace and joy and hope, and then we went out there and we talked about peace and joy and hope. I just think if you’re a quarter million miles away looking back at this impossibly unique planet, it’s the only words that we have in the English language that can convey even a small portion of what that felt like.

We saw sights on the far side of the moon, and especially when the sun eclipsed behind the moon that I can’t even describe the beauty, especially of that eclipse. It was otherworldly. And when I look at the moon now, I still think about that. I know when the right side of the moon is lit up at night, but not the left side of the moon, I almost don’t even look at it because we didn’t see that. But when the left side of the moon is lit up, that is very relatable to me, and I know what’s on that other side now.

Sources indicate that we only saw 18% of the far side on the left side, but I know what that looks like back there, and I think about it all the time. The moon became more of a friend when we were around it, I just felt comradeship with the moon. It was revealing its secrets to us. We were seeing parts of it that it doesn’t reveal to people on Earth, but we were seeing them, and it was very powerful.

It has been revealed that yeah. I think about all my family, all my friends, and now that I’ve talked to you on this, I’ll think about you next time I look at the moon.

Sources indicate that it’s the old TV. It’s the thing that we can look at from anywhere on Earth and we know we’re all seeing the exact same picture. I used to look at that and think about my brother when he went away to college, and I’ve always loved that. I was in the Navy; I love being at sea and watching the moon rise over the ocean when it’s just reflecting off the ocean. The moon’s a very powerful, very beautiful thing to get to look at. To me, it’s more a peace and togetherness than anything. ✦.

Surviving space is a group effort, and Wiseman has often sought expert wisdom on challenges “he’s dealing with at work.” Before retiring in September, he averaged a book a week, which he usually listened to while commuting to and from the Johnson Space Center in Houston. If a book really hit, the rest of his crew might read it too—effectively forming the world’s most high-functioning book club.

A version of this story originally appeared in the December 2026 issue of GQ with the title “Routine Excellence with Real Live Astronaut Reid Wiseman.”.

What are you most excited for this holiday season?

Sources indicate that ciara: This time of year has always been so special to me. Our schedules are so busy, and I really cherish the opportunity to slow down, spend quality time with our family, decorate the house together, and see the excitement on our kids’ faces throughout the season. This year, we are especially looking forward to soaking up those special moments together and getting ready to welcome Baby Cinco.”.

Industry observers note that you’re wearing a head-to-toe Macy’s for tonight’s celebration. How would you describe your personal style during the holiday season?

Ciara: Tonight I wanted something that felt elevated, but still comfortable for running around with the kiddos. I knew Macy’s would have exactly what I was looking for. With a busy career and a full house, are you someone who has all your holiday shopping done by November, or are you more of a last-minute, Christmas Eve kind of shopper?

Ciara: I’m definitely a planner and take holiday shopping very seriously! With a substantial family, you need the time to find something special and thoughtful for everyone. Especially with my kids, their interests are always changing, so I’m always paying attention to what they’re into and thinking about what would make them happy. I just love finding those special things that I know they’ll be excited to open on Christmas morning.

When it comes to gift-giving, what’s your signature style?

Russell: When it comes to giving gifts to my family, I get so excited. I love to go all out—go significant or go home! When you’re hosting for the holidays, what’s your secret to throwing a memorable celebration?

Butternut Pasta With Sausage and Dates

📅 13 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (522 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Epicurious

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that squash and sausage are a heroic autumnal pairing, especially in a weeknight-friendly pasta.
  • Rigatoni’s ribbed surface and large holes help chunky squash sauce cling and bites of seared sausage and date wedge—opting for a nutty whole wheat variety will only add to this meal’s autumnal earthiness.
  • More cozy pastas this way: Balsamic Mushroom and Sausage Pasta; Creamy Red Curry Pasta; and Baked Feta Pasta With Green Sauce.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that squash and sausage are a heroic autumnal pairing, especially in a weeknight-friendly pasta. Butternut is the easiest squash to source—not to mention easily found peeled and chopped (a blessing for those with more timid knife skills). But other winter squash like acorn or red kuri can stand in as desired. Whichever squash you select, a sharp, heavy chef’s knife is best for breaking down the chunky veg. But to make your life easier, microwave the squash for 1 to 2 minutes. It will slightly soften, making it simpler—and safer—to slice through.

Rigatoni’s ribbed surface and large holes help chunky squash sauce cling and bites of seared sausage and date wedge—opting for a nutty whole wheat variety will only add to this meal’s autumnal earthiness.

More cozy pastas this way: Balsamic Mushroom and Sausage Pasta; Creamy Red Curry Pasta; and Baked Feta Pasta With Green Sauce.

According to recent reports, cook 1 medium butternut squash (1½–2 lb.), peeled, halved, seeds removed, cut into 1" pieces (about 6 cups), in a large pot of boiling salted water until very tender, 12–14 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer squash to a medium bowl. Reduce heat to low, cover pot, and leave on burner to keep warm.

It has been revealed that heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium Dutch oven over medium-high. Add 1 lb. hot or sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, and break up into small pieces with a wooden spoon. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, about 3 minutes. Continue to cook, stirring occasionally, until browned all over and just cooked through, 3–4 minutes more. Transfer to a plate with a slotted spoon.

Reduce heat to medium-low. Cook 3½ oz. Medjool dates (about 6), pitted, sliced lengthwise ¾" thick, in same pan, turning halfway though, until deeply browned, 3–4 minutes. Transfer to plate with sausage; season with salt.

It has been revealed that add remaining 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil to pan. Add 6 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and reserved squash. Cook, scraping up browned bits and smashing squash with spoon to break up, until lightly browned and broken up into a chunky paste (pieces do not need to be even), about 5 minutes.

In a recent development, meanwhile, return cooking liquid in reserved pot to a boil over high heat. Cook 12 oz. short tube pasta (such as rigatoni) until very al dente, about 3 minutes less than package directions (it will finish cooking in sauce). Drain, reserving 3 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid to squash and break up squash with spoon until a saucy consistency. Add pasta, another 1 cup pasta cooking liquid, and reserved sausage and dates. Increase heat to medium-high; cook, adding more pasta cooking liquid as needed, until pasta is al dente and coated in sauce, 2–3 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. sherry vinegar or balsamic vinegar. Taste pasta and add more vinegar, salt and/or pepper if needed.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grand Theft Auto VI drops on November 19th, and there are many ways to prepare. I’ve been replaying every game going back to the original, with a particular soft spot for the 3D era: III, Vice City, and Rockstar's greatest achievement, San Andreas—yes, yes, I'm coming in hot. After some 13 years of GTA Online, with its perpetual content stream and microtransactions, it’s easy to forget how it all began. The franchise has consistently brought freewheeling chaos and mayhem, sure. But it has also always delivered memorable story missions, which evolved from basic lures and assassinations into something like GTA V's “Friend Request or “Reuniting the Family,” culturally scathing mini-movies which have to be played to be believed. “My least favorite mission involves Michael using a tattoo gun on me,” former Rockstar director, writer, and producer Lazlow Jones told me of the latter mission. “I still give Dan [Houser] shit about that one to this day.”.

What follows is a ranking of the greatest missions in the series’ history, with one caveat: I only allowed myself four missions per game, maximum. To help sort through the clear classics and happy accidents, I talked to some of the people who made these games come alive, including Jones, former Rockstar North technical director Obbe Vermeij, and West Coast rapper Young Maylay, the beloved voice of Carl Johnson. Shockingly, Maylay says he’s still fond of the infamous “Wrong Side of the Tracks.” “All we had to do was follow the damn train, CJ!” Maylay remarked, imitating his exasperated sensei Big Smoke. I’m not including that mission on here, though, partly because I’d like to make it out of this piece alive.

Industry observers note that bum. Budupup-budum. For a lot of us, that theme was the beginning of our Grand Theft Auto journey. What follows is barely prologue. There's an ambush on the Callahan Bridge, an escape with 8-Ball, and a drive to a safe house in Portland, Liberty City's Brooklyn-by-way-of-Queens industrial borough. You do not fire a single shot. And yet each playthrough already looked different. Did you open the short manual and splay the map across your bedroom floor, or drive blind to the edge of the Red Light District?

It has been revealed that "The most memorable mission for me was the first one I ever played, 'Give Me Liberty,'" Lazlow told GQ. Once the host of Technofile, a syndicated show about technology and video games, Lazlow showed up at Rockstar’s Manhattan offices in 2001 to report a radio piece. Not long after, he was spoofing American radio himself as the iconic voice of Chatterbox FM.

In a recent development, "[Former Rockstar CEO] Terry Donovan brought over a copy of the game the day it came out. Dan [Houser] had given me a PlayStation 2,” Lazlow continued. “I'd worked on the radio for the game all summer with Dan but I hadn't actually seen it. After the cinematic ended, I got into the car and Head Radio came on and I'm driving through town. It blew my mind.".

Recent findings suggest that crazy what a difference three years can make. The Donald Love of GTA III is a composed real-estate scion with a media empire. Liberty City Stories, set in 1998, shows you the man before the polish, who’s way more overt about his hunger for power — and human flesh.

The mayoral race is his project, and Toni Cipriani is his instrument. Toni guns down the incumbent mayor R.C. Hole, somehow engendering only one star. "Steering the Vote" then puts him behind the wheel of a campaign van, zooming across Staunton while the loudspeaker blares: “O'Donovan is a communist!” “O’Donovan hates America!” or “A vote for Love is a vote for happiness!” The van has to reach specific stops before the messaging triggers, which means the game is literally grading you on how much of the world you can seduce. GTA may have predicted everything from Ozempic culture to billionaire doomsday prep, but there was no forecast sharper than this one.

For most of Rockstar’s history, the studio—technically a U.S. firm, but with a British development team—has made its bread and butter satirizing America, and nothing has been off the table. But in London 1969, the first of two expansion packs for the original Grand Theft Auto, Rockstar transplants its crime sandbox to London in the late ‘60s, where the Brits take center stage. (“Who gave Paul McCartney a shotgun?” one YouTube commenter asks.) Broken up into chapters, the seminal “Dead Certainty” draws on the high-flying exploits of the real-life Kray twins, the foremost perpetrators of organized crime in London’s East End at the time, who rubbed elbows with politicians and entertainers before ultimately being locked away for life.

Grand Theft Auto is a game about many things, but one of the first things it was—and still is—is a game about cars. If San Fierro’s underrated main story missions aren’t enough (yes, I know, Cesar. The yay is leaving San Fierro again), head on over to Easter Basin for the best edition of “Exports and Imports.” The concept dates back to the original GTA, where it was called “Crane Bonuses,” but it’s a classic here because of its sheer scale. What starts at the docks turns into a mad hunt across the entire map of San Andreas, finding and then delivering 30 specific vehicles.

Industry observers note that san Andreas has 212 defined vehicles, more than twice as many as Vice City. You start learning the taxonomy—how to tell a Remington from a Sabre and an Infernus from a Cheetah—and figuring out where certain vehicles turn up. The Camper can be found on top of Mount Chiliad, meaning the hard part isn’t finding it so much as getting the lumbering thing back down in one piece. When I was younger, I never really appreciated these side missions. Now, I love how they slow the game down and make you observe all the GTA sandbox goodness you might otherwise race past.

It has been revealed that rockstar has a long, cruel history of giving you a remote control and trolling. But unlike “Supply Lines” or “Demolition Man,” there’s a certain genius to this one. Vic Vance pulls up outside the Mendez compound and, instead of going in like a cowboy, climbs into a van to command a newfangled robot servant, Domestobot. At this point the game becomes a butlering simulator: Fetch a drink, light a cigar, and clean the floor, all the while trying to crack a drug kingpin’s basement safe. Rockstar didn’t forget about our charming robot after this, either. In GTA V, Radio Los Santos host Major Boy laments the Domestobot future that never arrived: "We have internet glasses, but not our own robot butler!”.

In 1995, at age 17, Blair Renaud joined what became Rockstar Canada (now Rockstar Toronto), and stuck around long past his original contract, eventually becoming a technical director. “I basically walked into the boss's office and was like, ‘I'm not leaving. I'll do whatever you want,'” Renaud told me. After designing the London ‘69 map without ever having set foot in England (“I just winged it”), he and his entire Toronto office were put on QA duty for Grand Theft Auto 2, with its grim retro-futurist Anywhere City and sharper graphics.

GTA has always played with consumption (Donald Love likely ate his real estate mentor, Avery Carrington) but “Hot Dog Homicide!” is GTA2 at its most dastardly. In the original PC/Dreamcast version, you steal a bus, load it with civilian passengers, and deliver them to a Russian mob boss's meat grinder to satiate his army. “I think [GTA] was actually more controversial [in the beginning] about the crime, rather than just the violence,” Renaud stated. “It was like ‘Oh, I'm like stealing people's cars and running them over.' It was a little bit more real.” For all the creative choices the series has been pilloried for in the ensuing years, a mission like “Hot Dog Homicide!” wasn't nearly as explosive then as it would be today.

I always get excited about missions that let you revisit a location you've already seen, especially when the game gives you a reason to see it differently. “Bury the Hatchet” sends Michael and Trevor back to North Yankton, the snowy Midwestern state where GTA V began, where the two men start digging into the events of the botched bank heist that set their lives on their current course.

It’s San Andreas’s “St. Mark’s Bistro” done better. Instead of briefly dropping you into a familiar location for a quick hit of nostalgia, GTA V actually lets you spend some time knee-deep in the snow. Michael and Trevor each retrace the events of the heist; Trevor unearths a coffin marked with Michael’s name, only to find Brad’s decomposing body inside. Ultimately, the two men aim guns at each other. Michael has spent much of the game on his high horse insisting that he’s changed, while Trevor, always the firecracker, is at least honest about exactly who he is.

Recent findings suggest that another great LCS mission that adds to Liberty City lore. Donald Love sends Toni to explosives expert 8-Ball (who still has functioning hands at this point) to raze an entire neighborhood, Fort Staunton, and pave the way for his Panlantic deal. With the Forellis giving chase, Toni has to get a van loaded with explosives to the site, then race through tunnels planting charges beneath the neighborhood. No way those tunnels aren’t at least a little inspired by Die Hard with a Vengeance. After the biggest explosion in GTA history (not bad for a PSP game), the National Guard can be found roaming the neighborhood. And by GTA III, Fort Staunton is teeming with scaffolding, construction pits and Cartel members, a neighborhood still reshaping itself after Toni’s seismic contribution.

There are few things more San Andreas than being handed a shoddy military plane by a mysterious government agent and being told to fly it across the state without being detected by radar. “N.O.E.” is the greatest test of your skills acquired in the Pilotwings-esque gauntlet, “Learning to Fly.” Fly too high and the military shoots you down; fly too low and the terrain dings you first. The mission captures just how far Mike Toreno has pulled CJ from the streets and into the shadowy world of government conspiracies.

Industry observers note that greg Johnson, a hip-hop journalist who became Rockstar's senior researcher from 2003 to 2020, traces those wild Toreno missions to the 1992 film Deep Cover. Most people know it through its title song, Dr. Dre and Snoop Dogg's first record together. But the film itself touched on government corruption and drug trafficking in Southern California.

“Loved that Dan [Houser] put some Deep Cover-inspired missions in GTA SA with Mike Toreno basically playing Agent Carver and CJ as John Hull,” Johnson noted. “I definitely talked to [Houser] a lot about Deep Cover, but he was also having conversations with [West Coast hip-hop producer and Rockstar writer] DJ Pooh, who personally knows [drug lord] Freeway Rick [Ross] about that era, and reading up on books and reports…as they wrote the game.”.

Heavy metal band Love Fist is in a pickle. Think Speed, only with a limo, and even thicker Scottish accents than Groundskeeper Willie. The mission is straightforward, but not easy: drive the limousine across the city while keeping the momentum steady enough to hold off detonation. It’s also a testament to how Vice City could turn even its tertiary characters into stars. Love Fist barely occupies a sliver of the game, yet they've stuck around as memorable rockstars for more than two decades. Obbe Vermeij, longtime Rockstar North technical director, also has a soft spot for the mission. “Particularly funny,” he notes, “because the Love Fist voices are just guys from the office.”.

In a recent development, there isn't a single on-rails shooting sequence in Grand Theft Auto that I've ever passed easily. Doesn't matter how many times I've played. I’m no deadeye. Luckily, in “Reuniting the Families,” there’s plenty packed in before we get to that. This is back when CJ, Sweet, Ryder and Big Smoke are all still homies, and when the vast map of San Andreas is still centered on the few-mile radius around Grove Street. You head to a motel with the intention of saving the hood, only to find it crawling with SWAT. After battling your way through the rooms and taking down a helicopter on the roof, you escape by car with the cops still in pursuit. Smoke is behind the wheel while an AK with unlimited ammo is placed in your hands. The cops can even climb onto the car and try to wrestle the gun away from you. It’s a wild, arcade-style sequence, but also one of the last hurrahs for the homies before betrayal and more nonsense from that bastard Frank Tenpenny. Fittingly, the getaway car flies straight through a Sprunk soda billboard reading “A Taste of Things to Come.”.

It has been revealed that “Cop Land” is peak bromance between Tommy and Lance, before the latter decides to ruin the movie. It’s also a snapshot of just how much more active and assertive Vice City’s main character is than man-of-no-words Claude, made all the more credible by the late Ray Liotta’s swagger in the role. Tommy isn't merely taking orders and working his way up someone else's criminal ladder. By this point, he's building the Vercetti Estate into his own empire and making his own destiny.

In a recent development, in “Cop Land,” the entire northern portion of the first island experiences a demographic shake up and now consists of exactly two assets: cops on foot in tan and brown and cops in green police cruisers. First, Tommy and Lance have to steal cop uniforms, a step that can get clunkier than it should when the garage door won't shut with the right number of cops inside. From there, you head to North Point Mall in disguise, plant a bomb and hightail it out of there with a five-star wanted level. Vice City’s officers were particularly bloodthirsty, and getting to a Pay 'n' Spray with Lance still intact—my man is drawn to dumb deaths—was one of my greatest teenage achievements.

Dubai-born real estate heir Yusuf Amir can buy anything. So naturally, the thing he wants most is an experimental attack helicopter parked on an arms dealer’s yacht. Rockstar was mining Gulf excess for laughs more than a decade before Dubai Bling and Love Is Blind: Habibi. Yusuf’s gaudy apartment tells you everything you need to know about him. There’s a miniature model of Algonquin laid out in his penthouse, as if the entire city were already one of his properties, and a giant dollar sign mounted on the wall. He dances to “Arab Money,” peppers his speech with hip-hop slang, and adopts the mannerisms of a culture he knows nothing about. Luis, unsurprisingly, is not particularly moved.

In a recent development, that makes “Sexy Time” the perfect introduction to him. Boat out from the marina, slip past the patrol and steal the Buzzard. Only, mid-flight, Yusuf calls and asks you to turn around, blow the yacht apart and run down what’s left of the arms dealers. For those who felt GTA IV took itself way too seriously, The Ballad of Gay Tony was a breath of fresh air. “Yusuf Amir is one of my all time favorite characters Dan [Houser] created,” Lazlow said. “The dialogue in this mission is hysterical, and he's constantly trying to sound street while going on about building luxury condos.”.

The final chapter in the InterGlobal Studios asset arc turns Vice City into a formidable platformer. Tune in to Flash FM (Talk Talk’s “Life’s What You Make It”) or Fever 105 (Kool & The Gang’s “Summer Madness”) as Tommy leaps across rooftops on his trusted PCJ-600 bike in a single bound—though it’s far more likely that you’ll tumble to the streets at least once. There’s a delicate balance required for each stunt jump, but also a sense of reward once you master timing and speed.

In a recent development, this mission is, as the kids say, vibes. Something about scaling the ‘80s skyline by night while the rest of the city sleeps is unforgettable, along with the hilarious payoff, when Tommy triggers a spotlight that projects a massive X-rated image promoting adult performer Candy Suxxx (née Candice Shand) onto the side of a building. The most memorable GTA characters have a way of appearing in multiple forms: voices on the radio, bodies in cutscenes and, here, as advertising beamed across the world itself.

It has been revealed that small-town America gets the GTA treatment in “The Paleto Score.” Michael, Franklin and Trevor roll into sleepy Paleto Bay to rob the Blaine County Savings Bank, but the getaway swiftly becomes less Ocean’s Eleven and more like Terminator or even MechCommander. Even before the heist, Lester, the master of elaborate setups, proves to be an unlikely master of conflict resolution too. His dry little “Hello, Franklin” to break up another Michael and Trevor spat still has me in stitches.

It has been revealed that what starts as a relatively conventional bank job becomes a slow, lumbering march through an entire town, with our antiheroes mowing down cops, SWAT and eventually the military along the way. There’s even a reward for going overboard. One of the gold-medal requirements is to fire more than 4,000 bullets — because apparently, just robbing a bank wasn’t impressive enough.

It has been revealed that every time we see our hippie friend The Truth, his missions get better. In the apex of his mission tree, “Black Project,” CJ infiltrates Area 69, Rockstar’s twist on Area 51. There’s a stealth way of entering the maximum security facility, but that’s not nearly as fun as going in guns blazing. The level abounds with hilarious one-liners (“Get the General Mills on the line!”) and lab announcements (“Tonight’s menu is posted in the canteen. Barf bags can be ordered from Human Resources.”).

In a recent development, after GTA III’s and Vice City’s limited interiors, San Andreas gives you lively environments like Area 69, where you can disappear down corridors, into laboratories and through underground tunnels. And once CJ steals the coveted jet pack prototype, it becomes a way to fast travel across the state of San Andreas, bringing a whole new perspective to the final hours of the game. “The Truth. He stayed high as a motherfucker talking about conspiracy theory shit,” Young Maylay said. “But he would hit it on the head.”.

Niko spends much of GTA IV doing other people’s dirty work. By “Late Checkout,” the diamond deal has gone so badly that Ray Boccino has lost his money, his diamonds and what remained of his patience. Isaac Roth, the diamond dealer who helped blow up the deal, is hiding in the Majestic Hotel. Ray wants him dead.

It has been revealed that this mission is a choose-your-own-adventure affair. You can take the elevator and fight your way up through the guards, floor by floor, or use the window-cleaning platform outside to reach the penthouse from above and then fight your way back down. Either way, Niko eventually has to work his way through the hotel, killing Roth and his associates before making his escape.

It’s Rockstar’s take on the Plaza Hotel, minus Tim Curry, turned into a bonafide shooting gallery. Bonus points if you shove the front desk manager, who may respond by hopping over the desk to fight his own bellman.

Phil? Phil Collins? That's right. The former Genesis drummer and self-styled “Little Elvis” made gaming history by becoming the first real-life celebrity to lend his name and likeness as well as his voice to GTA. Like Vice City, VCS is inspired by the ‘80s TV drama Miami Vice; Philip Michael Thomas, who played Ricardo Tubbs on the show, voices Lance Vance in both VC and VCS, and Collins, as it happens, guest-starred on the series in 1985, as con man Phil Mayhew.

According to recent reports, in this mission the Mob is after the Brit, and Vic has to ward them off. It all comes to a head during “In the Air Tonight” at Hyman Memorial Stadium. You're up top clearing Forelli saboteurs looming in the rafters while Phil is down below working the crowd.

According to recent reports, for the man voicing Vic, this history wasn't lost on anyone. "Miami Vice was literally my favorite show as a little boy," stated voice actor Dorian Missick. "I still have pictures of me in what I call my Miami Vice suit. One year, my mom let me get a little suit that they used to wear, but the collar’s turned up. I wore something like that for Easter. So to me, it was my opportunity to kind of be on the Miami Vice episode that I never got a chance to do. So all of these things, the Phil Collins of it all, and just that energy of it — it was exciting to be a part of that.".

In a recent development, “Caida Libre,” Spanish for “free fall,” is one of those missions that finally makes the sprawling expanse of GTA V’s San Andreas feel like one cohesive playground. Michael and Trevor are hired by Martin Madrazo to take down a plane carrying his cousin Javier. Michael starts things off by shooting at the aircraft from Galileo Observatory with a sniper rifle.

The best part is the handoff, a seminal showcase of GTAV’s character-switch mechanic. First, Michael is coolly shooting down a plane from a mountaintop, and moments later you’re controlling Trevor, flying down country roads on a Sanchez motorcycle, chasing the falling debris like a man following his destiny. Eventually, Trevor finds Javier, kills him and climbs into the wrecked plane to retrieve the package. And, because this is Trevor, the mission ends with Trevor pining after Martin’s wife, Patricia, and kidnapping her. So much for the moral of Obsession.

When GTAIII first dropped, I spent the first few hours of the game gazing longingly across the river to Staunton Island, imagining what came next. Back in those days, Grand Theft Auto’s world opened up in stages and phases, trusting players to forgo instant gratification. That little stretch of water felt like the portal to another world entirely.

In a recent development, after Claude is victim of a double-cross, Maria helps him flee from Portland to Staunton where he meets his next boss, Asuka. But here’s the rub: Claude first has to prove he’s no longer the Mafia’s strongman, which means gunning down the beloved don Salvatore Leone in the heart of his turf. Once the deed is done, the Leones turn on you for the rest of the game, transforming the St. Marks neighborhood into a veritable “shotgun hell,” as YouTuber The Professional dubbed it in a video rant a few years ago. “Sayonara Salvatore” is thrilling enough. But its lasting impact on the open world is what players still can’t stop talking about.

It has been revealed that if “Three Leaf Clover” feels familiar, that’s because it is. The mission is Rockstar’s loving homage to Michael Mann’s Heat. Niko joins Packie McReary and his brothers to rob the Bank of Liberty, complete with suits, masks, enormous bags of cash, and a getaway that quickly turns into a war through the streets of Liberty City.

Industry observers note that there’s a little Point Break in there too: A civilian tries to play hero inside the bank, killing Michael Keane before being killed himself, echoing a similar moment in the 1991 film. Then comes the seemingly endless firefight through Algonquin’s neighborhoods, followed by an escape into the subway tunnels — the best transit system, by the way, in GTA history.

Sources indicate that vermeij claims that in GTAIV, missions were often centered more around story than gameplay, but both are top-notch here. “These scripts could get quite significant,” he said. “Thousands of lines in some cases…With every fix the script got a little more complicated.” This is GTA IV at its most cinematic, channeling the American crime movies and cop thrillers that have long shaped the series, all the while paving the way for GTAV’s slew of heists. “Four Leaf Clover,” though, remains the gold standard.

#7389. The USDA Thinks I Can Live on $65 a Week. Can I?

The USDA Thinks I Can Live on $65 a Week. Can I?

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1620 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Welcome to The Receipt, a series documenting how Bon Appétit readers eat and what they spend doing it.
  • In today’s special edition of The Receipt, we're unmasking the diarist and following James Beard Award-winning writer Paul Greenberg—a self-described cheapskate—on his quest to live on the USDA's Thrifty Food Blueprint.
  • My friends sometimes mistake me for a survivor of the Great Depression and not a Gen X-er raised in a household free from deprivation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Welcome to The Receipt, a series documenting how Bon Appétit readers eat and what they spend doing it. Each food diary follows one reader’s week of expenses related to groceries, restaurant meals, coffee runs, and every bite in between. In this time of rising food costs, The Receipt reveals how folks—from different cities, with different incomes, on different schedules—are figuring out their food budgets.

In today’s special edition of The Receipt, we're unmasking the diarist and following James Beard Award-winning writer Paul Greenberg—a self-described cheapskate—on his quest to live on the USDA's Thrifty Food Blueprint.

My friends sometimes mistake me for a survivor of the Great Depression and not a Gen X-er raised in a household free from deprivation. I don't just bargain hunt. I bargain scour as if it were 1931.

This habit stays with me no matter if I’ve got a book on the bestseller list or if the stock market has just tanked. As a lifelong fisherman, I love angling for opportunities lolling in the currents of American commerce. I can’t stand the idea of buying a $5 gallon of milk when I know that the same milk from the same cows is lurking at a supermarket across the street for under three bucks.

In a recent development, with the inflationary surge of recent years, my friends have at last started to take a curiosity in the methods of my madness. According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, the price of sirloin steak is up 21% since January 2024. Romaine lettuce? 27%. Even a gosh darn cup of coffee will cost you over 50% more in 2026 than it did when the Kansas City Chiefs last won the Superbowl. So when Bon Appétit asked my cheapskate self if I could get through a week of groceries for below what the USDA stipulates as its “thrifty food proposal,” I smiled the knowing smile of an old-timer. Bon Appétit and USDA, I accept your challenge.

Recent findings suggest that the USDA established the Thrifty Food Plan in 1975 and updated it in 2021 in an attempt to model a healthy diet that hits all the food groups. The TFP, as we’ll call it here forward (to economize on words in these lean times), proposes different shopping lists for different genders and age groups. I took those 2021 numbers and adjusted them for 2026 inflation. As a man in his 50s, I was given a total allotment of $64.90 per week, and recently, I took to the weird yet familiar corners all over Latest York City at which I procure my groceries. Using my usual regular shopping list, I mostly beat those numbers across the board—without, as US Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins recently suggested, resorting to a nutritionally suspect “$3 a meal for a piece of chicken, a piece of broccoli, you know, a corn tortilla and one other thing.”.

In a recent development, however, the experiment raised a deeper question: Should I have to? But first, here’s how I did it.

Out of habit or laziness, many of us have a “favorite grocery store.” In an era of rapacious capitalism that has pushed so many Americans toward insolvency, there can be no favorites. Rather, it pays to seek out places where merciless competition drives major chains towards a common bargain basement. In Manhattan, where I live, I call these places “golden corners”—spots where Trader Joe’s, Target, and the rising star of discount grocery chains, Lidl, cluster together around a single intersection.

In a recent development, I’m able to easily deduce which place offers the lowest prices and run between them in a single shopping outing. While I’ll occasionally venture elsewhere for my meat and dairy (see: Chinatowns, featured later in this article), I find a good cutthroat corner serves me best when looking for animal protein.

Note: There is no beef on this list. For climate change reasons, I’ve never been a fan of the world’s most carbon-intensive protein, and to my mind, the three-dollars-cheaper-per-pound ground turkey works just fine in a Bolognese. Also note that neither the TFP nor I put any cheese on our lists either. I’m not sure why TFP refrained, but after beef, cheese is one of the most climate impactful animal proteins on the planet. The environmentalist in me also says cut the cheese.

Professional economizers often encourage us to choose vegetables and fruits with longer shelf lives that can bang around in our fridges until we’re ready to eat them. I’ve found picking the cheapest fruits and vegetables when they’re available is ultimately a better deal. For this, I turn to a staple of American urban street life: the fruit cart.

According to recent reports, fruit cart vendors, common in Newly introduced York, Los Angeles, Miami, and Chicago, buy produce wholesale and offer deep discounts, especially when shelf life is short. My go-to cart-guy in Lower Manhattan nearly always has a $1 special (cauliflower, cucumbers, asparagus, berries of all kinds) and the relationship we’ve built means he steers me toward what’s good.

What if the nearly overripe berries go off? To this I say: There is no berry too off that can’t be made into jam (which saves you in the miscellaneous category at this article’s end). As for salad greens, while the mainstream shopping world wrings its hands over cyclosporiasis, I’ve found that joining a community garden circumvents the dreaded disease while also purging the scourge of inflation from your wallet. My community garden costs me about $50 a year in membership fees, seeds, and fertilizer, plus about an hour of my time a week in tending. The buy-in amounts to roughly $0.50 per salad.

According to recent reports, whatever fruit carts and my garden can’t supply, I usually find at great prices in Manhattan’s Chinatown, likely because vendors have connections to a handful of small farms and wholesalers that operate outside of most mainstream supermarkets. According to the California Migration Museum, there are roughly 50 Chinatowns across America in nearly every major American city, which is to say that a lot of the country should have access to one.

Note: Even with bargain basement shopping, I only barely hit USDA’s fruit mark. This was because nearly half of USDA’s fruit budget is juice, which, to my mind, is a bit like calling ketchup a vegetable.

It has been revealed that the TFP drives a hard bargain on grains, expecting the home shopper to plunk down $3.76 for an entire week’s worth of “refined-grain staple grains," which include rice, pasta, bread, tortillas and the like. That’s tough when a loaf of Wonder Bread at Walmart costs you $2.47. Add a single box of one-pound pasta and it could send you over-budget.

There’s a bit more give in the "whole-grain staple grains" category, which allows $6.94. But even a whole-wheat loaf from Walmart (priced at $2.97) eats up just over half of my weekly allotment.

The only way I was able to snag the bread, rice, and pasta in my weekly shop and stay under budget was by leaning on another Asian country and by working hard on my home turf.

Patel Brothers, a national chain of Indian grocery stores, sells brown and white rice as well as beans of all flavors and provenances for prices that range from $0.80 to $2 per pound. As for bread, Target’s house brand of whole wheat flour is $2.69 for a five-pound bag. About a pound and a quarter of it makes a loaf. Weekly sandwich bread therefore costs out at $0.67 per loaf.

Sources indicate that last and actually also least: pasta. Nobody but nobody beats Trader Joe’s buck a pound.

In a recent development, shopper beware—the last-minute, forgotten miscellaneous item is often the thing that stings you most at the register. Salt, sugar, cooking oil, and coffee purchased last minute, at even a cheap store, can be double what you’d pay if you are keeping careful track of who's charging what at your local golden corner. Keeping a passive list in your head of where the best buys on miscellany live helps these kinds of rookie mistakes from happening.

Sources indicate that additionally, as above, a little home elbow grease can be surprisingly effective in the condiment aisle. Fruit cart fruit made into jam and an immersion-blended home mayonnaise (a commitment of two minutes max) cost you pennies. And then there’s online. I have yet to find a better deal on coffee than on Amazon.

So I did it. I filled my fridge, stocked one shelf of my pantry, and even had a little left to treat myself to breakfast after this exhausting pan-city forage. Here’s what the final numbers looked like:.

It has been revealed that does this mean the USDA’s stingy allowance is appropriate for these ever more expensive times? That anyone can be a successful cost-cutter like me?

According to recent reports, um, no. My kids are grown. I’m a freelance writer with weird hours. I live in a vast, quirky city with odd corners that can cost out cheaper than parts of the developing world. A busy working mom in a food desert who can’t commit to a community garden would find the ordeal a heavy lift.

Industry observers note that thank you for joining me on this ride through my own personal Great Depression. But as for you, USDA, I think it’s time you upped your budget. Stop cutting things like food stamps and healthcare. Perhaps the newest iteration of Congress will be more inclined to make this happen than its predecessor. We are, after all, among the wealthiest sovereign nations in the world.

Sources indicate that C’mon, America! Don’t be such a cheapskate.

10 Best Sunscreens for Face That You’ll Actually Enjoy Wearing

  • As for the market itself, board-certified dermatologist Lindsey Zubritsky, MD, FAAD, attributes much of the category’s growth to increased consumer education.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When people talk about the “good old days,” I stay quiet—I’m pretty certain I was born in the right generation. I love waiting in line for $10 artisanal matcha, and I love having access to hundreds of sunscreens that don’t pill, feel greasy, or leave behind a ghoulish white cast. Considering that sunscreen is arguably the most vital step in your beauty routine (every dermatologist and aesthetician worth their license would agree), having so many options feels particularly worth celebrating, especially given how much the global sunscreen market has evolved.

Industry observers note that if you need a refresher on why we talk about sunscreen so much at Vogue, board-certified dermatologist Marnie Nussbaum points out that while our skin-care routines may include plenty of salmon sperm and copper peptides, the most effective step is also the least exciting: sunscreen. Used diligently and consistently, it can help prevent much of the damage we might otherwise try to address later, including collagen and elastin loss, skin laxity, hyperpigmentation, fine lines, and, most importantly, skin cancer.

As for the market itself, board-certified dermatologist Lindsey Zubritsky, MD, FAAD, attributes much of the category’s growth to increased consumer education. “In the past few years, there has been so much incredible education about the importance of wearing sunscreen every day,” she states. “With more people looking to incorporate SPF into their daily routines, the market has drastically expanded.” Today, that means everything from invisible formulas and tinted sunscreens to SPF lip balms and on-the-go sticks.

Sources indicate that another perk of being alive in 2026? Having easier access to formulas that were once largely limited to their home countries. Whether you’re discovering Korean, Japanese, and Australian sunscreen innovations on TikTok or asking a friend to bring back a French pharmacy favorite, it’s never been easier to explore what the rest of the world has to offer. The US has historically been slower to approve newer sunscreen filters than other markets, although that’s beginning to change. In June 2026, the FDA approved bemotrizinol, a UV filter already widely used abroad and the first new sunscreen ingredient permitted in the US in more than 25 years. Still, international markets offer formulators a broader range of UV filters, helping explain the variety of textures, finishes, and formulations available overseas.

Sunscreen has come a long way from formulas that focused primarily on UVB protection. Broad-spectrum options added UVA protection, and newer formulas have made daily SPF easier to wear. Board-certified dermatologist Dara Spearman, MD, FAAD, adds that newer formulas are not only more wearable but also easier to incorporate into everyday routines. “They’re more lightweight and suitable for everyday use across skin types,” she explains. Many newer tinted formulas are designed to blend more seamlessly into a wider range of skin tones. Several also contain iron oxides, which help protect against visible light, making them especially beneficial for those with melasma or hyperpigmentation.

But knowing how key sunscreen is and actually wearing it every day are two different things. According to board-certified dermatologist Sandra Oska, MD, daily use remains inconsistent. “There has been a genuine shift in how consumers think about sunscreen, but the majority of people still aren’t wearing it every day,” she indicates. Men, in particular, tend to underuse SPF, while women and Gen Z are generally more consistent. Even among regular people, common mistakes like underapplying can limit protection.

Recent findings suggest that ultimately, usability is what drives consistency. As Oska notes: “What are consumers actually going to use first thing in the morning, and what’s going to make it into their bag for reapplication?” Formulas that layer well with skin care tend to win out for daily use, while sticks, powders, and SPF lip balms have become essentials for touch-ups throughout the day.

After testing dozens of sunscreens—from the classics to each fresh bottle that hits our desk—and speaking with esteemed dermatologists and estheticians, we evaluated them all to bring you this edit of the best of the best. (Each of them has been tested and worn IRL!) Below is a look at all the best facial sunscreens of 2026 so far.

British Vogue’s Ellie Davis tests the Beauty of Joseon Relief Sun sunscreen.

According to Dr. Nussbaum, sunscreen helps protect against both UVA and UVB rays, which cause different types of damage. UVB rays primarily cause sunburn and can damage DNA, increasing the risk of skin cancer. UVA rays penetrate deeper into the skin, contributing to collagen and elastin breakdown, fine lines, and premature aging. They can even penetrate windows, making daily protection crucial when you’re indoors, too.

According to recent reports, when it comes to sunscreen formulas, there are two main types of UV filters: mineral and chemical. Mineral sunscreens use zinc oxide, titanium dioxide, or both to protect the skin, primarily by absorbing UV radiation, with some reflection and scattering. Chemical sunscreens also absorb UV rays and convert that energy into less harmful forms, primarily heat. Both can provide effective sun protection, although their textures and how they feel on the skin can vary. Mineral formulas are often recommended for sensitive skin, while chemical formulas tend to be lighter and less likely to leave a white cast.

What to Look For in a Face Sunscreen.

Recent findings suggest that SPF Level: “Picking a sunscreen does not have to be complicated!” Los Angeles dermatologist Chris Tomassian notes. “Look for a sunscreen that is SPF 30 or higher and broad-spectrum, meaning it blocks both UVA and UVB rays. You want to use at least two finger lengths of sunscreen for the full face, and when you are out in the sun, reapply every two hours to maintain adequate sun protection.” Apply sunscreen at least 15 minutes before going outside.

Type: Mineral sunscreens use zinc oxide, titanium dioxide, or both to protect against UV radiation, primarily through absorption, with some reflection and scattering. Chemical sunscreens also absorb UV rays, converting their energy into less harmful forms. “Although both can be incredibly effective, chemical sunscreens can be somewhat more irritating to sensitive skin,” explains Dr. Nazarian. “Physical sunscreens are a bit more stable, but are also a little more occlusive and can trap heat, so it may feel a little heavier than the chemical sunscreens.” Zinc oxide and titanium dioxide are mineral sunscreen ingredients to look for.

Texture: How the sunscreen sits on the skin can make all the difference in how it wears. Those looking for something under makeup might appreciate a lightweight formula or something with a primer-like texture. Conversely, someone with dry skin might consider a richer, emollient formula similar to a face cream. That being said, keep your routine (and skin type) in mind when selecting your SPF this year.

In a recent development, white Cast: A white cast is a whitish, almost purplish hue left behind after applying some sunscreens. This often happens with mineral formulas that utilize zinc oxide to provide a physical barrier between the skin and sun rays. Fortunately, most sunscreens these days—even mineral options—do not leave a white cast.

Broad-Spectrum: Broad-spectrum means your sunscreen protects against both UVA and UVB rays. If a sunscreen is not labeled “broad-spectrum,” it may not provide adequate UVA protection, leaving your skin more vulnerable to sun damage and premature aging.

It has been revealed that editors’ Review: Our editorial team has tested each sunscreen on this list (and more that weren’t featured!), so we can speak to everything from texture and finish to how well they layer under makeup. Where our editors feel particularly strongly about a formula, you’ll find their firsthand experiences alongside insights from our dermatologist experts.

What Is Broad-Spectrum Sunscreen?

“Broad-spectrum describes the quality of providing sun protection against a wide range of ultraviolet wavelengths,” Dr. Murphy-Rose explains. “Broad-spectrum sunscreens protect against both UVA and UVB rays.”.

How Much Sunscreen to Use on Your Face.

Recent findings suggest that dr. Murphy-Rose recommends applying two finger lengths of product to the face each application. “One of the most common mistakes in sunscreen application is not applying enough product,” she continues. “Always remember to apply to your whole face, including over the brows, ears, and around the lips. These are areas where I very often see pre-cancerous skin growths, and I believe that’s partly due to less sunscreen use on these areas.” She also recommends using an SPF lip balm.

There’s an ongoing debate about mineral versus chemical sunscreen. In fact, you might be wondering what those terms even mean, and which you should use in your routine. Here’s what you need to know:.

What Sunscreen Is Recommended by Dermatologists?

In our reporting, dermatologists often recommended broad-spectrum sunscreens with SPF 30 or higher from EltaMD, SkinCeuticals, La Roche-Posay, and Supergoop!. For more insight into their picks, see the expert recommendations featured throughout our product reviews.

Should You Wear Sunscreen Every Day—Even Indoors?

Wearing sunscreen every day helps protect against cumulative sun damage, which can contribute to skin cancer and premature aging. And while you might think you’re safe from UV rays indoors, UVA radiation can penetrate ordinary window glass, making sunscreen particularly worthwhile if you spend time near sunny windows. Visible light from the sun can also contribute to hyperpigmentation, especially in people with darker skin tones or melasma. However, there’s little evidence that the blue light emitted by phones, computers, and other electronic devices has a meaningful effect on the skin.

How to Apply (and Reapply) Sunscreen Properly.

It has been revealed that now that you know what to look for in a sunscreen, it’s notable to apply it with care. “It is a common glitch that consumers are not applying it correctly, whether applying a product that is substandard, applying an insufficient amount, or neglecting to reapply appropriately,” Dr. Murphy-Rose explains. “A good guideline for sufficient coverage is about a shot glass’s worth of product for one application for the whole body or the equivalent of two finger lengths for the face.”.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re in direct sunlight, you should reapply sunscreen at least every two hours, as well as after swimming, sweating, or towel drying. This means applying the same amount you did initially (read: the two-finger rule!). Sunscreen sprays and powders can be convenient for touch-ups, especially over makeup, but it can be difficult to apply enough to achieve the SPF protection stated on the label. For the most reliable coverage, stick with a lotion or cream when reapplying. According to Dr. Tomassian, another misconception is that makeup with SPF is sufficient for your daily sunscreen: your SPF-laced makeup must be layered on top of a layer of sunscreen. “Always remember the sunscreen that you will use is the one that is going to be most effective!” Dr. Karen adds.

In a recent development, sunscreen should generally be reapplied at least every two hours when you’re outdoors, and more frequently after swimming, sweating, or towel drying, according to the product’s water-resistance instructions. Over time, sunscreen can wear off or become less effective, so regular reapplication is essential to maintain protection.

You might be wondering: Does SPF matter? It’s a common question we beauty editors get, especially with so many different sunscreens on the market. Not to mention, you might receive different advice based on who you’re talking to.

“SPF (Sun Protection Factor) measures the amount of UV radiation needed to produce sunburn on protected skin (with sunscreen) compared to the amount of UV radiation required to produce sunburn on unprotected skin (without sunscreen),” Dr. Green explains. “The higher the SPF, the more UV radiation exposure your skin can handle before getting sunburned.” Generally speaking, most experts recommend an SPF of 30 or higher, but Dr. Green advises a minimum of SPF 50.

When we test and review a product, we take a holistic approach to deliver well-rounded product recommendations. First, we lean on Vogue’s vast network of experts—from board-certified dermatologists to celebrity estheticians—for professional insight into the industry’s standout products that specialists use themselves or recommend to clients. We pair their expertise with our editorial best practices to curate the thoughtful edits you read on our site.

For sunscreens, we selected the best based on the following characteristics: ingredients, texture, finish, SPF level, and the skin-care concerns they address. To do this, we paired our own tests of each formula with expert guidance and reviewer insights to determine which we would recommend.
