💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that after a whirlwind month of speculation, unsubstantiated rumors, and endless Kalshi prognostication, white smoke has finally emerged from the Amazon MGM chimney.
  • Recent findings suggest that the announcement ends the long-running—and quite frankly, exhausting—mystery over Daniel Craig’s successor and starts a fresh creative era for the 007 franchise, which Amazon acquired from longtime Bond custodians Michael G.
  • “James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime,” Pattinson said in a statement to The Hollywood Reporter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that after a whirlwind month of speculation, unsubstantiated rumors, and endless Kalshi prognostication, white smoke has finally emerged from the Amazon MGM chimney. There’s a fresh James Bond—and his name is Robert Pattinson.

Recent findings suggest that the announcement ends the long-running—and quite frankly, exhausting—mystery over Daniel Craig’s successor and starts a fresh creative era for the 007 franchise, which Amazon acquired from longtime Bond custodians Michael G. Wilson and Barbara Broccoli in February 2025, four years after No Time to Die was released. Now, Pattinson will tux up as the seventh cinematic Bond under the stewardship of super-producers David Heyman and Amy Pascal and the vision of GQ’s Director of the Year Denis Villeneuve, marking arguably the biggest role of the 40-year-old London-born actor’s career.

“James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime,” Pattinson said in a statement to The Hollywood Reporter. “I’m deeply grateful to Denis, Amy, David, Tanya, and everyone at Amazon MGM Studios for their belief in me. To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement. I couldn’t be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team.”.

Rumors of Pattinson’s selection caught fire in October, when delays on The Batman Part II gave him a window to audition for Bond at Berkshire’s Bray Studios, alongside peers Callum Turner, Josh O’Connor, Jack Lowden, and an unnamed fourth actor. The chatter heightened a couple weeks later when various British tabloids suggested that Turner, O’Connor, and Lowden were each the preferred choice to satisfy the demands and responsibilities of the beloved British action hero—heightening suspicion that a final decision was looming. According to THR, the finalists were judged “based on stunts, camera presence.” But Pattinson’s last-minute arrival clearly tipped the scale.

“Before anything else, I want to express my deep gratitude to the remarkable actors who joined us on this journey. We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007,” remarked Villeneuve in a statement to THR. “I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our newly introduced James Bond. He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin.”.

It’s both a particularly inspired and obvious choice. Pattinson’s physical traits and characteristics hue close to Ian Fleming’s original Bond—tall and slim, with dark hair. He’s already a bona fide movie star, the current face of DC Studios’ Batman franchise; meanwhile, the selection catches him at the tail end of another booked-and-busy year. Unlike his auditioning peers, the acclaimed actor will enter the franchise well-experienced working in IP and with big-name directors. After co-leading this spring’s The Drama, he chewed up scenes as Antinous in Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey (the second time working with Nolan after Tenet), made a creepy turn as Chris Hansen in Primetime, and will close 2026 as Scytale in Dune: Part 3—now the first of future Villeneuve collaborations, a relationship that surely helped him acquire his license to kill.

It has been revealed that “James Bond is one of the most beloved, inspiring, iconic, and yet enigmatic characters in literature and movies,” Pascal and Heyman stated jointly to THR. “The legacy of this character is in great hands with Robert Pattinson. His fearlessness as an actor, his self-deprecating wit, and his ability to continually reinvent himself make him the perfect Bond for our times.”.

The decision to hire a movie star isn’t a risky choice, but there’s not much precedent within the franchise—especially recently. When he succeeded Pierce Brosnan as Bond in 2005, beating out Clive Owen, Michael Fassbender, and Henry Cavill, Craig boasted an under-the-radar resume. He’d just come off Matthew Vaughn’s crime thriller Layer Cake, but otherwise had played supporting roles in Road to Perdition, The Mother, and Enduring Love. His only massive-budget studio experience came several years earlier as Angelina Jolie’s love interest in Tomb Raider.

Naturally, the British press drew its fangs upon his selection, critiquing everything from his general obscurity to his physical features, which stood in stark contrast to previous Bond actors. “The Mane’s Blond, James Blond,” chirped The Irish Times, while The London Daily Mirror played with the same pun: “The Name’s Bland … James Bland.” At his official introduction to the press along the Thames, Craig arrived on a speedboat wearing a life vest, attracting instant mockery—the first of several digs about his less-than-sleek aesthetic and physical abilities. (One tabloid insulted an on-set sunburn and his inability to drive a stick shift car.).

It has been revealed that pattinson, however, has mostly conjured genuine excitement—not in spite of, but because of, his extreme familiarity with moviegoers, dating back to his Young Adult days in the Harry Potter and Twilight franchises. Since then, over the last decade-plus, his eccentric characters and commanding screen presence immediately qualifies him as someone “stirring and exciting and different,” descriptors that Pascal noted she prioritized in their methodical search.

Thanks to director Martin Campbell, Casino Royale returned the Bond franchise to earth and established Craig as a grounded, gritty action star in the mold of Jason Bourne. The movie ended up raking in $616 million globally, the highest earning Bond film to date, and launched Craig into four more sequels. Similarly, Pattinson will have the benefit of a highly-respected, Oscar-nominated director in his corner with experience shepherding IP into new places and eliciting compelling performances about tortured male protagonists.

Sources indicate that with Villeneuve at the helm of this 26th installment, don’t expect another hard creative pivot; the man behind Prisoners, Blade Runner 2049, and Dune wasn’t hired to bring back the colorful, absurdist, gadget-heavy era that Austin Powers parodied throughout the 90’s. Still, latest leadership means a new direction—a clean slate for Pattinson to burnish an already diverse, robust career and prove his chops again at the highest level of scrutiny.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that mushroom fans: Bookmark this recipe immediately. It will give you everything you want when you crave a creamy mushroom pasta as soon as the crisp fall air sets in. The hardworking trio of miso, Parmesan, and touch of soy sauce delivers an umami bomb of flavor that doesn’t overwhelm, but magnifies, the best of earthy mushrooms. Coupled with luscious noodles enrobed in a creamy (but not heavy) sauce, what’s not to love?

According to recent reports, A few helpful notes for pasta success: (1) While any pasta will work, egg-based noodles, like the fettuccine I recommend here, are the best complement to the sauce. The nests (Rummo and De Cecco are great accessible brands) cook far faster than standard straight pasta, almost as fast as fresh. (2) Don’t be afraid to season your mushrooms! Yes, I know this goes against all that we’ve learned about salting them too early in the cooking process, but just a bit of salt will get them going and releasing their water faster for eventual crisp-browned edges. Don’t be alarmed if you see a pool of water at the start of the mushroom cooking—that’s to be expected and just keep going until it evaporates. (3) Don’t forget to reserve plenty of pasta cooking liquid, which is critical to the eventual sauce’s success. I prefer transferring the al dente noodles from the pasta pot to the skillet, letting any residual water come with it (and to ensure you don’t accidentally drain away that liquid gold).

Find more fall favorite meals here: Weeknight Pumpkin Chili; Cream-ish of Mushroom Soup; Mushrooms au Poivre.

Industry observers note that cook 12 oz. egg-based pasta (such as fettuccine nests) in a large pot of boiling salted water, stirring occasionally, until al dente, about 1 minute less than package directions.

Industry observers note that meanwhile, heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet over high. Add 1 lb. crimini or mixed mushrooms (such as button, maitake, oyster, and/or shiitake), sliced ¼" thick or torn into bite-size pieces, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and toss to coat evenly. Spread out into an even layer and cook, undisturbed, until mushrooms are starting to release their liquid, 2–3 minutes (do not be alarmed; there will be a lot). Continue to cook, tossing occasionally, until moisture is almost completely evaporated and edges of mushrooms are starting to brown, 6–8 minutes.

Reduce heat to medium-high; add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, tossing often, until garlic is fragrant and golden, 1–2 minutes. Pour in ¾ cup dry white wine, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan with a sturdy spatula or flat-edged wooden spoon, and cook until wine is mostly evaporated (you should have about 1 Tbsp. liquid left in pan), about 4 minutes. Reduce heat to medium-low. Add 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, cut into pieces, and 2 Tbsp. white miso and stir until melted and combined. Slowly pour in ½ cup heavy cream, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan; simmer until thickened slightly, 2–3 minutes. Add 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce; season with freshly ground pepper. Taste and add more salt if needed.

It has been revealed that using tongs, transfer pasta to mushroom mixture and add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Increase heat to medium and bring to a simmer. Cook, tossing constantly and adding ½–1 cup more pasta cooking liquid to reach desired sauce consistency if needed, until pasta is al dente and liquid has thickened slightly, about 3 minutes.

Sources indicate that remove pan from heat. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about ½ cup) to pasta and toss to combine. Season generously with more pepper; taste and season with more salt if needed.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with more Parmesan and pepper.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Last night, ahead of the 2026 Governors Awards, Primetime actor Skyler Gisondo put the finishing touches on his Louis Vuitton look in a rather unusual location: the projection room at the Aero Theater in Santa Monica.

Sources indicate that the theater hosted a Gisondo-themed double feature: Primetime and Licorice Pizza (you may also know him from his scene-stealing performance in Booksmart). Still, this is all latest to him. Though Gisondo has been a working actor since childhood, Primetime marks his first-ever awards season campaign. “It’s not even a dream come true because it’s almost like something I never even allowed myself to dream of,” Gisondo tells Vogue.

With an awards blitz comes extra attention to fashion. “I’m 30, and I feel like I just recently started to figure out what I like,” claims Gisondo, who loves a vintage workman jacket and admits, “I seem unable to eat anything without spilling on myself, so that is kind of prohibitive for me wanting to get nicer shirts and stuff.”.

According to recent reports, enter menswear maestro Jason Bolden, who is helping Gisondo achieve a look inspired by his favorite actors: Redford and Newman. “I think there’s a certain timelessness to it—it’s cool in any era at any time. That’s certainly the stuff that I find myself responding to,” he says.

Recent findings suggest that while he’s kicking off awards season with a classic black suit (though the Vuitton tuxedo blouson adds a cool, unfussy touch), Bolden is nudging the actor toward bolder pieces. “I’m pretty tame in my fashion decisions,” Gisondo notes. “I’m probably Jason’s most boring client, but to me, the stuff he has me in, I’m like, oh my God, this is crazy.” What is crazy, you may ask? “He’ll put me in a leather jacket or something, and I’ll look at him and say, ‘Jason, I don't know if I’m this guy, man.’ And he’ll say, ‘Oh, you’re this guy.’”.

Bolden isn’t the only one encouraging Gisondo to broaden his fashion horizons. “My girlfriend is also lovingly pushing me to dress cooler,” he says. He recalls an instance when she suggested he buy a pair of baggy pants. “I was like, ‘I just can’t do it. They’re too major. This just isn’t me.’ Now they’re not even the biggest pants I own.”.

It has been revealed that up next on Bolden’s agenda? To get Gisondo into a pair of leather pants.

Industry observers note that “If I learned anything from Primetime, it’s that you just got to try things. You can’t be afraid to fail,” he notes. “You can’t be afraid to fail at work, in your fashion choices. You only live once. Let’s try some things. Put on the leather pants. Let’s see how it goes.”.

According to recent reports, I haven’t made a meal in the French countryside in fall; but sometimes I dream, and these slow-cooked lentils are what I’d make in such a situation. If your shop only carries sweet Italian sausage or something like an apple-stuffed chicken sausage, both work in a pinch. Just this past weekend, fans were still pinning red strings on their bulletin boards between Jack Lowden and the MI6 superspy when images resurfaced of the Slow Horses star wearing Omega. Since 1995’s Goldeneye, Bond has been an Omega man—a relationship later canonized in one of cinema’s most iconic line readings, when Daniel Craig confirmed his brand of choice in three stretched-out syllables: Oh-Mee-Guh.

If, like me, you were only basing your predictions on what the reported pool of potential Bonds wore on their wrists, Robert Pattinson would have been an easy name to cross off. The newly confirmed 007 only signed on as an ambassador for the Swiss luxury brand Jaeger-LeCoultre two short months ago! When I interviewed Pattinson about the appointment over the summer, he was effusive about his new partner: “I very rarely even wear watches, but when I tried it on, I was like, ‘That’s my favorite watch.’ I wanted to just buy it.”.

Now, in addition to juggling his other iconic role as Batman, Pattinson will presumably need to balance his existing commitment to JLC with his new gig’s long-held ties to Omega. During our conversation earlier this summer, Pattinson revealed what he looks for in a watch. If it’s attention-grabbing badass watches Pattinson is after, he’s in good hands with Omega. The brand is best known for supplying the watches Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin wore when they landed on the moon in 1969. Omega has been happy to create special versions of the Speedmaster for its current partners to dial up its profile. And, of course, the Swiss house continues to expand its Bond-inspired offerings: The maker recently added a “Spectre” version of the Seamaster, 007’s preferred model, to the lineup. And whenever Omega needs to drum up buzz around soon-to-be-released models, they tend to show up on former Bond Craig’s wrists during public appearances.

Recent findings suggest that speculators trying to pin down the next Bond would have had better luck if they’d read some less recent watch tea leaves. Back in 2020, Christopher Nolan released Tenet, his inscrutable but enthralling time-warp thriller in which Pattinson plays a mysterious, dapper, and charming spy involved in a high-stakes mission to save the world—about as good a preview of what the 40-year-old actor will look like as 007 as you’ll find in his filmography. And the watch on his wrist in that flick? An Omega.

#7382. In Puerto Rico, It's Not Thanksgiving—It's Sanguiving

In Puerto Rico, It's Not Thanksgiving—It's Sanguiving

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1765 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Puerto Rican Thanksgiving is an exhilarating holiday remix.
  • Thanksgiving is just as cherished in Puerto Rico as it is on the mainland.
  • In a recent development, I meet with Huyke, widely considered the Puerto Rican answer to Julia Child, on a hot summer day at SatoFino, a neon-hued, woman-owned restaurant in San Juan.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Puerto Rican Thanksgiving is an exhilarating holiday remix. Think turkey marinated in garlic, lime, and oregano, then stuffed with fried green plantains and chicharrón mofongo. Gravy is more likely to be made with guava than with giblets, and flan stands in for apple pie. “Pumpkin spice” is nowhere to be found; here, the local winter squash calabaza takes center stage. And in lieu of warm apple cider, sweet coconut water is sipped beachside straight from a coco.

Thanksgiving is just as cherished in Puerto Rico as it is on the mainland. Celebrated locally since the early 20th century, shortly after the United States invaded in 1898, it marks the beginning of the island’s rambunctious holiday season. It is also a favorite of chef and restaurateur Giovanna Huyke, who over four decades has become the feast’s culinary authority in Puerto Rico.

In a recent development, I meet with Huyke, widely considered the Puerto Rican answer to Julia Child, on a hot summer day at SatoFino, a neon-hued, woman-owned restaurant in San Juan. The bartender swiftly spies her—Huyke is a regular, and her signature red hair makes her easy to spot—and prepares the chef ’s go-to drink, a stiff Manhattan. We settle into our barstools, readying to initiative what will ultimately unfurl into an epic cooking adventure. Huyke has a propensity for them, she tells me. In the preceding days she traveled to Atlanta to cook for Ser Familia—a nonprofit that specializes in supporting Hispanic families—before she rushed back to Caguas, a city 20 miles south of San Juan, where she fed VIPs attending the Miss Universe Puerto Rico pageant. Then she raced across the island to teach a traditional-methods cooking class in San Germán, the second-oldest city in Puerto Rico. Now, she’ll show me how to prepare a Puerto Rican Thanksgiving feast.

A vueltita through the Plaza del Mercado de Río Piedras with a fresh haul of groceries, in preparation for Sanguiving.

“We have a rich and resilient food history—it came from necessity, lack, and a bounty from the land,” Huyke states. It’s a complex cuisine informed by both a deep agricultural heritage and a modern reliance on imported and shelf-stable ingredients, which, despite many obstacles, manages to emerge beautiful and full of flavor—the continuation of a culinary evolution ongoing for centuries. “Our food comes from Spain, Indigenous Taíno people, and [enslaved] West Africans,” Huyke continues. “But it grew from our land and from our history, mixing every influence in our pilónes and our cauldrons.”.

Being around Huyke is a joy. A local TV personality, newspaper columnist, and cookbook writer since the late ’80s, Huyke has taught generations of Puerto Rican home cooks how to prepare the island’s most treasured dishes. Among them was my grandmother, Sara, who I call Tata. Like many members of the Puerto Rican diaspora, my family traveled back to the island for the festivities, alternating each year between Thanksgiving and Christmas. We’d enter Hartsfield- Jackson International Airport in Atlanta in heavy winter coats and leave San Juan’s Luis Muños Marín in shorts and tank tops.

Tata’s Thanksgiving table centered on the expected turkey, but her stuffing was exceedingly Puerto Rican. To a base of Pepperidge Farm stuffing mix, she added picadillo: ground beef cooked with sofrito—the fragrant blend of garlic, onions, peppers, and the punchy native herb culantro that is the cornerstone of the Puerto Rican palate—and pimiento-stuffed Manzanilla olives, all seasoned with the golden spice blend sazón. When Tata died I inherited a weathered copy of Huyke’s 2004 recipe booklet Celebraciones. Within it were recipes that clearly informed Tata’s tremendous Thanksgiving menu; it turned out Huyke had been influencing my holiday for even longer than I knew.

Sources indicate that although formally known in Puerto Rico as El Día de Acción de Gracias, in true Boricua fashion, Thanksgiving is often referred to as Sanguiving, a play on words that gestures to the Roman Catholicism that remains the region’s predominant religion. It’s also El Día del Pavo, which directly translates to “Turkey Day,” and Sangiving, spelled like it sounds. We islanders have a fondness for clever, shortened expressions, an example of our natural tendency toward Puertorriqueñizar—in English, “to make Puerto Rican.”.

A stall brims with large slabs of local calabaza.

“Our adobo goes on the turkey, and all the sides have something to do with sofrito,” Huyke tells me, walking me through the standard Puerto Rican Thanksgiving table. In Puerto Rico, adobo takes two forms—one wet and one dry. Each is a spectacular blend of Spanish, African, and Indigenous ingredients and techniques—garlic, onion, peppers, and herbs pounded in a wooden mortar and pestle with Taíno roots called a pilón, binding the island’s ancestral and colonial cultures.

It has been revealed that puerto Ricans officially became American citizens (and draft eligible) in 1917, just weeks before the US entered World War I. As many as 20,000 locals served, and Puerto Rican soldiers have played a role in every US military conflict since. In many respects, Thanksgiving traditions rooted en la isla are part of a broader military promise: American soldiers always eat well on Thanksgiving Day. Puerto Rican soldiers brought many wartime foodways home with them, and this combined with government subsidies means that today staples can at times feel military-adjacent—especially given the reliance on shelf-stable foods required by a storm-prone island. Over time, the territory’s once agrarian economy (centered around sugar, coffee, and tobacco exports) was transformed into an industrial manufacturing system. Puerto Ricans still consume many foods like tinned corned beef, Vienna sausages, Spam, club soda crackers, and canned vegetables; roughly 85 percent of all food in Puerto Rico is imported.

When Huyke’s father, Hector, served in the Korean War, he encountered the military’s famously bland instant mashed potatoes. From then on, he flat-out refused the dish except during holidays, when Huyke’s mother, Alice (herself a trained cooking instructor), made an impossible-to-resist version: yellow potatoes slowly simmered in cream, enriched with chicken bouillon, then whipped until fluffy with butter. Today a garlicky variation features on Huyke’s Sanguiving table.

Huyke, for her part, wants to steer Puerto Rican cuisine away from processed ingredients and back toward fresh foods—not only because they’re healthier, but also because they are richer in flavor and better convey the layered story of the island’s culinary heritage. She favors from-scratch dishes that lean on regional bounty, from Indigenous staples like maize, peppers, yuca, and other root vegetables to later introductions like plantains and coconuts.

Ají dulce (sweet peppers) are essential to local cuisines across Latin America and the Caribbean—and Chef Giovanna's Sanguiving table.

The best way to explain, she tells me, is to cook together. A few weeks later Huyke joins me in my own kitchen in North Carolina. I rapidly learn that cooking alongside her is a lot like having your own personal instructor. At each step she explains how she’s arrived at a certain preparation and why she uses specific ingredients over others. It’s clearly a familiar role: Education remains a central focus for Huyke, and she counts among her mentees young women like Natalia Vallejo, the island’s first James Beard Award–winning chef. She frequently enlists up-and-coming chefs to cook alongside her and makes herself available for mentoring phone calls. I now feel lucky that I can count myself among them.

Although Huyke auditions new Sanguiving dishes every year, Puerto Rican favorites are always on the menu, many of them influenced by her mother’s recipes. Key among them is yuca stuffing—or “estuffing,” as Puerto Ricans commonly pronounce it. Huyke’s family version, Agüeybaná stuffing, is named for the island’s powerful Taíno chief who led the local people at the time of the Spanish invasion in 1493. Huyke peels and then grates fresh yuca before grinding it to a paste in the food processor. Meanwhile, she instructs me to sauté sofrito in olive oil before adding ground and salt pork, annatto, herbs, and aromatics. It’s all piled into a high-walled dish and baked.

According to recent reports, next we turn our attention to pastelón, a lasagna-like layered casserole of fried sweet plantains and creamy queso fresco. The dish was likely born in Latest York City, where Puerto Rican and Italian communities converged, before finding its way to the island.

“The Puerto Rican and Italian diasporas were physically close in Latest York during the ’50s—they were exposed to lasagna and mozzarella,” she explains.

Industry observers note that then come more sides. Gandules, or pigeon peas, are a treasured crop. Though they’re frequently served with rice at Sanguiving and other times of year—arroz con gandules is Puerto Rico’s national dish— Huyke instead opts for an escabèche-style salad that marries gandules with tomatoes, avocado, and herbs in a tangy vinaigrette. Another island staple, canned beets, gets a fresh reinterpretation as Huyke roasts a local-grown variety and tops them with crumbled queso fresco.

Huyke’s Sanguiving turkey rests on a banana leaf bed and is adorned with freshly picked wildflowers from the rainforest.

In a recent development, many Puerto Rican families choose pernil, or roast pork shoulder, as their Sanguiving centerpiece. It is typically marinated overnight in an adobo of minced garlic, sour orange juice, olive oil, oregano, salt, and pepper. But Huyke sticks to turkey, brining it first in a mixture of salt, brown sugar, dried bay leaves, fresh herbs, and peppercorns before pushing butter under the skin and brushing the bird with a blend of rum, melted butter, and guava jelly. Huyke preserves the drippings for a tangy-sweet guava-infused gravy. She also shows me how to make ajilímojilí, a highly adaptable, herbaceous sauce of garlic, ají dulce peppers (similar to bell but fruitier and more delicate), culantro, cilantro, olive oil, vinegar, and her own signature addition: a copious amount of capers. Guests will drizzle it over nearly every dish on her Sanguiving table, she tells me.

After hours of cooking and using every imaginable tool, from a traditional pilón to a modern Vitamix blender, we sit down to enjoy the fruits of our frying, molding, steaming, sautéing, and roasting. The result is unmistakably an American Thanksgiving spread, refracted kaleidoscopically through a fresh, colorful Puerto Rican lens.

Recent findings suggest that puerto Ricans have both embraced and resisted US imperialism at various points. There always lingers the question of statehood, which exists alongside the island’s long-standing and active independence movement. As Huyke’s cooking demonstrates, this push-pull relationship only continues to play out in all sorts of dynamic ways.

In a recent development, “I believe every cuisine evolves,” she indicates. “But traditions should be kept and taught. So we do not lose the roots that make us unique.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that david Duchovny has been famous for as long as I have been alive.
  • According to recent reports, duchovny went on to star in Californication, a raunchy dramedy about a divorced novelist navigating the sexually and professionally parasitic Hollywood studio system of the 2000s.
  • In addition to his six books, Duchovny has released four records, and written and directed a number of feature films.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that david Duchovny has been famous for as long as I have been alive. From 1993 to 2002, The X-Files made government conspiracies a staple of primetime television. Duchovny’s FBI special agent Fox Mulder, with his skeptical counterpart, Gillian Anderson’s agent Dana Scully, personified the imminent breakdown of consensus reality in the coming century, delivering the paranoid fringe into 20 million American living rooms. The show belongs to a world of monoculture that no longer exists, and it launched Duchovny into a realm of visibility that’s hard to imagine now, when famous people are produced and consumed at an industrial rate. A few weeks ago, as my boyfriend shopped for a suit jacket at Crowley Vintage in Brooklyn and I edited this story on my phone, I watched a college-age boy put on a long, gray trench coat and announce to his girlfriend: “Mulder mode.”.

According to recent reports, duchovny went on to star in Californication, a raunchy dramedy about a divorced novelist navigating the sexually and professionally parasitic Hollywood studio system of the 2000s. Many viewers interpreted Californication as a kind of autofiction, although Duchovny did not write for the show. The actor has written a number of novels, but it’s apparent to anyone who has spent 30 seconds with him that this soft-spoken, reluctant celebrity has nothing to do with the character Hank Moody. Still, Californication did anticipate something about art, celebrity, and self-commodification: Anybody who writes today must contend with marketing an artistic persona for a public that does not, as a rule, read.

In addition to his six books, Duchovny has released four records, and written and directed a number of feature films. He greets the degraded state of American arts with a charming blend of rigor and self-deprecation. “I’m not Jonathan Franzen,” he states of his fiction-writing process. “But if I work on something every day, it deepens. And eventually, hopefully, I can achieve one tenth of what Jonathan Franzen achieves.” But he has an aversion to the sort of publicity that might make his various artistic ventures more lucrative. He tells me he finds it “spiritually impoverishing.”.

I meet Duchovny with his band—millennial slackers half his age—at their practice space in Carroll Gardens, where they’re preparing to tour their fourth LP, Prince of Pieces. He wears a white Hanes T-shirt, tight underneath his athletic arms, and he has a tattoo on his ankle—a compass pointing west, something he got when his daughter, West, was hospitalized as an infant. (She’s 27 now, an accomplished actor. “She wanted to be a doctor,” he says. “I was so happy when she told me she was going to pursue acting. Thank God.”).

It has been revealed that the albums are composed of subdued, easy-to-listen-to folk-rock tracks, not dissimilar from early Kurt Vile. It’s the band’s first rehearsal in ages, and one of their only chances to prepare in advance of a European tour. In person, they play the songs harder and heavier, sprinkling in crowd-pleasing covers: “Godzilla” by Blue Öyster Cult, “The One I Love” by REM, and—“sadly only one time,” Duchovny says—“Hotline Bling.” The energy in the room is high. These men like one another. Duchovny’s manager offers me a beer from the cooler I’m perched on. I gesture to the tallboy in my purse. He looks disappointed. “You didn’t trust us,” he says. Duchovny steps aside to take a sip of water and picks up the microphone.

“You can sing along,” his keyboardist, Colin Lee, notes.

“I can sing along?” Duchovny asks.

Duchovny at rehearsal with his band.

Sources indicate that at 66, David Duchovny remains a sex symbol. He’s in better shape than he was on The X-Files. He’s in better shape than the boys in the band. The night after practice, during a Q&A for a screening of his 2023 film Reverse the Curse, he mentions that the wardrobe department had to fashion a “BDSM harness” for him to wear under his clothes to remind him to hunch like an old man. He plays a Red Sox fan who bonds with his estranged son over baseball, marijuana, and their shared lust for a beautiful, young death doula. Duchovny’s character has terminal cancer. “I’m in my dying era,” he tells the crowd. “I die in every film. ”.

According to recent reports, for the most part, the audience at Westchester County’s Irvington Theater is old enough to have watched The X-Files as it aired. At least two esoteric-looking old men carry David’s poetry collection like a prayer book. There are a handful of young people. A college-aged girl in a KN95 mask raises her hand to ask about Bucking Fucking Dent, the novel adaptation of the Reverse the Curse screenplay, which Duchovny wrote while the movie was in production purgatory. “In the book, Ted and Marty’s last name is Fullilove. In the movie you change it to Fullaker. Why did you do that?”.

In a recent development, “Good question,” Duchovny states, stalling. “Full of love. Full of shit. It’s all the same.”.

Inevitably, someone asks about the fresh X-Files. Ryan Coogler is rebooting the show for Hulu. Duchovny will later suggest to me that Chris Carter, the show’s original writer, has designs on a reboot of his own—“He has looks, and wants to end with the original show.” As for Coogler’s version, he notes, “I know he noted he wants me to come do something, but we haven’t figured out what yet.” During the audience Q&A, Duchovny seems to have misheard the question, and spoils the ending for The Exiles, his forthcoming Taiwanese crime film: “I die in that one too.”.

Duchovny’s latest book, About Time, a collection of poems published last year by Akashic, is also largely about dying: the death of his father, the death of his first marriage, the ambient death that hung in the air at the beginning of the decade. He started writing the poems when his therapist encouraged him to talk to dead people. “He was talking about Rudolph Steiner’s belief that you can talk to the dead. And he remarked: You can talk to your father and you should. My dad and I didn’t connect like we might have,” Duchovny says. “When you’re younger, you think you have all the time in the world to get the relationship you want. But the relationship doesn’t end.” In conversation, he is cerebral without being annoying. “There’s a power struggle when you read a really good novel,” he says. “Somebody’s mind is taking over your mind. I think about language a lot and how we take it for granted as being an accurate signifier. When I was younger I thought communication was possible. I’m not so sure now. But it’s fun to try.”.

According to recent reports, duchovny’s humility complicates the sexual charisma that still lives at the center of his public persona. His introduction to About Time begins, “I know what you’re thinking: Just what the world needs now—a bunch of poems from an actor.” There’s a sense that he wants to get ahead of the reader’s skepticism. But there’s also plenty of perceptive lines in the poems themselves: “You dreamt you wrote something so good, / so ambivalent and destructive, so creative, / so lacking in morals, decency, or instruction, / so sad and so funny, / so useless and old, / so familiar and new, / so full of theft and power / that they had to name a god after it.” I ask him if good writing is necessarily amoral. He says, “Probably. Which is why any politically correct work of art is usually super successful and really bad. Usually artists are difficult people, and I have no problem separating the art from the artist. But people do now.”.

In college, Duchovny wanted to be a poet. “I thought it was an actual occupation you could have,” he says. When an underclassman turned up in his workshop who was better than him, he quit writing poems on the spot. “It was actually Walter Kirn,” he says. “He showed up at 16-years-old. He was a genius. I was like okay—I’m not a poet.”.

Sources indicate that the two men have become close in the last decade. Kirn, who wrote Up in the Air and founded the newspaper County Highway, tells me what Duchovny was like at Princeton: “He was golden. He had an aura. I was a little starstruck by him.” Duchovny has agreed to play paranormal radio host Art Bell in American Nights, a biopic that Kirn is developing alongside director Alex Lee Moyer. Bell’s Coast to Coast, a cult AM show during the ’80s and ’90s, was beloved by long-haul truckers and compound preppers alike, who called in to report UFO sightings, cattle mutilations, and crop circles. “I, like the rest of my generation, grew up on The X-Files,” Moyer tells me. “It made a massive impression on me, and I’ve been a fan of David ever since. The synchronicity of him being a part of this is not lost on me.”.

I ask Duchovny if he always needed to be the best. “I at least needed to be the best in my class,” he notes.

Industry observers note that in LA, I meet Duchovny in a quiet restaurant to talk about his books. He describes his first novel as “an act of cowardice.” Holy Cow is narrated by an anthropomorphized barnyard animal who uncovers the conspiracy theory that is factory farming. “I thought: Well, they’re not gonna cut me off at the knees on this. Because I’m clearly not that serious. It was calculated. I didn’t want to try for the great American novel the first time as an actor.” The books that followed are more ambitious, each one better than the last. By the time he was promoting his fourth book, 2021’s Truly Like Lightning, he made his ambition plain. “I want to be taken seriously,” he mentioned on Marc Maron’s podcast. “That’s my weakness. I want that book to be taken seriously.”.

“You don’t want people to be like the guy from The X-Files wrote a book,” Maron mentioned.

“That’s what they’re gonna say,” Duchovny remarked, “but I hope and I believe that eventually people will see that I mean business.”.

According to recent reports, truly Like Lightning centers on a Mormon polygamist family forced to enter the godless world of Los Angeles when their homestead is upended. “When I started to read about Mormonism, it struck me as super optimistic. Everyone’s gonna get their own planet and everyone’s gonna be able to propagate souls. As opposed to a European perspective, which was always about the end of something, being 2,000 years removed from this thing. The Mormons noted no, this is still happening.” The novel takes cues from the literary critic Harold Bloom, who wrote that Mormonism was an “American original” and called its founder a “religious genius.” Duchovny studied under Bloom at Yale, where he earned some of an English PhD. “Everything goes back to Bloom,” he says. “And you never really leave grad school. I’m not sure I’ve left grad school. They might still be waiting for my dissertation.”.

But Duchovny did leave grad school. He signed with a talent agent one summer to try to earn some money acting in commercials. His agent told him that if he wanted to go out for theater or film roles, he’d have to get into an acting class. “I remarked: I’m not doing anything. When I stepped into acting class, something happened. I wasn’t a demonstrative person—I was an intellectual person. So it was like: Yeah, be unreasonable. Be irrational. It opened up a different world, a world of fiction, a world without consequences. I’m doing a scene, and I’m yelling at this person and I’m going to murder them, but I don’t have to go to jail.”.

For someone with half a dozen good books and an enormous public profile, it’s surprising there haven’t been more reviews. Johnny Temple, who published Duchovny’s two most recent books on Akashic, tells me, “It’s certainly frustrating that there hasn't been more review coverage of David’s books. For any well-known actor, musician, or other type of public figure, there’s always going to be obstacles to being taken seriously in a different medium.” Kirn tells me, “That makes writing fiction a much purer achievement in my mind. You’re doing this because you love it, and you know that two thirds of your fans will only remember you as a TV character. It’s a brilliant, Sisyphean task. Also, he’s a superb writer.”.

Sources indicate that I ask Duchovny whether he still thinks about being the best. “I think now I can acknowledge that it’s a hollow designation,” he says. “Especially in the arts. Even though we give awards, which is silly. Holy Cow made the Times bestseller list. Ever since, everything I write sells less and less.”.

In a recent development, “It’s hard for someone to champion it,” he adds. “If I wrote a memoir, I’m sure it would get reviewed in the Times.”.

Talking to Duchovny, one is reminded that wanting to be taken seriously and being in on the joke aren’t mutually exclusive. As band practice winds down in Brooklyn, the guys are excited to cover Lou Reed’s “Perfect Day.” Duchovny crosses his arms in front of his lap like a schoolboy as he sings. To my ear it sounds just fine, but Lee, the keyboardist, asks the mixer to lower the reverb on David’s voice.

“Maybe lower David’s mic in general?” the bassist, Mitchell Stewart asks.

“Lower than zero,” Duchovny says. “Less than zero.”.

Recent findings suggest that A few days later, he texts me. He just screened an early cut of Soapbox, a Hollywood satire he wrote and stars in opposite Laverne Cox. At first, he’s bummed that the test audience has decided that his character shouldn’t get killed in the final moments of the movie. But a couple hours later, he writes me again: “People don’t want me to die. I guess I should be flattered.”.

The name is Pattinson—Robert Pattinson.

After a much-talked-about worldwide hunt, the actor was confirmed as the next James Bond. As such, the British star will soon be slipping into 007’s signature slick suits in an upcoming Bond film to be directed by Denis Villeneuve. While it will be a while before we see what stamp Pattinson puts on the beloved franchise, one thing is for certain: His red carpet history definitely proves he’s got the style DNA to play Bond.

For years now, the star has been sticking to wearing a sleek array of suits and tuxedos for his public appearances—a uniform that his new secret agent character almost wears exclusively in the films, too. (Looking good in a tux, after all, is half the job, if not more.) On past red carpets, Pattinson has favored classic black tuxedos and bow ties, but he’s also worn unlined styles with unbuttoned shirts—and no tie!—that feel just a little bit less stuffy.

Pattinson’s effortless approach to tailoring, then, could be a preview to a new era and mood for Bond—something a little more relaxed and contemporary, compared to the rigid, slim-fit suits that past Bonds have worn on-screen. Where Bond goes traditional, Pattinson has favored slouchier-fit silhouettes, undone ties, and chunkier shoes that add a more modern edge to dressing up. It’s all very Bond, but cooler Bond.

Of course, in Hollywood, it’s not uncommon for actors to dress for the part they want—so perhaps Pattinson has been method-dressing to play Bond all along. Or, maybe his innate penchant for suiting up is what got him cast over all of the other auditioning heartthrobs. Whatever the case may be, the actor’s style feels like the correct inspiration for guiding Bond’s wardrobe today. The film’s costume department should start pinning some of Pattinson’s best suiting hits to the mood board now: He is the perfect reference.

In a recent development, from Sean Connery’s immaculately tailored suits in Dr. No to Daniel Craig’s thigh-bearing trunks in Casino Royale, each man who has played James Bond has brought a new aesthetic sensibility to the role. For Connery, this meant soft-shouldered Savile Row tailoring, polo shirts, and knit ties to suit the era of Ivy Style, while Roger Moore’s wardrobe of safari jackets and nylon ski suits embodied the sporty hedonism of the 1970s. In the 21st century, Daniel Craig’s Bond was built around a timely blend of Brioni, Tom Ford, and stalwart British brands that complemented the contemporary #menswear scene. Today’s news that Robert Pattinson—a longtime Dior ambassador and one of the most consistently thrilling dressers in Hollywood—has been cast as 007 suggests Bond’s most fashionable era may be yet to come.

It has been revealed that daniel Craig is no slouch in the clothing department, but before donning the tux for Casino Royale, he was primarily known as a stage actor with a penchant for distressed jeans and Chuck Taylor high-tops. Pattinson, meanwhile, has been the face of Dior’s menswear for a decade, during which he’s established his impeccable taste and a willingness to take significant swings with his outfits—not to mention a reputation for wearing the absolute heck out of a gray suit. Now, with fellow Brit Jonathan Anderson (who cast Craig in Loewe’s quirked-up fall 2024 campaign and posted this heartwarming pic today) running the show at Dior, the stage is set for a Bond with a taste for capital-F fashion.

Tradition dictates a vibe shift whenever a latest Bond is chosen, but whatever James Bond wears has an outsized impact on menswear. Pierce Brosnan’s era had structured Brioni suits and made the Omega Seamaster a star, while Daniel Craig helped cement Tom Ford’s tailoring as a red-carpet staple and juiced sales of N.Peal ribbed Army sweaters and Drake’s suede chukkas. As GQ’s Cam Wolf noted in a 2018 article about Skyfall, Daniel Craig’s Barbour jacket, sweater, jeans, and brogue boots from that film—a classic but fairly unremarkable outfit—became the aspirational template for untold numbers of men on r/malefashionadvice. A few years later, when Craig wore a Rag & Bone slim-fit henley in No Time to Die, the brand sold out of the unassuming undershirt in a matter of days.

It’s been five years since No Time to Die’s release, and it will likely be at least a couple more before Pattinson’s first outing as 007 hits screens. That’s a long wait to see how the next Bond era aesthetic comes together, but given Pattinson’s distinctive approach to fashion, it should be well worth it for the clothes alone.

Ancient European Trees Just Solved a 3,500-Year-Old Cold Case: When Did Babylon Fall?

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (665 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mesopotamia in the second millennium B.C.E.
  • Babylon may be best known today from sacred texts, from the Hebrew Bible to the Quran.
  • On paper, Mesopotamia should be easy to date.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mesopotamia in the second millennium B.C.E. left behind an unusually rich written record. Yet historians still can’t agree on exact dates. Rival chronologies hinge on when Babylon fell, and they disagree about that by more than a century, so it’s hard to line up events across the Near East and eastern Mediterranean.

Babylon may be best known today from sacred texts, from the Hebrew Bible to the Quran. But long before those books were written, the fabled city on the Euphrates was the capital of one of the ancient world’s great powers. It was home to King Hammurabi, whose law code ranks among the oldest written legal systems on record.

On paper, Mesopotamia should be easy to date. Scribes left behind king lists, administrative records, and royal inscriptions that lay out what happened and in what order. The catch is that they counted time by kings’ reigns, not calendar years, so the whole sequence had no fixed link to dates we’d recognize.

Venus should have fixed that. Babylonian scribes watched the sky for omens, believing the planets’ movements foretold harvests, wars, and the fate of the king. During the reign of King Ammisaduqa, they wrote down when Venus appeared and disappeared on the horizon, dating each sighting by year of his reign. Because Ammisaduqa also appears in the king lists, those sightings tie the whole sequence of kings to the sky, and modern astronomers can work out when they could have happened.

According to recent reports, the trouble is that Venus repeats itself, so the observations fit several possible points in history. That left four rival timelines (high, middle, low, and ultra-low) that place Babylon’s fall as much as 150 years apart.

The key witness turned out to be wood. Timbers from ancient buildings in Anatolia, in modern-day Turkey, had tree rings that could be lined up in order, but no one could pin that sequence to actual calendar years. Yet those same sites are tied to Mesopotamia through the Old Assyrian trade network, whose merchants left records that line up with Mesopotamian kings. So dating the wood would date the history, too.

Recent findings suggest that now, researchers believe they’ve done just that. In a study published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, the team wrote that they used “patterns captured in single-year radiocarbon measurements from tree rings to calendar-date Anatolian wood samples from sites with direct archaeological links to Mesopotamia.”.

According to recent reports, led by Charlotte Pearson of the Laboratory of Tree-Ring Research at the University of Arizona, the team measured carbon-14 in single annual growth rings from the Anatolian timbers. They partnered with ETH Zurich’s Laboratory of Ion Beam Physics to make the measurements.

To anchor the Anatolian wood, the team turned to precisely dated Tyrolean stone pine from Austria and oak from Germany. That pinned the Anatolian tree-ring sequence to the calendar, with each ring now tied to a specific year from 2072 to 744 B.C.E. The payoff reaches beyond Mesopotamia. “These data can now be used for samples from anywhere else in the world,” Kurt Nicolussi of the University of Innsbruck told Austria’s public broadcaster, ORF, in a translated report.

“Tree-ring dates are combined with archaeological and high-resolution ice-core evidence to evaluate the competing chronological frameworks for Mesopotamia between 2000 and 1500 B.C.E.,” the authors wrote.

The verdict: The Old Babylonian Empire fell in 1587 B.C.E. The authors found “strong support” for what they call a middle-low chronology, a timeline that falls between the middle and low models.

“This illustrates how high-precision radiocarbon methods, in combination with other interdisciplinary evidence, can enhance chronological accuracy across many time periods,” the authors wrote.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

No holiday table—or really any dinner table, for that matter—is truly complete without a substantial side of creamy, buttery mashed potatoes. While it may seem like simple, classic comfort food, there are a few ways to take mashed potatoes from good to great. That's why we retested this recipe again and again until we achieved potato perfection.

It has been revealed that what People Are Saying:"So good! I don’t typically like sour cream on its own but it was a huge improvement for basic mashed potatoes. Will definitely be making this again." – PurpleStrawberry.

It has been revealed that "Easily my go-to mashed potato recipe. I've made it for Thanksgiving, and got requests to make it again. It's so good, doesn't even need gravy." – kitkat123.

Really, the only chopping you'll have to do is cut up the potatoes. I do suggest peeling them (more on that later), and be sure to try to cut the potatoes into equal-sized pieces so they cook evenly. Around 1" chunks are ideal. Time to cook 'em! In testing, I found that covering the potatoes with cold water first yields the best consistency and ensures the potatoes don't become too mushy. Don't forget to add a pinch of salt to the water! Let the potatoes cook until softened—the best way to test is to use a paring knife and make sure it can be inserted with no resistance. This should take about 20 minutes. Make sure to drain when they're done so they don't overcook.

Now comes the fun part: Mashing the potatoes until smooth. You can use a masher, a ricer, or even a handheld mixer for this step. I think the smoother, the better, but you do you, of course.

On to what makes these potatoes the best ever: Heat up some whole milk and butter until the butter is melted in a pot.

Then, pour over the still-warm potatoes and mix to combine. Then add the sour cream, some salt, and pepper, and you're basically good to go! Mix everything well, transfer to your prettiest serving bowl, and proceed with the finishing touches: a couple of pieces of butter to melt into the potatoes, plus fresh parsley for some color and brightness. Brace yourself for the compliments.

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

According to recent reports, if you have any leftovers, store them in an airtight container in the fridge for a max of 3 to 4 days. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Before Anthony Boyle and I begin our interview, we’ve already covered a fair amount of ground. Serendipitously, we’ve ridden up alongside each other on our bicycles. Boyle is still acquainting himself with the city’s two-wheeled possibilities; he’s a recent but enthusiastic convert. “It opens up the world!” he declares.

Recent findings suggest that our first stop is a tiny gallery in east London, where an exhibition of contemporary Irish art is on display. Boyle, a Belfast transplant, has lived in London off and on for the past few years. “Is that the Significant Fish? It’s surely the Big Fish,” Boyle asks of one painting, invoking the giant salmon sculpture that sits on the waterfront in Belfast. The actor is wearing jeans, low-profile sneakers, and a blue T-shirt with a horse printed on the back, a recent impulse purchase—it reminds him of childhood summer vacations spent riding in Donegal.

Recently, Boyle, 32, has established himself with his shrewd portrayal of IRA commander Brendan “The Dark” Hughes in the TV series Say Nothing and his assured turn as the flamboyant Arthur Guinness in Steven Knight’s House of Guinness. Earlier this year, the film I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning—in which Boyle plays a college-educated food-delivery cyclist—premiered to impassioned reviews at Cannes. “The film feels like a socialist war cry,” Boyle notes, describing its portrayal of working-class communities in modern Britain.

In a recent development, and this November, he took another exhilarating left turn, starring opposite Julia Garner in Netflix’s The Altruists, an eight-part series about the spectacular collapse of the cryptocurrency exchange FTX—and one of a handful of fresh films and TV series that spin our recent techno-history into entertainment. Boyle plays the tech giant’s disgraced founder, Sam Bankman-Fried, whose dizzying ascent and precipitous downfall have made him a hubristic emblem of the crypto age. The show casts Bankman-Fried and his on-again, off-again girlfriend and colleague Caroline Ellison (Garner) as hyperintelligent idealists, at once fiercely competitive and committed to “effective altruism”—a philosophical movement that seeks to optimize charitable giving.

Recent findings suggest that the awkward physicality, unruly hair, and peculiar vocal inflections that Boyle brought to the role are a world away from the steely conviction of an IRA soldier or the patrician swagger of a Guinness. For his first meeting with The Altruists’ creators, he went to the budget retailer Primark, bought a black sweater, smeared it with Cup Noodle stains, and mussed his hair. He logged onto Zoom in character, improvising that he had Mark Zuckerberg waiting on another call. His childhood friend and Say Nothing costar Lola Petticrew, with whom he rehearsed, offered invaluable feedback. “When you do that voice, I want to throw a cup of tea over you,” Boyle remembers Petticrew saying. He was delighted. “There’s an inner conflict in him that makes his performances unpredictable,” says Garner. “Whatever he’s thinking or feeling, you can see it in his eyes. You can’t teach someone to have those eyes.”.

Industry observers note that once he was offered the role, Boyle watched footage of Bankman-Fried, fascinated by an awkwardness at odds with his extraordinary influence. He even corresponded with Bankman-Fried in prison: “This is the smartest person I’ve ever been in contact with,” he says of their exchange. “People don’t think they’re doing evil,” Boyle says, reflecting on Bankman-Fried’s motivations. “They believe they’re doing things for the greater good.”.

PARALLEL LINES Anthony Boyle wears a Dries Van Noten sweater, JW Anderson jeans, and Paul Smith belt.

It has been revealed that as a boy in West Belfast, Boyle trained at the Royal Welsh College of Music & Drama before his onstage breakout at age 21 as Scorpius Malfoy in Harry Potter and the Cursed Child, which earned him an Olivier Award. “Before that, my longest play was a five-day run at a community center,” he says. In addition to his striking Say Nothing and House of Guinness performances, Boyle’s career has encompassed roles in the World War II drama Masters of the Air and the John Wilkes Booth–inspired series Manhunt. “I met with a bunch of cowboys,” he says of that role, “it took me a while to lose the habit of picking up random things, chewing, spitting them out.” He delights in the contrasts in his work: “I’m always trying to do what I haven’t done,” he says. As we walk through the park, a few men practicing martial arts catch Boyle’s attention, and he acquires a pair of nunchucks, giving them a whirl with enough confidence that I can’t discern whether this is a genuine skill or a gloriously committed bluff. “Pretty good, right?” he asks.

Since The Altruists finished shooting last November, Boyle completed the forthcoming dark comedy The Worst (with Keira Knightley and Alicia Vikander) and has been filming Charmer, a newly introduced series in which he plays a professional seducer hired to test the fidelity of his wealthy clients’ partners. Next comes a second season of House of Guinness, with just two days off between filming. “I need to find little bits of joy and craic where I can,” he says.

One of those joys is returning home. Boyle has lived in London and New York and recently moved back to Belfast, although his schedule means he seldom spends much time there. Recently at a McDonald’s with his cousin, Boyle’s order was supersized without any prompting. “Anything for The Dark,” the server said—a reference to his Say Nothing role, and, Boyle reckons, just about the coolest thing that could have happened on his home turf. He’s been honored by his hometown in additional ways: Belfast artist Colin Davidson recently painted his portrait and unveiled it at the city’s Lyric Theatre. Davidson offered him some sage advice while the actor was sitting for him: “He said, ‘Never soften your edges, Anthony.’ ”.

According to recent reports, “Coming from where we come from, this career seemed a world away, but seeing him chase it made it feel more tangible for me,” says Petticrew. Working together on Say Nothing, Petticrew adds, was meaningful beyond the acting: “To reflect the place we both love so deeply and tell its story was probably one of the most crucial things we’ll ever do.”.

An upcoming project will bring Boyle even nearer to his origins. In a four-part adaptation of Michael Magee’s acclaimed 2023 novel Close to Home, he plays Sean, a young man returning to a Belfast reckoning with the aftermath of the sectarian violence of the Troubles. Boyle attended the same school as Magee a few years apart, and the novel depicts a world Boyle recognizes—down to the hardscrabble streets and poorly paid nightclub jobs. “I felt like someone was reaching out of the book and grabbing me,” he says. “It articulated thoughts and experiences I thought only I had.” Boyle urged the book on everyone around him. “I bought a hundred copies,” he says—one Christmas, he distributed 10 among his family. “None of them opened it.” Television, he realized, might be a way to get the story into their lives.

In a recent development, playing Sean demanded a fresh methodology from Boyle: “It was almost coming back to myself in a way and not performing,” he notes. Boyle, who is also executive producing the series, championed local talent and developed it closely with Magee, running scenes with him until the dialogue felt lived-in. “I wanted to make Close to Home for people in the areas I grew up in.”.

We’re wrapping up our walk when he tells me he is meeting his father to help his younger sister move apartments. She recently arrived in London for college and was temporarily living in his house with a friend while looking for a place of her own. Boyle would leave for work before dawn and return late to find them blasting Sinéad O’Connor and dancing in the kitchen. “It was infectious,” he notes. We’re now in front of Hackney City Farm, a cloistered urban oasis with livestock and gardens. His new T-shirt has reminded him how much he misses riding, and he wants to know where in London he can get on a horse. When I mention that the farm has donkeys, he’s thrilled: “I love a donkey.”.

A week later, I run into Boyle again, shouting to me as I bike past. This time he’s accompanied by his older sibling and their partner. He’s showing them around before heading to Newly introduced York for The Altruists press tour. Swaggering along the road, he is just as buoyant as before, taking himself off on another adventurous detour.

In a recent development, marvel has filled most of the seats for its latest X-Men film. Sadie Sink is Jean Grey, Kit Connor is Cyclops, Christopher Abbott is Professor X, Samara Weaving is Emma Frost, Inde Navarrette is Rogue, and Maya Boyd is Storm. But there’s still one grizzly gap in the line-up: Wolverine.

According to recent reports, earlier this month, Jeremy Allen White was linked with the role after insider Jeff Sneider reported that he had met with Marvel about a small part that could become much bigger later on. Nobody has confirmed that the part is Wolverine (and Sneider has since stressed that White isn’t officially in talks) but the internet did the math pretty rapidly. And now there’s a smoking gun: facial hair.

According to recent reports, while walking around the Studio City Farmers Market over the weekend (because, of course), The Social Reckoning star was spotted carrying a bouquet of flowers bigger than his torso and wearing some extremely Wolverine-y mutton chops. Normally, growing out your sideburns wouldn’t count as casting news. But when you’ve just been linked with Logan and suddenly look ready to join the X-Men, people are going to ask questions.

It has been revealed that white would make a lot of sense. He’s 5’7”, which puts him much closer to the comic book Wolverine’s famously stocky 5’3” frame than Hugh Jackman ever was. He also spent months getting absolutely massive for The Iron Claw, so the muscle is already there. And after years of watching him play Carmy in The Bear, we know he can do angry and exhausted and permanently one minor inconvenience away from losing it. That’s basically three quarters of the Wolverine job description.

In a recent development, jackman has owned the role since the first X-Men film landed in 2000. He’s played Wolverine across 10 movies, most recently returning for 2024’s Deadpool & Wolverine. His version became so definitive that it’s difficult to picture anyone else with the claws (other than the time Troye Sivan briefly had them in 2009’s X-Men Origins: Wolverine), even though the 6’2" actor looked very different from the shorter character drawn in the OG comics.

Maybe White just fancied some giant sideburns. Maybe the flowers are covering three adamantium claws. Either way, Marvel should probably give him a call—assuming it hasn’t already.

Tech Report: No Central Air? No Sweat. These Tested Window Air Conditioners Cool Down Spaces Fast
