📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

If you’re a fan of soft, crunchy, chewable ice, a countertop nugget ice maker can bring that sought-after texture right to your kitchen. Also known as pellet or “Sonic” ice, nugget ice is made of compacted flakes that are soft, airy, and easy to munch on and slow to melt. It’s especially good for soaking up the flavor of whatever you’re drinking, making it a favorite for everything from sodas and cocktails to iced coffee and just plain, old water.

Nugget ice makers have become increasingly popular home appliances, but the machines themselves can be relatively advanced. They require more complex internal components than basic ice makers, and thus tend to cost more—often starting around $400 for a high-quality design. Depending on the appliance, you’ll also find features like large ice baskets, water reservoirs, self-cleaning cycles, and high daily production.

To help you find the right machine for your kitchen and budget, we researched, tested, and reviewed the best nugget ice makers from manufacturers such as GE, Euhomy, and Gevi. Whether you’re entertaining friends or just ready to retire the built-in ice maker on your fridge, these are the models we recommend.

The selection of countertop nugget ice makers available from trusted and reliable brands is limited, so we dug to find and test the best options by considering product specs, capabilities, and prices. During testing, we ran cleaning cycles to get the systems ready to go. We then timed how long it took for each machine to produce one batch of ice, and again for how long it took to fill the ice basket completely.

Industry observers note that throughout our setup and testing, we evaluated each model’s ease of use, reliability, and the quality of the ice they made. We took note of any cool or unique features like app compatibility, storage options, and more.

Our home appliance writer, Nick Hilden, also spoke with Jessica Randhawa, founder and head chef at the Forked Spoon, and Yu Jiang Zhao, mixologist, about what to keep in mind when choosing a nugget ice maker.

It has been revealed that this was the nugget ice maker that made our tester throw out their ice trays once and for all. It takes everything we liked about the previous version, GE Profile Opal 2.0, and boosts the ice production speed, upgrades a smattering of components and functions to make it easier to clean and enhance its lifespan, and includes an external water tank and ice scoop to boot.

According to recent reports, we’ve found that it churns out ice at a rapid enough pace to keep round after round of cold beverages for a sizable gathering. It has an easy-to-use app that offers smart functions such as scheduling alerts for maintenance. Additionally, its sleek design has a timeless vibe that won’t look dated two years from now.

Recent findings suggest that it’s got a footprint nearly that of two shoeboxes side by side, which is a bit major for a smaller kitchen. It can also get somewhat noisy when it’s actively producing ice—about the volume of a loud refrigerator—though it’s basically silent when it’s just keeping it cool. But if you’re looking for reliable, convenient ice on demand, there’s none better.

Full GE Profile Opal 2.0 Ultra Nugget Ice Maker Review.

Industry observers note that this little unit packs a surprising amount of ice production power, churning out as much or more than any of the larger models on our list (40 pounds per day). Additionally, its compact size makes it perfect when you have less countertop real estate to spare, or if you want portable ice production for a backyard barbecue or camping in an RV.

It has been revealed that our testing found that it churns out ice fast, with the first batch in under ten minutes. Its operation is as straightforward as they come, and its cleaning is easier than most other machines, with an automatic cleaning mode that requires little effort on your part besides draining out the water that runs through the system.

It has been revealed that all told, it’s a great ice maker for anyone who wants a no-fuss model that will look nice in the kitchen without taking up too much space. It also offers similar performance to larger, more expensive models, minus the roomy storage capacity.

Full Euhomy Smart Countertop Nugget Ice Maker Review.

Recent findings suggest that the Gevi 2.0 is the kind of ice maker you won’t mind taking up prime countertop real estate, given its polished design. The bin holds almost five pounds of ice (the largest capacity on our list), and the machine has thick insulation on all sides to keep cubes frozen for longer.

One of our favorite features is the door on the ice maker that opens to a 90-degree angle. To achieve this, the Gevi ditches the viewing window that’s present on other models, but this design choice allows you to pull the ice basket forward. This made it very simple to scoop our pellet ice once the container was full.

It has been revealed that the instruction manual claims that it takes about 15 to 30 minutes for the first cubes to form, but I noticed a couple of pellets had dropped around the 9-minute and 20-second mark. They were fairly wet to start but began forming more compactly over time and were the perfect, crunchy texture. However, it takes a few hours to get a full basket, which is tricky if you need ice immediately.

The water reservoir is kind of awkward to access with the door style, but the Gevi also comes with a hose that hooks up to your tap if you want it to fill automatically.

According to recent reports, ice makers require regular cleaning to ensure both quality ice and a long lifespan for the unit, and we found that the Silonn Nugget Ice Maker makes it easier than the rest. Most notable is its self-cleaning function, which is as effortless as it gets: Push a button to start the clean cycle, and let it do its thing. This is unlike other models that require removing a lot of parts or going through a complex series of steps. We also like that you can just toss its removable water reservoir and ice bin in the dishwasher, with no hoses or bottles to clean.

In terms of operation, it delivers most everything you want from a solid ice maker. It produces a hefty 44 pounds of ice a day, and its 2.6-pound bin holds plenty of ice for several rounds of drinks. It’s straightforward and intuitive to use—all you need to do is fill it with water—and is somewhere in the middle in terms of countertop footprint.

According to recent reports, it does produce more noise than other popular models. Most nugget ice makers crank the volume up when actually producing ice, but this one has a noticeable hum even when on standby. For reliable ice with no-hassle cleaning, however, it’s hard to beat.

Sources indicate that one of the key benefits to a good nugget ice maker is that it can churn out upward of 30 or even 40 pounds a day, making it ideal for hosting large, thirsty groups. The best models can have the first cubes ready within about 10 minutes, and will have a full bin within an hour or so.

A countertop machine, of course, can’t store three dozen pounds of ice. Most ice bins hold 1 to 3 pounds, which will replenish as depleted. It’s rare to go through a full bin, so unless you expect to host a particularly large number of people, this may not be the most pressing concern.

The vast majority of home nugget ice makers are equipped with a built-in water reservoir. These are great for at-home use as they don’t require installation and are highly portable, making it easy to pack them away for storage.

Industry observers note that the larger the tank, the more ice the machine will produce. However, this also means that it will require more counter space. Models with smaller water reservoirs eat up less room, but require you to refill them frequently.

You can plug some models directly into your home plumbing system, which eliminates the need to fill a tank as it will draw water continuously. These, however, may require expert installation depending on your DIY skills, and will usually end up in a cabinet or closet rather than on your countertop.

Sources indicate that the bigger the ice maker, the more countertop space it uses, so consider how much room you have in your kitchen. Our top pick, the GE Opal 2.0, is a great ice maker, but it has a pretty big footprint for a kitchen with limited counter real estate. When measuring dimensions, don’t forget about the inch or two of clearance that you’ll need for the fan, which keeps the motor from overheating.

If you have the space for it, Randhawa recommends placing the model in the pantry. This not only keeps your countertops open, but can muffle the operating noise.

Recent findings suggest that “With most nugget ice machines you should expect some sound when operating on standby, but they can get pretty noisy when producing ice,” says Randhawa. “That might not matter in the din and clatter of cocktail hour, but could be more bothersome when things quiet down.”.

It’s difficult to determine how loud a particular model will be without actually hearing it as there is no standardized noise rating. Your best bet is to check reviews for what previous buyers or reviewers have to say.

Sources indicate that nugget ice makers use a large metal cylinder with an auger inside that freezes as the machine runs. Water then pours into the cylinder and starts to freeze along the walls, producing a thin sheet of ice that the auger scrapes and pushes through the machine as ice flakes.

Sources indicate that the machine then squeezes the flakes to push out excess water and compacts them into small, airy pieces so that what you end up with is a soft, porous nugget of ice that (probably) won’t crack your teeth when you chew it. They’re ideal for beverages because they take on the flavor of the drink, and there’s really nothing quite like that taste and texture.

Unfortunately, nugget ice makers aren’t ready to use right out of the box. Once you’ve gotten your unit, it’s best to let it sit upright on a level surface for at least two hours before plugging it in. This helps the refrigerant settle. The time may vary depending on the model you have, so it’s best to refer to the manual for the specific time.

It has been revealed that you should also run the self-cleaning or sanitizing cycle before getting started. A combination of equal parts water and vinegar can get the job done. By doing this, you’re clearing the machine of any lingering residue or grime that could affect the clarity and taste of the ice. After completing a cycle with the solution, you can run another one with just water for a full wash-down.

Nugget ice makers are not a set-it-and-forget-it machine—they require regular cleaning and additional upkeep. One of the main concerns with these appliances is calcium buildup, or limescale, which accumulates if you have hard tap water.

To prevent this, it’s a good rule of thumb to occasionally descale your ice maker. You can make a 1:1 solution of distilled white vinegar and water, put it in the reservoir, and run it through the machine for a few cycles. Another tip is to use filtered water.

Industry observers note that self-cleaning modes should be run at least once a month, but if you’re a frequent party host, every other week couldn’t hurt. If you’re using a nugget ice maker that hooks up to a water line, you would benefit from an inline filter. Vacuuming the fan and blowing out the condenser also prevents clogs from dust and debris that may cause overheating.

Nugget ice makers make anywhere from 24 to 44 pounds of ice in a 24-hour period. They start up relatively promptly (as little as 10 minutes) but may take up to an hour to fully fill the ice bin.

Models with large capacity bins are best for big groups, while smaller ones are good for home bars and entertaining a couple of friends. Some options have ice bins that are insulated to keep ice from melting, while others just have an acrylic bucket in which ice melts faster.

Recent findings suggest that for those that regularly host large gatherings or just don’t want to run out of nugget ice, we suggest running your nugget ice maker the day before and storing nugget ice in the freezer. Alternatively, you could stockpile extra nugget ice just in case you’re burning through more than expected the day of your event.

Industry observers note that most nugget ice machines are countertop units, so special installation isn’t necessary. We’ve specifically recommended models that don’t require you to install them, as the vast majority of owners will want something user-friendly and easy to store when not in use. Typically speaking, ice makers that require installation are heavy-duty, professional-grade units for serving large groups of people.

According to Randhawa, “Most nugget ice machines just use a standard outlet and require space around it to vent per the instructions.” Without proper ventilation space, your unit could overheat and break down.

“[Nugget ice makers] run compressors constantly and consume more power than people think it should for a countertop appliance,” notes Zhao. “If energy consumption is a concern to you, look for those with an Energy Star rating, and factor in that it will likely be running a good portion of the day.”.

Newer models tend to need about 0.05 to 1 kilowatt-hour per day, depending on your ice use. The more ice you make, the more power you’ll need. That’s roughly the equivalent of an energy-efficient fridge, which increases electric bills by about $10 to $15 a month.

If you always want ice at the ready, then you’ll have to run your nugget ice maker at all times, but it’ll likely shut off once the bin is full. “This is a normal operating procedure,” says Zhao. “Turning it off and on [manually] every day reduces its life and means you are waiting 15 to 20 minutes for your first batch every day.”.

Sources indicate that however, these machines don’t technically need to run year-round if you’re worried about possibly running up your electric bill. “You can turn them off and put them away when you don’t strategy on using them,” states Randhawa. “We put ours away during vacations and over the winter, after the temperature drops, which is generally when we don’t want ice in our drinks.”.

The Data Highlights It: The Faux Fur-Trimmed Coat Is the Coat of the Season

📅 15 Jan 2024 | ⏱️ 4 min read (856 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A very specific coat has taken the internet and fashion people alike by storm.
  • Industry observers note that with searches for the designer up 967% on The RealReal, vintage dealers racing to list their versions, and creatives DIYing it at home, it’s safe to call this the coat of the season.
  • Industry observers note that “The coat taps into a growing appetite for pieces that feel expressive and one-of-a-kind, qualities that have always made vintage compelling,” states Noelle Sciacca, head of fashion at The RealReal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A very specific coat has taken the internet and fashion people alike by storm. Conner Ives’s robe coat looks like a piece pulled from a 1920s opera house coat check, and everyone from Sienna Miller to Zoë Kravitz have worn iterations of it. First introduced in his fall 2025 collection, it pairs antique silk with reclaimed fox at the lapels and cuffs, and sells for a cool $9,000. And it’s in extremely high demand.

Industry observers note that with searches for the designer up 967% on The RealReal, vintage dealers racing to list their versions, and creatives DIYing it at home, it’s safe to call this the coat of the season. While the Ives version might top many of our wish lists (and budgets), its essence is rooted in the feeling of a bygone era, maybe one we’re craving more than ever these days, if the style is any indication.

Industry observers note that “The coat taps into a growing appetite for pieces that feel expressive and one-of-a-kind, qualities that have always made vintage compelling,” states Noelle Sciacca, head of fashion at The RealReal. “We’re seeing a real shift toward everyday opulence, rich textures, and a sense of history,” she shares. “The Conner Ives coat captures that mood. It feels glamorous and eccentric, but still effortless enough to throw over jeans.”.

The proof for demand is in the data. According to Sciacca, searches for fur-trimmed jackets and coats are up 33% year-over-year, while jacquard searches have increased 60% and tapestry prints have surged 170%. “What’s great is shoppers don’t necessarily need the exact coat to capture the look. They’re exploring vintage and archival pieces across designers and decades, looking for ornate prints, beautiful fabrics, and unexpected details.”.

Retailers are also quickly catching on with similar-style coats from Ciao Lucia, Rixo, Doen, and Maison Essentiele selling out within days of appearing live on their sites. “I had a gut-feeling that it [the Taimi Satin Bouquet coat] would be a top-seller,” Lucy Akin, founder of Ciao Lucia, shares with us. “It was validating to not only see it sell-out so quickly, but also have my entire Instagram feed flooded with these vintage inspired jackets. They are having a moment, no doubt!”.

Stylist Bailey Moon echoes this. “I think there’s a real appetite for clothes that have personality again,” he notes. “The Conner Ives coat taps into a sense of nostalgia, but it also feels playful and a little irreverent, which I think is part of its appeal.” That’s also what separates it from the Penny Lane coat. Where that style reads bohemian and casual, this one trades suede for silk and leans closer to evening wear, so the rest of the outfit has to do less.

According to recent reports, “Fur and shearling inherently have a sense of drama, so I prefer to let the coat be the centerpiece and keep everything else relatively understated,” Moon shares. “A great pair of trousers, beautiful knitwear, or even a simple dress can make the look feel incredibly modern. I love the contrast of something quite extravagant paired with something very utilitarian.”.

Laura Harrier in a short Conner Ives coat.

Recent findings suggest that but the appeal extends beyond ornament. Memory and timelessness, play a part, too. Nour Hammour’s Sima Coat was designed after founder Nour Hammour’s grandmother’s coat, and the way she carried herself in it. “It is the balance between exceptional materials, craftsmanship, and a silhouette that will remain relevant long after the season has passed,” shares marketing director Zeina El Zein Hammour. “The quality of the shearling, the depth of the trim, and the way the coat falls on the body are what distinguish a piece that you’ll keep for decades.”.

For vintage hounds, it’s also a real marker of the shift away from all-neutral everything that’s dominated for so long. “After years of quiet luxury and minimalism, I think people are ready for a little romance and extravagance,” says Susan Kim of Estella NYC, who sells similar vintage iterations on her site and at vintage fairs.

Kendall Jenner wearing a Conner Ives duster.

Secondhand enthusiast and influencer Katie Casper tried her hand at recreating the coat using pieces she already owned, a Shanghai Tang silk jacket from her mother-in-law and a removable fur stole from an old Zara coat. “In its simplest terms, the coat is a colorful brocade base with a fur trim,” she states. “Both are easy to source secondhand.” The trickiest part was proportion, she says, since the stole overpowered the jacket and she’d choose a narrower one next time.

It has been revealed that whether the style lasts beyond this season is another question. “I fear we may all be a little exhausted by 2027,” Casper muses. But Moon sees it differently. “A beautiful statement coat can live in someone’s wardrobe for years,” he says. “The question is whether you’re buying it because you genuinely love it or because you’ve seen it on everyone else. The best clothes should still feel exciting to wear long after they’ve stopped being the thing everyone is talking about.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Take the edge off those chilly winter nights without ballooning your energy bill.
  • The top space heaters run quietly and efficiently, offer multiple heating levels, and come with safety features like automatic shut-off for accidental tipping.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Take the edge off those chilly winter nights without ballooning your energy bill. Space heaters offer immediate warmth for cozy nights in the bedroom and for brisk days in a drafty office. The small radius of heat also makes them ideal for improving the temperature in your immediate surroundings without wasting energy turning up the thermostat and heating the entire house. Some even double as fans during the summer.

The top space heaters run quietly and efficiently, offer multiple heating levels, and come with safety features like automatic shut-off for accidental tipping. We researched and tested the most promising models from brands like Vornado, Lasko, and Dreo. Below, you’ll find our selections for the most efficient, durable, and safest space heaters out there.

It has been revealed that we tested space heaters by first evaluating each model based on important factors like safety, setting variety, and size. We paid attention to how well the appliances were able to warm up a space by using them around our homes and offices. We also took note of the number of heat settings each unit had and the temperature range they offered.

According to recent reports, to evaluate the unit’s heat capabilities, we took into account its temperature range and wattage, and prioritized heaters that offered a broad range with good control and output of at least 1,200 watts or more. We’ve made a point to include options that operate via remote-controlled desktops and smart picks that come with a companion app as well.

For heaters that we haven’t had the chance to try in person, we heavily vetted specs and assessed each space heater based on the same factors we used during testing.

Lasko calls the CW100 bladeless because it doesn’t technically have a fan, per se. Instead, it uses a multi-vane impeller. That design contributes to the appliance’s quiet operation because it pulls in air through its base and into the tower. It comes with a cleanable air filter, which is accessible via a tool-free hatch at the back of the heater—no tools required.

We appreciate the slick touchpad on the front for adjusting the wattage for the heating element, tower oscillation, and the eight-hour timer. The space heater only has two actual heat settings—high and low—but there is a manual thermostat for controlling temperatures, which helps make up for the lack of power options.

In a recent development, the wide window of airflow and consistent heat distribution helps bring a room up to temp faster than most space heaters on this list, and this unit covers up to 300 square feet. One gripe: The battery hatch cover on the remote is tricky to remove. There is a holster for that remote control, though, making for one tidy package.

Full Lasko Oscillating Bladeless Ceramic Tower Space Heater Review.

For a low-cost option, the Vornado MVH Vortex Heater heats a surprisingly large area—up to 256 square feet—with minimal noise. This unit worked well in a bedroom that has exterior walls on five sides, even during cold overnight temperatures. We like how simple, compact, and lightweight this unit is, and the appliance case stays cool to the touch, so you can move it around safely without concern.

Industry observers note that the unit’s controls are a miss for us, though. While we liked the simple on/off button and the three-position toggle for heat levels, the thermostat dial is vague. The numbers on this dial range from 1 to 7, which don’t really show how warm each setting is.

Recent findings suggest that as a result, we had to experiment with different settings until we figured out what worked best for us (you’ll likely have to do the same). Despite this drawback, the thermostat feature is helpful for when temperatures dip or get too high, as it manages the unit’s auto shutoff/on feature.

Full Vornado MVH Vortex Space Heater Review.

It’s rare to come across a space heater that oscillates both horizontally and vertically, and that’s the feature we liked the most while testing the Dreo Whole Room Heater. It rotates 60 degrees up and down and 90 degrees from side to side for noticeably more coverage. Better yet, you can use both oscillation modes at the same time.

This space heater also has three heat and fan settings, and we appreciated being able to control the fan speed separately, even if we were running on high heat. Temperatures range from 41 to 95 degrees Fahrenheit, so we were able to truly customize the output. We kept our space heater at 73°F a majority of the time, and we never felt overheated or chilly.

According to recent reports, the space heater comes with a remote, but there’s also a control panel on the base of the unit. The main thing we don’t like is that the remote was a little confusing to navigate at first. You have to use one button to access the fan speeds, heat levels, and temperatures, so we found ourselves clicking through a few times to get to the setting we wanted.

Full Dreo Whole Home Room Heater Review.

In a recent development, if your office is generally cold, then a heater small enough to sit on your desk might be the perfect solution for dealing with the frigid temperatures of your building. At only 12 inches tall, the Ellipse ceramic heater from Lasko is truly a compact model— discreet enough to tuck into the corner or underneath a workspace.

Sources indicate that the highest settings pump out powerful heat in seconds, but there are medium and low settings if you want toned-down warmth. Temperatures are adjustable through the touch panel on the space heater.

We appreciate that even though this is a smaller design, it comes with its own remote. You can make the space heater oscillate and conveniently set a timer with the press of a couple buttons, and everything is viewable from the LED panel on the front.

The only thing we didn’t particularly like is that the Ellipse turns on at the highest setting automatically, so you’ll have to make adjustments almost immediately to find the ideal temperature and power.

Recent findings suggest that A tech-facing space heater certainly has its benefits. The Lasko Therma-Smart tower heater has WiFi connectivity and pairs with the Aria home app for a virtual remote.

In a recent development, connecting the heater was fairly easy: simply hold the WiFi button on the space heater for five seconds so it enters “pairing mode,” and then connect the device to the app. You can see wattage use and heat levels, and there’s a temperature dial in the center of the page to adjust to your liking. The Therma-Smart heater also pairs with Google and Alexa if you prefer to use voice commands.

Otherwise, the space heater has similar settings to other Lasko models that we recommend, like touch-sense controls and a digital window for viewing purposes. There are low, medium, and high heat settings, a max heat output of 1,500 watts, and a 12-hour timer function for running most of the day. One thing we noticed is that the oscillating feature seems to move very slowly, so you still might get hit with targeted heat if you’re sitting directly in front of the heater before it starts the rotation again.

The Lasko 751320 Ceramic Tower Heater is a reliable, mid-range option for homes and offices. Tester and Popular Mechanics editor Tom Price loves this model for its versatility. “The tower design and mid-sized build mean you can comfortably place it on a coffee table in the living room without it taking over the space. At the same time, it isn’t so small that I don’t feel the heat in larger spaces.”.

The space heater has programmable controls that will turn the unit off and on after a certain period of time (or once the room has reached the desired temperature). It’s also equipped with an oscillating mode and comes with a multi-functioning remote control, too.

Although the gate on the front of the heater is designed to be cool to the touch, one aspect to keep in mind is that this unit does not come with an auto shutoff feature in case it gets tipped over.

In a recent development, A cold bathroom early in the morning feels like punishment, but a space heater on the floor near a bathtub or shower isn’t exactly a safe alternative. This fixed, wall-mounted unit from Dreo is a more reliable alternative. It’s IP24 waterproof-rated, so it’s protected against splashes from every direction, and has the same kind of ALCI plug you typically find on hair tools.

It has been revealed that the bathroom heater accommodates spaces up to 200 square feet. With smart functionality, the companion app allows you to schedule timers, adjust temperatures, and change heat levels remotely.

Though this model has a child lock and a cool-touch exterior, we recommend mounting it out of reach of littles because the exhaust vent gets pretty warm.

Sources indicate that if noise is one of your biggest concerns while shopping for a space heater, then an oil-filled radiator heater might be the right option. The Pelonis heater doesn’t use an internal fan, and offers the quietest noise operation on our list, maxing out right around five decibels.

It offers just about the same features as the ceramic heaters we recommend, with three different heating modes, tip-over security, and overheat protection. The heater has 360-degree warmth circulation, so you’re covered from every angle.

Recent findings suggest that the radiator sits on four casters so it easily moves from room to room. It has a carrying handle, but it’s relatively small compared to the overall size of the unit and may overheat, so we recommend moving to your desired space before turning it on.

Simple, affordable, and versatile, these use electrical resistance to warm your space. A ceramic block or element is electrically conductive and heats up, and that heat is transferred to the air with an internal fan. The majority of the heaters on our list fall into this category.

Ideal use: These are great for general household use, shared offices, or wherever quiet heat is needed. Their simplicity makes them quite rugged; they have fewer parts to wear out or break.

Recent findings suggest that this style of space heater emits infrared radiation rays that heat objects and individuals rather than the air, and it’s one of the more straightforward designs. They provide warmth almost instantly and aren’t loud while running, but they do have limited range.

Ideal use: Spot heating or small areas that need to be warmed up in a short amount of time.

According to recent reports, these appliances burn propane or kerosene to warm an infrared emitter that projects the energy to heat your space. They’re considered convection heaters because they transfer thermal energy through a fluid, either by gas or oil.

They elevate the temperature of the air in certain spaces and are most suitable for delivering warmth in an area where you might walk around, like the surroundings of your desk or workshop.

Ideal use: Construction sites, garages, or work areas are the best places to use these heaters, since you want to place one at a comfortable distance and keep the work area unobstructed. Gas or liquid-fuel heaters direct the heat wherever you’re working.

Most residential space heaters use about 1,500 watts of power. If you’re using one of these devices as a primary heat source, it’s recommended to choose a model that offers 10 watts of heat output per square foot of space. 150 square feet is the common standard for coverage. You may consider investing in more than one unit if you’re trying to warm a larger space, or finding a design that has the right power combined with a fan or oscillating mode to disperse heat more evenly.

If you have pets or young children, then choosing a space heater with safety features is especially crucial for avoiding accidental burns and fires. The majority of the heaters on our list come with an automatic shut-off feature if it tips over. A good portion of our recommended heaters also include a timer to prevent the device from running for the entire day if you forget to shut it off.

Sources indicate that during our testing and research journey, we learned some other valuable safety tips along the way such as the “three feet rule” (keeping the space heater at a distance from anything flammable) and not using these appliances in moist areas. But most importantly, you should never plug a space heater into an extension cord, power cord, or power strip. They’re not equipped for the electrical load that these devices require, and can be a potential fire hazard.

The short answer is it depends. Whether it’s “a lot” depends mainly on how long you run the heater and your local electricity rate. In the U.S., residential electricity prices typically range from $0.12 to $0.20 per kWh, with the average being around $0.17 per kWh as of December 2025.

In a recent development, because most space heaters operate at 1,500 watts, they can cost between $0.18 and $0.30 per hour at average electricity rates. To find a more accurate estimate, divide the heater’s wattage by 1,000 to convert to kilowatts, then multiply that number by the number of hours the heater is running, and multiply that result by your electricity rate per kilowatt-hour (kWh).

These appliances aren’t intended to replace your home’s central heating system, so it’s better to use them supplementally if you don’t want to pay more on your electric bill.

It has been revealed that you should turn them off when sleeping or left unattended. Common overnight hazards like a unit tipping over, bedding sitting too close to the heater, or an outlet overheating pose significant risks that you might not notice until you wake up. While most space heaters have preventative safety features like automatic shutoff or built-in thermostats, and may even be rated for continuous use, it’s best to resist the temptation of 24-hour warmth for safer operation.

Industry observers note that season 1¼ lb. skinless, boneless chicken thighs (4–5) all over with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

In a recent development, heat 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large pot over medium. Add 1 tsp. crushed fennel seeds, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. ground cardamom, and ¼ tsp. ground cloves and cook, stirring, until fragrant, about 20 seconds. Partially cover pot, reduce heat to medium-low, and simmer until an instant-read thermometer inserted into thickest part of a thigh registers at least 165°, 15–18 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board and let cool slightly. Reduce heat to low and cover pot. Using 2 forks, shred chicken.

Melt 4 Tbsp. (½ stick) unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add 1 cup orzo and cook, stirring often, until golden brown and fragrant, about 5 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. finely grated lemon zest, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper.

Industry observers note that scrape orzo mixture into pot with broth. Increase heat to medium and simmer broth, uncovered, until orzo is just al dente, 8–10 minutes. Remove soup from heat and add shredded chicken, 5 oz. baby kale or spinach, and 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice. Stir until greens are just wilted. Taste and season with more salt if needed.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This creamy, always comforting slow-cooked rice pudding is scented with cardamom and sometimes topped with nuts or dried fruit. Versions of it exist across South Asia and beyond, each one slightly different but speaking the same nostalgic language. I’m serving it with a little twist here—a brûléed top for that crackly crème brûlée moment, and a scoop of mango sorbet for brightness and as a nod to the classic sticky rice flavor.

Note: If you are not using a nonstick pot, be extra careful and stir every 4 to 5 minutes; otherwise the rice pudding will definitely stick to the bottom. In the event it does, promptly empty the contents into a new pot and start simmering from low heat again. If you do not have a kitchen blowtorch, you can skip the brûlée. Serve warm or chill for 2 to 4 hours and garnish with saffron threads.

Find more Rachel Gurjar recipes here.

Sources indicate that to a medium heavy-bottomed nonstick pot, add 5 cups (1.2 L) whole milk, 1 cup (240 ml) water, one 14-oz. (415 ml) can sweetened condensed milk, 3 green cardamom pods, and one 1" (2.5-cm) cinnamon stick. Bring to a boil and add 1 cup (200 g) jasmine rice or any short‑grain rice, then turn the heat down to low and simmer, stirring often and scraping all the way down to the bottom of the pot to make sure the mixture doesn’t stick or scorch, until the rice is tender and the mixture is thickened, 50 to 60 minutes. Add ¼ tsp. fine sea salt and stir to combine. If the consistency feels too thick add, ¼ cup [60 ml] water and stir to reach your desired consistency.

Recent findings suggest that scoop the kheer into heatproof serving bowls and top each with 1 to 2 Tbsp. granulated sugar, ensuring the surface is covered completely. Then carefully brûlée using a kitchen blowtorch, moving in a circular pattern, until the sugar is melted and a deep amber color. (You want a thin, smooth crust that shatters when broken.) Top with a scoop of sorbet and serve immediately.

Recent findings suggest that I'll try just about anything Taco Bell puts on its menu, and whatever I order usually ends up drenched in hot sauce. So when I heard the chain was adding a upcoming FLAMIN' HOT offering (and bringing back a punchy fan favorite), I was curious whether they'd finally give me enough spice to leave those packets alone. I like my food hot enough to get a few beads of sweat forming on my nose, and with a name like FLAMIN' HOT, I don't think that's asking too much.

According to recent reports, there were two contenders: the returning FLAMIN' HOT Grilled Cheese Burrito ($5.49), which I'd missed during its first run, and the brand-new FLAMIN' HOT Mini Taco Salad ($2.49). Both feature Fritos FLAMIN' HOT, so I figured I was in for some decent spice. Here's how that worked out.

Industry observers note that I love a good taco salad, especially when the bowl itself is edible. But my first impression of this mini version was that it looked like a pretty ordinary Taco Bell salad. And after a few bites, I wasn't finding much to convince me otherwise.

In a recent development, you've got seasoned beef, refried beans, lettuce, tomatoes, cheddar, and Creamy Chipotle sauce tucked into a crispy flour tortilla bowl. Beneath everything was a layer of reddish rice, which Taco Bell says is seasoned with FLAMIN' HOT Fritos. I could definitely see the color, but whatever was making that rice spicy wasn't doing much for my taste buds.

And speaking of Fritos, I'm still trying to figure out where mine went. They're supposed to be in there, but I genuinely couldn't tell whether they'd been included in my particular serving. I would've loved more of the chipotle sauce, too, because the other ingredients seemed to overpower whatever heat was hiding underneath.

The shell itself was fine, although a little bland and greasy. I’m still pro-taco salads, but I just wish the spice had been more noticeable—especially with a name that makes such a big promise.

The returning burrito is stuffed with seasoned beef, spicy rice, crunchy FLAMIN' HOT Fritos, nacho cheese sauce, sour cream, and Creamy Chipotle sauce. And because Taco Bell clearly believes there's no such thing as too much cheese, the entire thing gets a three-cheese blend grilled onto the outside of the tortilla.

It has been revealed that I took a pretty substantial first bite, making sure to get into those Fritos and all its FLAMIN’ HOT components. The nacho cheese had that gloriously gooey, movie-theater quality (complimentary), while the rest of the fillings worked together much better than they had in the salad. There's a lot happening inside this thing, and I was enjoying every bit of it.

Industry observers note that most importantly, I could actually taste the heat. There was a satisfying punch of spice, followed by that little tickle at the back of my throat that tells me something's doing its job. I wasn't desperately reaching for a drink, but the burrito had enough kick to make me happy.

It has been revealed that I even went back for another bite of the mini taco salad afterward, and it tasted better with the burrito's lingering heat still in my mouth. Who knew it needed a little help from its menu companion?

It has been revealed that ultimately, the burrito is the one I'd order again. The mini taco salad has potential, and for $2.49, I wouldn't be opposed to giving it another shot. But next time, I'm bringing the extra hot sauce packets it should've saved me from needing.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.

When you were a child, did you ever wonder what happened to the sea at the horizon? Perhaps you imagined it stretching forever. Or perhaps, like me, you believed that where the blue ended, the water simply fell off the edge of the world, spilling over in some enormous, invisible waterfall. It made perfect sense at the time, and there was quite a lot of magic involved, too. Then came geography lessons, maps, explanations, terminology, and the gradual realization that the world did not end where your vision did—that it was, in fact, far vaster than anything the eye could take in. So why has it become so difficult to recapture the purity and intensity of that experience as an adult?

Could there be a chance, however counterintuitive it sounds, that you were actually more conscious back then?

It sounds counterintuitive, but Alysson Muotri, PhD, a professor of pediatrics and cellular and molecular medicine at the University of California, San Diego, has given this poetic—almost philosophical—idea scientific legs. To do so, he used one of the most futuristic tools that right now exists for investigating the human brain: brain organoids, tiny clusters of living neural tissue grown from stem cells in a laboratory. He wondered whether these tiny lumps of living human brain tissue could illuminate that elusive inner experience. What he found was that as we grow and learn about the world, this process might really be changing how we perceive reality.

But before you can explore consciousness in a lab, you need to build the organoids. The process begins with ordinary human cells, often collected from the skin. Scientists reprogram them into induced pluripotent stem cells, which regain the ability to develop into almost any cell type in the body. Researchers use chemical signals to turn these cells into neurons and other brain cells. The cells multiply, gathering into tiny clumps of tissue. Inside them, neurons begin making contact, and electrical signals pass between them. However, calling these organoids “brains in a dish” is rather generous, though tempting; they lack much of the anatomy of a developed human brain. Still, organoids allow scientists to watch human neural tissue take shape in ways that would be impossible to witness inside a living person’s skull.

Muotri’s team discovered in 2019 that maturing organoids produced electrical rhythms resembling certain features of brain activity recorded in premature infants. Here was human neural tissue, deprived of the sights and sounds accompanying a child’s development, nevertheless organizing itself into patterns observed in living brains. Four years later, researchers at Indiana University Bloomington incorporated brain organoids into an experimental computing system that used their electrical responses to help recognize spoken sounds and predict mathematical patterns. By 2025, other scientists had reported that repeated electrical stimulation could alter how individual neurons in organoids responded, with some changes lingering for hours after the stimulation came to a halt—evidence of cellular mechanisms associated with learning and memory.

Sources indicate that muotri, meanwhile, had begun wondering whether the electrical activity of his brain organoids could offer any clues to that elusive inner experience we call consciousness. Of course, even if we assume that consciousness arises entirely from the brain, there is something peculiar about trying to measure it. It’s not as though you can insert a thermometer into someone’s head and pinpoint the experience of being alive and aware—or the feeling of experiencing the world as a child.

Muotri decided to investigate by borrowing an approach from consciousness research called the perturbational complexity index (PCI). In humans, the method involves delivering a brief magnetic pulse to the brain and recording the resulting electrical activity through electrodes placed on the scalp. Earlier researchers have analyzed the responses and calculated a score that has helped distinguish wakefulness from deep sleep and general anesthesia; a higher score indicates greater conscious awareness. While PCI cannot measure consciousness directly, it offers clues about the brain’s capacity to sustain it.

It has been revealed that in preliminary findings, Muotri measured the organoids’ electrical activity before exposing them to repeated stimulation, using an approach similar to PCI. To say that he found a startling degree of complexity in the way their neurons communicate with one another—with scores that exceeded those typically recorded in awake human brains—is an understatement. Because the organoid and human measurements use different methods, however, the scores cannot be compared directly. Still, he wasn’t expecting the organoids to have this PCI level, he indicates. “It’s very latest, and I’m still thinking about what it means.”.

Industry observers note that muotri also found something shocking about how the organoids behaved as they were stimulated repeatedly with light. Gradually, the cells began reacting differently to the stimulation, and some of those changes lingered after the light was switched off. “So there is some kind of a memory embedded in those networks,” he says. But even more astounding was that, as the organoids adapted to the stimulation, their complexity score actually fell, similar to the way human brains with lower PCI scores were less aware.

Sources indicate that he thinks the reason is that a brain organoid increases its bias as it learns, just as we become more biased as we learn more over the years. By bias, Muotri means that experience makes certain neural responses, particularly those reinforced through repeated exposure, more likely than others. Learning, apparently, does more than give us knowledge. It may also condition us to overlook parts of the world we once experienced more freely.

“It’s almost like when you are born…as soon as your brain is naive and fresh, you’re more conscious than when you are an adult,” Muotri continues. By adulthood, however, experience has cramped your brain’s style. “Because you already experienced so many things, you’re already [so] attached to the physical environment, that you become less conscious than you were [as] a baby.”.

The suggestion is extraordinary, especially coming from experiments involving tissue that has never seen a sunset, heard a lullaby, obeyed a teacher, or encountered anything resembling a childhood whatsoever.

Yet there is a recognizable human parallel. Developmental psychologist Alison Gopnik has compared adult attention to a spotlight, concentrated on what matters for an immediate goal, and children’s attention to a lantern, illuminating more of their surroundings. A toddler entering an unfamiliar room might become absorbed by a patch of sunlight that an adult barely notices. The adult knows more about the room, but familiarity helps determine what deserves attention. Noticing more of the world doesn’t necessarily mean being more conscious of it.

In a recent development, however, a baby’s brain, already shaped by months of development in the womb, is hardly comparable to an organoid that has never experienced the world outside a laboratory. That’s why Kenneth Kosik, MD, a neuroscience professor at the University of California, Santa Barbara, is skeptical. In a 2024 paper published in the journal Patterns, titled Why Brain Organoids Are Not Conscious Yet, he argued that organoids lack much of the organization and communication between brain regions that may be necessary for consciousness. And electrical activity, however complicated, is not enough to prove an inner life. Neurons firing independently can produce unpredictable signals that are difficult to reduce to a simpler description, even when there is no evidence that anything is being experienced. “So we still have a little bit of a jump there, yeah, to say that compressibility is related to consciousness,” Kosik states.

Muotri himself is cautious about what the numbers mean and says they are still preliminary data. Nor does he claim that his organoids actually experience anything. “I should not say they are conscious outright,” he says.

In a recent development, for now, Muotri’s experiments cannot definitively tell us whether we were more conscious as children than we are as adults, but they do open a window onto something just as intriguing: what happens to our experience of the world if learning itself changes how our brains encounter our environment? After all, the day I discovered that the sea did not plunge into an abyss, I gained precious knowledge that generations before me had strived to acquire. But have I ever again experienced the sea quite as fully as I did when I was a child, believing it could spill over the world’s edge? That is a whole different question, and we don’t have the answer yet.

Industry observers note that stav Dimitropoulos is a Gold and Community Anthem Award–winning journalist, and writes about consciousness, science, and culture for Popular Mechanics, Nature, and the BBC. Her work often explores mind-stretching angles where science meets philosophy. Her debut nonfiction book, Slow, Lazy, Gluttons (Greystone Books, 2026) asks: What if the traits society shames — laziness, darkness, nostalgia, and more — are actually survival superpowers?

This Three-Day Wedding Brought Persian Traditions, Dramatic Design, and an Ibiza-Style Rave to Oaxaca

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that brian Downs and Sarvenaz Shahbazi had a classic college library meet-cute.
  • According to recent reports, the couple got engaged two-and-a-half years later, over July 4th weekend on a trip to Puglia.
  • In a recent development, sarvi’s family, who were in on the plan, told everyone to meet for sunset drinks at the beach club of the masseria where they were staying.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that brian Downs and Sarvenaz Shahbazi had a classic college library meet-cute. One day, while they were both at Columbia Business School, Brian was tutoring their mutual friend—and future wedding officiant—Alex in a study room. Sarvenaz, who goes by Sarvi, walked by and jumped right in, taking the lead in guiding everyone through accounting problems. “I remember immediately thinking how pretty she was, but also how smart and confident she was,” notes Brian. The two became friends, and by the time they were back from winter break, Brian asked Sarvi out for drinks at The Commerce Inn on January 7, 2022. Says Sarvi, “I had mentioned to him in passing that I had been wanting to go a month or two earlier since it had just opened, so I was very impressed with his thoughtfulness and planning!” The two were inseparable from that point on.

According to recent reports, the couple got engaged two-and-a-half years later, over July 4th weekend on a trip to Puglia. Sarvi’s parents had planned a week-long vacation in the region, and Sarvi and her brother decided to join last minute with their partners. Brian, who was already on an engagement ring search, expedited the process to have it ready for the trip. “At the time, I genuinely did not think an engagement was on the table for at least a few more months,” claims Sarvi. “We had only recently started talking about it, and Brian had very strategically staged our first-ever ring shopping trip the week before we left, which I then learned was just a decoy.”.

In a recent development, sarvi’s family, who were in on the plan, told everyone to meet for sunset drinks at the beach club of the masseria where they were staying. When the couple arrived, one of Sarvi’s favorite songs was playing, and a single table was set with flowers and Champagne with views of the water. “I looked at the setup and immediately said to Brian, ‘Oh my God, I think someone is going to get engaged here. We’re going to see it,’” Sarvi claims. When they walked towards the deck, Brian pulled out the ring and got down on one knee. “She was in utter shock,” recalls Brian. “I had thought a lot about what I was going to say, but the only thing I actually remember saying is ‘eshgham,’ which means ‘my love’ in Farsi.”.

When choosing a destination to tie the knot, Brian and Sarvi found themselves constantly drifting back to Mexico, ultimately deciding to exchange vows in Oaxaca City on November 15, 2025. The couple went on their first trip together to the country and had each visited countless times before and after they started dating.

The bride took charge to bring their dream wedding to life. “I work in hospitality as the director of strategy and development at Catch Hospitality Group, so what I truly find most fulfilling in life is creating experiences for others centered around exceptional food and drink and a carefully curated ambiance,” she says. Alongside planners Gutierrez F Studio, Sarvi helped orchestrate three days of events that blended this ethos with traditions from her Persian culture. The weekend would kick off with a rehearsal dinner full of delicious food and speeches at Criollo, followed by a Persian wedding ceremony and party at the historic Proyecto Murguía, and finally, the big day at Loma Noble. “We had so much fun creating a completely different world, each with a distinct personality, for every part of the wedding day—leading our guests on a journey from a ceremony in a bucolic agave field, to an energetic and dramatic dinnerscape, all the way to an after-party rave in a cactus garden,” says the bride.

While Sarvi had clear ideas of how to bring together all the events, it took some work to come up with her wedding wardrobe. “I wasn’t a bride with a pre-constructed Pinterest board, so when I first started thinking about what I would wear, I was completely overwhelmed by the sheer number of options,” she claims. “I never wanted to wear anything that felt stiff, stuffy, or overly traditional.” This drive to find something unique led her to a pale butter-yellow dress with a sheer cape from Harithand for her rehearsal dinner, which she paired with diamond and ruby flower earrings from her aunt. “I felt immediately comfortable in it—it was soft, ethereal and subtly sexy—and felt perfect for our dinner under the stars at Criollo,” she says.

Sources indicate that her ceremony dress search ultimately led her to two iconic bridal designers: Danielle Frankel and Vera Wang. When Sarvi first saw Wang’s Ariel dress, it reminded her of Van Gogh’s Starry Night. “It ultimately felt perfect for our Persian ceremony,” she states. “There is so much artistry, symbolism, and craftsmanship that goes into an ‘aghd’ and the ‘sofreh’—the traditional ceremonial table—with countless individual symbolic items and details coming together to create something incredibly beautiful. There was a similar sense of artistry and romance in the Vera Wang gown that felt especially fitting for that night.” She paired the look with pink sapphire and diamond flower drop earrings from her maternal grandmother, who recently passed.

For the Western wedding day, Sarvi wore a strapless gown by Frankel. While she wasn’t planning to try it on before she entered the showroom, the style called to her. “I loved the contrasting shades of white, the different textures, and the subtle lace throughout the skirt, which gave the dress so much dimension and movement,” she claims. Once again, the bride wore a jewelry piece from her grandmother: a pearl choker with a gold flower and a tiny ruby. “They were playful, distinctive, and deeply personal, with those unexpected touches of color that I always love,” she says.

After dinner, the bride changed into a custom look she made with Brooklyn-based designer Delfina Balda. The two-piece look featured a mix of textures and fabrics with varying degrees of sheerness. “It felt like the perfect party look—artful and completely unique, but something I could actually dance in,” she states. For the after-party, which was modeled after DC10 in Ibiza with a completely red lighting scheme, Sarvi decided to change out of bridal white and donned a red dress by The Attico. “It has this intricate soutache detailing and a fringe skirt that gives the dress incredible texture and movement, especially on the dance floor,” she says.

The groom wore a mix of vintage and bespoke looks throughout the wedding weekend. For Friday night, Brian donned a relaxed suit found at Ebreo Vintage in Williamsburg that fit him perfectly. “Even the owner basically mentioned, ‘Honestly, you should just buy that.’ I got pretty lucky,” he notes. His next two looks were made alongside Tyler Sequeira at P. Johnson. The groom wanted to wear a double-breasted chocolate brown suit for the Persian ceremony to complement the natural tones throughout the celebration. “On my second visit, when I was picking fabrics and locking everything in, Sarvi’s uncle Mohammad, or Momo, insisted on joining me,” says Brian. “It’s a tradition in their family to buy a new suit for the groom joining the family, so he ended up helping me design the suit for the aghd. I loved that the suit became something more meaningful than just something I had picked out for myself.” For the black-tie wedding day, Brian wore a bespoke tuxedo made in midnight blue.

The wedding weekend began at Criollo, for an open-air dinner filled with mezcalitas, tacos, and chickens roaming freely through the space. “It immediately gave everyone a sense of the place we had fallen in love with,” says Sarvi. The night full of speeches ended with a night of dancing at a local vinyl bar. “It was one of the first moments where I looked around and really processed that all of these people we loved had traveled to Oaxaca to be there for us,” says Brian.

On the Persian wedding day, the couple paraded with their guests through the streets to their venue, where the space was filled with florals, Persian food, music, and a sofreh table ready for the ceremony. The bride’s uncle officiated the aghd and her mother and other family members participated throughout. “By the time the ceremony ended, the night very rapidly became a full-on Persian dance party,” states Sarvi. “We had hoped Friday would have just as much energy and dancing as Saturday, but even we underestimated it.” Adds Brian, “Seeing my parents and friends dancing to Persian music alongside Sarvi’s family is one of the funniest and most joyous memories I’ll have from the weekend.”.

In a recent development, the ceremony the next day was held at sunset among the agave fields of Loma Noble, an agronomic project outside the city of Oaxaca. “We wanted the ceremony to feel as though it belonged within the landscape rather than creating something that completely competed with it,” says the bride. Sarvi walked down the aisle to a string rendition of “Creep” by Radiohead. “Certainly not the most traditional wedding choice, but one of my favorite songs of all time and, to me, one of the most beautiful songs ever written,” she says. The couple’s business school friend Alex officiated, weaving in sentimental passages from Brian’s late grandfather Jack, and the groom’s mother shared a reading. The couple wrote their own vows, including an entire section Brian prepared in Farsi. “I learned afterward that my younger cousin had secretly been tutoring him so he could learn and practice that portion,” says Sarvi. “It was one of the most deeply sentimental gestures I could have imagined.”.

The couple share they were both emotional, yet calm and present for the ceremony. The two recessed to “California Dreamin’,” which they sang with joy down the aisle. “It was this perfect release of all the emotion we had been feeling, and immediately shifted the energy from the ceremony into pure excitement for the night ahead,” says the bride. The two spent a moment alone together in the bridal suite before joining guests at cocktail hour along a tree-lined pathway.

Industry observers note that when guests moved into the reception tent, they found the space decorated with a nod to an eclipse, complete with a glowing orb above a circular central stage and serpentine tables along the room. Dinner was punctuated with speeches, assigned “table captains” to keep the energy alive, and dances with their parents. The newlyweds shared their own first dance at the end of dinner to “Sunny” by Bobby Hebb. “As soon as it ended, Brian and I grabbed the microphones and essentially confirmed, ‘Now, it’s time to party.’ At that exact moment, trays of carajillos came out for everyone, giving the room one more jolt of energy before the curtains separating the dinner space from the dance floor opened,” says the bride. Their 300 guests moved to the disco-ball-filled space complete with a martini bar and music by DJ César.

“At one point, Brian and I ended up dancing on top of the bar and apparently were dancing hard enough that the staff became concerned it might come crashing down—so the bartenders were literally holding it up beneath us while we were dancing,” states Sarvi. “That probably sums up the energy of the night better than anything else.” The party didn’t stop as guests next moved through a glowing red tunnel. “Once you emerged into the cactus garden, everything was washed in red light, with an enormous triangular LED structure framing the dance floor,” says the bride. “It felt almost otherworldly and created exactly the kind of late-night atmosphere we wanted.” The couple danced until 6 a.m.

Looking back, the couple describe it as the most magical weekend of their lives. “I constantly find myself wondering what I did to end up married to someone so cool and so loved by her friends and family,” indicates Brian. “She draws people into her orbit, and getting to stand next to her while all of those people highlighted up to celebrate us is something I’ll never forget.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Inspired by the towering Praline Pecan Pie served at Das Dutchman Essenhaus in Middlebury, Indiana, this pecan cream pie brings together the best parts of pecan pie and cream pie. A gooey, nut-packed base sits beneath silky brown sugar custard and a pillow of whipped cream, with crunchy candied pecans scattered over the top. It’s a lot of pie—in the best possible way.

Sources indicate that the pecan layer is jammed full of butter-toasted nuts, but the secret ingredient is a dollop of sour cream, which helps prevent crystallization and keeps the filling from becoming overly sweet. More sour cream goes into the whipped topping, adding tang and helping it hold its shape. Dark brown sugar and plenty of vanilla give the custard its toffee-like flavor.

According to recent reports, this is admittedly more involved than a classic pecan pie, but the work is straightforward and easy to spread over a couple of days, making this a particularly good project to tackle before Thanksgiving Day. Toast the pecans once for both the gooey filling and crunchy topping, and make the crust and pecan layer ahead so all that’s left is the custard, whipped cream, and a little patience while everything chills.

What size pie pan should I use?

Industry observers note that use a standard 9" metal pie pan. Metal promotes even browning and can accommodate more filling than a standard glass or ceramic dish of the same diameter. This is a generously filled pie, so pan capacity matters.

Can I make pecan cream pie ahead of time?

Yes. You can bake the crust and pecan layer up to one day ahead and store them, covered, at room temperature. Once you’ve added the custard, the pie needs at least four hours in the refrigerator to set. The fully assembled pie can also be refrigerated for up to one day. For the crunchiest topping, scatter the candied pecans over the whipped cream just before serving.

How do I know when the brown sugar custard is thick enough?

In a recent development, the custard should start to bubble, then become glossy and thick like pudding as you stir it over medium heat. This generally takes 3–4 minutes. Don’t rely on refrigeration alone to thicken it: The cornstarch needs to cook sufficiently on the stovetop for the custard to set properly. Keep stirring to prevent lumps or curdling.

2 hours (plus 6 hours for chilling).

Industry observers note that whisk 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour, ¼ tsp. baking powder, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces; rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until combined (mixture will be very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat, then smash into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea size). Make a well in the center; pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead dough in bowl a couple of times to bring together (some dry bits may remain).

Recent findings suggest that turn dough out onto a lightly dusted surface; dust top of dough with rice flour or all-purpose flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more flour as needed. Pat into a ½"-thick disk; wrap in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Place racks in upper and lower thirds of oven; preheat to 425°. Let dough sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Unwrap and roll out on a lightly floured surface to a ¼"–⅛"-thick round. Wrap around rolling pin; transfer to a standard 9"-diameter pie dish (preferably metal). Unfurl into dish, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into dish. Trim overhang to 1". Fold overhang under and crimp edges as desired. Prick bottom and sides of dough in several places with a fork. Freeze 15 minutes.

Recent findings suggest that crumple up 2 sheets of parchment paper; smooth out and place over dough. Fill dish with pie weights or dried beans. Set pan on a foil-lined baking sheet and bake crust on lower rack, tenting edges with foil if browning too rapidly, until edges are golden brown and bottom is opaque, 35–40 minutes. Remove from oven; reduce oven temperature to 350°. Lift parchment and weights out of pan.

While the crust is baking, whisk 2 large eggs, ⅔ cup (packed; 133 g) dark brown sugar, and remaining 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl. Set egg mixture aside to use for the candied pecan topping and the pie filling.

Melt remaining 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a medium saucepan set over medium. Add 2½ cups (300 g) raw pecans and cook, stirring gently, until nuts are slightly darkened in color and fragrant, 5–7 minutes. Pour through a fine-mesh sieve set over a small bowl, reserving both the pecans and the browned butter. (You’ll use the same pan to make the custard; no need to wash it.).

Transfer ½ cup toasted pecans to another small bowl to make the topping: Add 1 Tbsp. reserved egg mixture and toss to coat. Spread on a parchment-lined baking sheet and bake on upper rack until dry to the touch and a honeycomb-like texture appears on surface, about 5 minutes. Let candied nuts cool.

For the filling: Finely chop remaining toasted pecans and add to the remaining egg mixture along with the reserved browned butter, 2 Tbsp. sour cream, and 1 tsp. vanilla extract. Stir to combine. Scrape into crust and bake on lower rack until pecan layer is mostly set but still jiggles slightly in the center when gently shaken, 15–18 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack; let cool until barely warm, at least 30 minutes.

It has been revealed that do Ahead: Candied pecan topping can be made 3 days ahead; store airtight at room temperature. Crust with pecan layer can be baked 1 day ahead; store, covered with foil, at room temperature.

Heat 1½ cups heavy cream and 1 cup whole milk in the same saucepan you used for the nuts over medium until steaming, about 2 minutes.

Meanwhile, whisk 6 large egg yolks, ¾ cup (packed; 150 g) dark brown sugar, ⅓ cup (40 g) cornstarch, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining ½ cup whole milk in a medium bowl.

Sources indicate that gradually pour warm cream mixture into egg mixture, whisking constantly until combined. Pour mixture back into pan and cook over medium heat, stirring constantly, until it starts to bubble, then becomes glossy and thick (like pudding), 3–4 minutes. Scrape into a medium bowl, add 6 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, cut into pieces, and 4 tsp. vanilla extract, and whisk until butter is melted and custard is emulsified. Cover with plastic wrap, pressing directly onto surface. Let custard stand at room temperature while the pecan layer cools. The pecan layer can still be slightly warm when you add the custard; neither needs to cool completely.

Uncover custard; whisk until smooth. Spoon over gooey pecan layer, spreading evenly to edges. Cover and chill at least 4 hours and up to 1 day.

According to recent reports, whisk ¼ cup sour cream, 3 Tbsp. powdered sugar, remaining 1 tsp. vanilla extract, a pinch of kosher salt, and remaining 1 cup heavy cream in a medium bowl to medium peaks. Spoon over custard and spread into an even layer. Break candied pecans into large pieces and scatter on top.

Sources indicate that do Ahead: Pie can be assembled 1 day ahead. Chill.

Recent findings suggest that every cuisine has a sauce that’s an absolute essential—a ride or die, if you will. For South Asian food, this is a cilantro mint green chutney. It brings a punchy, herb-packed burst of flavor that goes with pretty much everything. This recipe combines cilantro, mint, and just the right amount of heat from green chiles, creating a balance of spice and freshness. Lime juice adds brightness, while cumin, sugar, and chaat masala add complexity. Use this as a zesty topping for your favorite dish or as a base for pani puri water (just add 1½ cups [360 ml] of water and strain), or make it creamy with yogurt or sour cream to use for spreading and dipping.

Slow-roasting Japanese sweet potatoes flesh-side down releases their natural sugars, caramelizing and deepening their sweetness. The flesh becomes incredibly tender, almost custard-like in texture, while the skin turns a rich golden brown and becomes slightly crispy. So don’t bother peeling them! Top them with tamarind concentrate (I like Tamicon, Cock Brand, Pure Indian Foods, or Dragonfly—anything without citric acid), green chutney, fresh onions, tomatoes, and cilantro for a chaat-inspired appetizer.

Pulse for a few seconds in intervals until the ingredients are pulverized into a smooth paste. Transfer to an airtight container and store until ready to use, up to 1 week in the refrigerator or 1 month in the freezer.

Preheat the oven to 375°F (190°C) and line a baking sheet with parchment paper.

Let rest for 5 to 8 minutes. Once cool enough to handle, cut the sweet potatoes into 1" to 2" [2.5 to 5 cm] pieces.

To a small bowl, add ½ cup (120 g) plain whole-milk yogurt or sour cream and ½ tsp. fine sea salt and whisk to combine. If you’re using sour cream, thin it out with a little water.

It has been revealed that place the sweet potatoes on a serving platter and drizzle the yogurt, ½ cup Evergreen Chutney, 3 Tbsp. tamarind concentrate or paste, and 2 Tbsp. lime juice evenly all over. Sprinkle with 1 medium red tomato (5 oz. [140 g]), finely chopped, 1 small red onion (7 oz. [200 g]), finely chopped, 2 Tbsp. chopped cilantro leaves and tender stems, 1 tsp. chaat masala, 3 green Thai chiles or 1 serrano, stemmed, thinly sliced, and crispy sev and serve immediately.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.

Sources indicate that roughly 11 percent of American adults are on a GLP-1 for weight loss, according to a 2026 Gallup survey; so chances are, you likely know someone who is using one for diabetes management, obesity treatment, or heart health—but the benefits might not stop there. Now, semaglutide, the popular GLP-1 medication found in Ozempic and Wegovy, is drawing serious attention from longevity experts.

A recent study published in Nature found that semaglutide administered to female mice late in life significantly extended their life span. The results pose a legitimate question: Could GLP-1 drugs lengthen human lives as well?

To understand whether GLP-1s have anti-aging benefits, researchers put mice that were 20 months old—or roughly 60 human years—on a semaglutide regimen for the rest of their lives. There was also a control group of female mice the same age that received saline injections instead of the semaglutide. The team targeted older, non-obese, non-diabetic female mice to minimize the effects of male aggression and injury, consistent with previous long-term aging research, according to study author Danica Chen, PhD, professor of metabolic biology and nutrition at the University of California, Berkeley.The results? The median life span of the mice that received the GLP-1 drug increased from 742 days to 834 days, roughly a 12 percent extension. The researchers also saw reduced inflammation and preserved cognitive and muscle function in the GLP-1 group.

In a recent development, but there’s a rub here: This study was done in mice, which are a far cry from human adults, meaning we don’t yet know the effects of GLP-1s on people—at least not yet. However, there has been research that suggests lower-calorie diets lead to longer life spans in humans. “The general cause of aging is accumulation of cellular damage,” Chen says. She explains that calorie restriction can reduce cell damage and improve the function of tissues (a group of similar cells working together to perform a specific task), both of which contribute to a longer life span.

Sources indicate that michael Corley, PhD, associate professor of medicine at the University of California San Diego, thinks the Nature study is “important and exciting” because it looks beyond the established metabolic benefits of GLP-1 drugs and tests whether they can influence the biological aging process. (Biological age denotes how well the body is functioning on cellular and molecular levels, while chronological age refers to the number of years a person has been alive.).

Industry observers note that “The finding that semaglutide extended life span by approximately 12 percent in older female mice, while improving several measures of physical and cognitive function, adds notable evidence to the emerging field of GLP-1 therapies as potential gerotherapeutics,” or treatments that target the root of aging, Corley says. In fact, Corley was involved in a separate study, published earlier this year in Nature Communications, that found that 32 weeks of semaglutide treatment improved multiple epigenetic aging clocks, including measures of biological age and the pace of aging.

Findings presented at the 2026 Aging Research and Drug Discovery Meeting have also strengthened this emerging picture, Corley explains. Novo Nordisk, a Danish pharmaceutical manufacturer with locations around the world, reported that semaglutide improved measures of biological aging across multiple organ systems, including the heart and kidneys.

Likewise, Eli Lilly, an American pharmaceutical company headquartered in Indiana, presented findings that tirzepatide—another GLP-1 medication, which is found in prescriptions like Mounjaro and Zepbound—positively influenced several epigenetic aging clocks, including organ-specific markers that measure the biological age of the heart, kidney, liver, and immune system.

“Together, these independent observations suggest that GLP-1-based therapies may affect biological aging through multiple molecular pathways,” Corley states. “The new mouse study is particularly interesting because it extends these molecular observations to actual life span, while also demonstrating improvements in several hallmarks of aging.”.

Industry observers note that so, could GLP-1 drugs actually extend the life span of humans? Corley thinks the more compelling opportunity isn’t necessarily extending life span, but extending health span—or the number of years people live in good health, free from chronic disease and disability.

It has been revealed that “Human life span has biological constraints, and it is unlikely that GLP-1 drugs alone will dramatically extend the maximum limits of human longevity,” he states. “However, by reducing the burden of cardiovascular disease, metabolic dysfunction, and other age-related conditions, these medications could help more people remain healthy and independent for longer, potentially increasing average life span without fundamentally changing the upper limits of human longevity.”.

However, improvements in biological aging don’t necessarily translate into longer lives, Corley cautions.

According to recent reports, “The critical next step is determining whether these molecular changes predict meaningful improvements in physical function, cognition, and resilience,” Corley says. “I think the greatest potential of GLP-1 therapies is not to push humans beyond the limits of longevity, but to help more people reach older ages while maintaining their health, function, and independence.”.

It has been revealed that to find out whether or not GLP-1 drugs can eventually be used as a legitimate longevity tactic in humans, Chen notes clinical trials in humans are an notable next step. For now, GLP-1s remain a titan of diabetes and weight management—but their role in human longevity remains to be seen.
