This recipe is inspired by the garam masala my mother used to make back in India. Just a pinch adds incredible depth and flavor to both meat and vegetable dishes—it’s the secret ingredient that often leaves my guests wondering why my Indian food tastes so exceptional. And now you can use it too! This version perfectly balances the warming notes of cloves and nutmeg, and it’s the one I return to time and time again. If you prefer a sweeter blend, add more cinnamon and fennel seeds; if you want a spicier kick, increase the black pepper and cloves.

Find more Rachel Gurjar recipes here.

1 hour (plus 1 hour for marinating).

According to recent reports, in a small bowl, toss 12 dried bay leaves, 12 whole cloves, 5 black cardamom pods, 4 whole star anise pods, three 3" (7.5-cm) cinnamon sticks, 1 whole nutmeg, 3 Tbsp. coriander seeds, 3 Tbsp. whole mace fronds, 2 Tbsp. cumin seeds, 1 Tbsp. black peppercorns, and 2 tsp. white poppy seeds to combine.

Heat a medium dry skillet over low heat until hot. Add the spice mixture and toast until slightly fragrant, about 45 seconds. Transfer back to the bowl and let cool.

In a recent development, transfer the whole nutmeg to a mortar and break into smaller pieces with a pestle (this is just to make it easier to grind, so don’t worry about being too precise!). Repeat with the cinnamon. Tear the bay leaves into smaller pieces. Transfer all of the spices to a spice grinder and grind into a fine powder (it will be slightly warm when you remove the lid). Transfer to an airtight container (do not cover yet) and let cool completely. Then close the lid.

Do Ahead: Garam masala can be made 1 month ahead. Cover and store in a cool, dark place.

Recent findings suggest that to a small heatproof bowl, add 1 medium yellow onion (9 oz. [255 g]), halved, thinly sliced into half-moons, 2 Tbsp. lime juice, 2 Tbsp. Kashmiri red chili powder, 2 tsp. chaat masala, ½ tsp. cayenne powder, and ½ tsp. fine sea salt.

According to recent reports, in a small pan over medium-high heat, warm 2 Tbsp. peanut oil or any vegetable oil or avocado oil until it shimmers. Add 1 tsp. cumin seeds and cook until fragrant and they start to turn brown, about 1 minute. Be careful not to let the seeds burn or they will taste bitter. Remove from the heat and pour the hot oil over the onions. Toss to coat the onions in the spice mixture.

Serve immediately or let cool and store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 1 week.

To a mortar and pestle or food processor, add one 2" (5-cm) piece fresh ginger, chopped, 4 garlic cloves, peeled, and 3 green Thai chiles or 1 serrano, stemmed, chopped, and pound or pulse into a chunky paste. To a medium bowl, add 2 lb. (910 g) boneless, skinless chicken thighs, excess fat trimmed, cut into 2" [5-cm] pieces, along with the ginger-garlic paste and 1 tsp. fine sea salt and toss to combine. Cover and place in the refrigerator to marinate for a minimum of 1 hour or overnight.

It has been revealed that in a medium heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven over medium-low heat, warm ⅓ cup (80 ml) vegetable oil or avocado oil, then add 1 tsp. cumin seeds, ½ tsp. black mustard seeds, ½ tsp. black peppercorns, 5 whole cloves, 1 fresh or dried bay leaf, 1 star anise, and one 3" [7.5-cm] cinnamon stick, broken into small pieces, and lightly toast and until fragrant, about 1 minute. Increase the heat to medium, add 1 medium red or yellow onion (9 oz. [255 g]), finely chopped, cover, and cook until the onion is translucent and beginning to turn brown around the edges, stirring halfway through, about 10 minutes.

Recent findings suggest that add 1 Tbsp. ground coriander, 1 Tbsp. Kashmiri red chili powder, 1 Tbsp. Garam Masala, 2 tsp. cayenne powder, and 1 tsp. powdered turmeric. Stir to combine and cook until fragrant, about 1 minute. Drain off the excess marinade from the chicken, then add it to the pot along with 3 Tbsp. tomato paste, 1 Tbsp. packed fresh fenugreek leaves, and remaining 1½ tsp. fine sea salt and stir until everything is mixed thoroughly and the chicken is covered with the spices and tomato paste. Add ½ cup (120 ml) water and mix again. Cover and cook until the chicken is cooked through and tender, 30 minutes, stirring halfway through.

According to recent reports, remove from the heat and sprinkle with the remaining 1 tsp. Garam Masala, remaining 1 tsp. fresh fenugreek leaves, and cilantro leaves. Serve immediately with lime wedges, Insanely Addictive Pickled Onions, and steamed rice or Indian flatbread.

Do Ahead: Store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days or in the freezer for up to 1 month.

  • How long a power station lasts has the most impact on your experience when using one, whether you’re experiencing a blackout or enjoying a weekend off the grid.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

How long a power station lasts has the most impact on your experience when using one, whether you’re experiencing a blackout or enjoying a weekend off the grid. This year, Anker has upped its game with the S-series stations. Advanced algorithms have improved how its inverters deliver power and extend battery life. Not long ago, I reviewed this technology in the small but powerful S2000 and was impressed. Now, I’ve put the newer and larger S5000 power station through its paces, and it didn’t disappoint.

According to recent reports, for context, I also compared the S5000 to Anker's other large power station, the F3800 Plus (now only available as a bundle with other home power accessories), which has been on our list of the best portable power stations. Each model offers both 120- and 240-volt output, but the S5000 has a much larger battery capacity of 5,024 watt-hours (compared with 3,840 watt-hours with the F3800 Plus), and the S5000 is much smaller in size. While it offers less total power output (4,500 watts versus 6,000 watts for the F3800 Plus), I think the S5000 represents an overall improvement for those looking to buy a home backup station that’s more powerful than a typical portable power station.

This is what I cared about the most because better inverter efficiency is the primary feature Anker touts with the S5000. To evaluate its efficiency, I ran two tests. The first was to turn on the AC output and let it run overnight with nothing plugged into it, making sure to deactivate any auto-off features. I did this because, even when idling, most power station batteries lose some stored energy. But after 18 hours, the S5000’s battery capacity was still at 100 percent—that’s impressive. To make a comparison for context, I ran the F3800 alongside it for the same amount of time, and its battery capacity dipped to 81 percent.

For the second test, I plugged a watt meter into the station and plugged a space heater into the meter. I then ran the heater at full power, drawing around 1,500 watts, until it drained the battery fully. Using a resistive load like this (a device that turns energy to heat) can drain a battery pretty quickly, but this also gives you a good read on a power station's performance. It lasted just over three hours, and my meter measured just under 4,900 watt-hours. Compared with its official spec of 5,024 watt-hours of capacity, I determined that this station is around 97 percent efficient. Many stations hover around 89 percent on average, so this was a big win for the S5000.

It has been revealed that the technology behind this ability enables the inverter to throttle itself up and down to meet the demands of the devices plugged into it. This is especially significant for lower-powered devices and cyclical appliances with fluctuating power needs, like refrigerators, because the inverter maintains its efficiency, regardless of what’s plugged into it. That means longer run times across the board. This station could easily power my full-size refrigerator for more than 48 hours.

Recent findings suggest that the size of this station in relation to the battery capacity is its second most striking feature. It’s two-thirds smaller than the F3800 but offers 1,184 more watt-hours. At 99 pounds, I wouldn’t call it light, but with two wheels and a telescoping handle, it’s easy enough to roll around, and it’s not too hard to lift in and out of a vehicle. It would be easy to transport this to and from a second home or a job site.

There are a few other enhancements, as well. The 30-amp, 240-volt connection (great for powering an electric dryer or other 240-volt appliance) has its own on/off button, so it won’t create any unwanted drain when all you need is 120-volt AC power. It also accepts both low- and high-powered DC input, which means you get up to 3,000 watts of solar power if you have enough panels to achieve that.

Sources indicate that there’s also a port connection for adding up to five expansion batteries, potentially increasing the total battery capacity to as much as 30,000 watt-hours. That same port can be used to connect to Anker’s Solix 5000 Smart Tri-Fuel Generator for direct DC recharging, which is three times faster than standard AC charging. I had this very generator on hand and was able to test this out. I observed around 4,000 watts of input while the generator was running on gasoline. In an emergency where the power has gone out for several days, you could use this method to fully recharge the S5000 in less than two hours.

According to recent reports, the only downside is the maximum total output of 4,500 watts. While that’s perfectly fine for very basic home backup and RV use, it’s not going to power a heating/ventilation/air-conditioning system, let alone a full bank of circuits on a manual transfer switch, no matter how many expansion batteries are attached (they only add capacity, not output). True whole-home backup would require a larger station.

According to recent reports, sometimes, newer power station models are just more of the same, with only minor tweaks to power output, capacity, or outlet configuration. But the Anker S5000’s inverter efficiency technology is a notable upgrade that delivers on its promise of longer runtime than comparable models with the same capacity.

It’s not a contender for true whole-home backup (Anker’s E-10 system is a better option for that) and doesn’t have as much output power as the F3800, but it can bring substantial power during an emergency to several appliances or a couple of critical circuits, and it’s much more portable. And if you’re an RV owner looking for a compact yet powerful station, this should definitely be on your list for consideration.

Shop the Anker Solix S5000 Power Station.

Industry News: Best Knife Set After Years of Testing Knives (2026)

📅 14 Mar 2025 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3878 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that I’m just going to say it: You don’t need an 18-piece knife block with a blade for every conceivable kitchen task.
  • Sources indicate that after testing dozens and dozens of knives and talking with our Test Kitchen editors and professional chefs, the consensus is that the best knife set really only needs three essentials: a chef’s knife, a bread knife, and a paring knife.
  • When it comes to the core pieces of a knife set, though, many of the best knife makers make great versions of multiple knife types.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that I’m just going to say it: You don’t need an 18-piece knife block with a blade for every conceivable kitchen task. If you find one of those sets out in the wild, what you’ll probably find is that a lot of knives in the block still have a factory-sharp edge, because they’ve never been used. At the same time, it’s hard to ignore the sheer value a lot of knife sets offer. For most home cooks, buying every knife piecemeal is akin to adding a 15%–20% tax.

Sources indicate that after testing dozens and dozens of knives and talking with our Test Kitchen editors and professional chefs, the consensus is that the best knife set really only needs three essentials: a chef’s knife, a bread knife, and a paring knife. As you get more confident or curious in the kitchen, you might choose to add a versatile nakiri knife, a handy petty knife, or a versatile cleaver, but we generally recommend doing so on an ad hoc basis with an eye for how it will fit into your cooking and how much you truly want to spend on a knife.

When it comes to the core pieces of a knife set, though, many of the best knife makers make great versions of multiple knife types. In that spirit, the sets here offer high performance and great value without compromise. Nearly every knife recommended in these sets has been tested individually, so I feel confident saying you’ll be happily slicing, sawing, and coring with every recommended option.

Read on for our top knife set picks, including a couple of slightly more expansive options with a knife block and steak knives for those who want some extra pieces.

New in this upgrade: Editors spent some extended time with our top picks and we’ve added their long-term user notes.

Industry observers note that individual Mac knives have come out on top in our testing time and time again for their high-quality construction, ultrasharp blades, lightweight feel, and middle-of-the-road price point. This three-piece set is made up of a chef’s and petty knife that are the top overall picks in their respective categories, and a bread knife that’s essentially a luxe version of our favorite serrated knife.

It has been revealed that in testing, the Mac Professional Chef’s Knife was versatile and comfortable to use thanks to its ergonomic pakkawood handle, able to work through a giant mound of veggies efficiently without making our hands cramp up. Its blade was one of the sharpest we tested and combines the best qualities of Japanese- and Western-style chef’s knives in both its material and shape. Made of molybdenum high carbon steel, it strikes a balance between the brittle (but extra-sharp) steel used in Japanese blades and the softer, more durable steel typical of a Western knife. Similarly, its shape is a hybrid of the rounded edge of a Western-style blade and the straighter edge of a Japanese knife.

Perhaps unsurprisingly, we are also significant fans of Mac’s Professional Series petty knife, and for similar reasons: It’s razor-sharp and offers a unique shape that splits the difference between a utility knife and paring knife.

The bread knife included in this set is also part of Mac’s Professional Series. It’s a tier up from the Superior Series knife that won our bread knife test, which is evident in its build quality: While it features the same scalloped blade of the Superior Series knife, it has a metal bolster that makes for a more seamless connection between the blade and handle, and a more balanced overall feel while slicing.

Industry observers note that in the long run: I used these Mac knives for more than a year (the chef’s knife I used for five) and they served me well the whole time. The paring knife is on the long side so it’s better suited to things like cutting hard cheeses than peeling or coring, though I prefer using a Y-peeler and an apple corer anyway. But because it’s longer, it was also easier to sharpen. The bread knife is perfect. The shape of the serrations and curve of the blade provide excellent leverage, and because they’re wavy instead of pointy, I didn’t notice loss of sharpness at all. It’s also heavy enough that its weight helps me push through without tearing.

Recent findings suggest that and then there is the chef’s knife. The old standby, loved by every reviewer and Test Kitchen editor who has tried it. The balance, weight, and shape made it versatile, and the steel sharpened fantastically. However, after a couple years, my Mac did chip. I was able to resharpen and salvage it, but I’m not the only one who ended up with a chipped blade. The Mac we kept in house for long term testing also chipped after a few years. As reviewer Jesse Raub has noted in a number of his knife pieces, Japanese knives like the Mac are made from harder steel, so they don’t dull easily but they do chip. Personally, I find it one of those trade-offs you have to make when you’re picking a knife, and there is much good about the Mac that I still happily endorse it.

—Noah Kaufman, senior reviews editor.

Classic Damascus 3 Piece Knife Set.

Recent findings suggest that if you like the high-end look of beautiful Damascus steel and prefer a more rounded belly to your chef’s knife (better for rocking chops on the board), this set from Shun may be the one for you. Shun’s knives consistently perform well in our testing, and each of these knives has earned a spot as a top pick in its category. And by buying them as a set, you’ll save a modest amount of money off the total cost of the individual knives.

It has been revealed that one of the things that sets Shun’s Classic line apart is that it features the brand’s proprietary VG-MAX core, a high carbon steel with additional metals like chromium and molybdenum added in the mix to help with corrosion resistance and sharpness. In testing, we found this made for blades that cut effortlessly through anything we threw at them and retained their sharpness over time.

The rounded pakkawood handles of the Classic line knives made each of them extremely comfortable to hold, and because the handles maintain an even thickness throughout their length, they allow each user to find the grip and hand positioning that’s best for them.

Shun’s knives are routinely some of the sharpest in our testing, and we appreciate the more Western-leaning hybrid shape of their blades. It makes them great options for anyone who wants the versatility of a Western chef’s knife while looking for the precision edge of Japanese gyuto. While Shun’s bread knife is a little short for our tastes, it was also the sharpest and easily sliced through everything during its round of testing, earning it a top pick in that category.

It has been revealed that in the long run: I’ve had these Shun knives for a year now, and they’re my go-to set. The chef’s knife is incredibly comfortable to hold. A smooth notch where the blade meets the handle gives me a comfortable spot to pinch-grip, and the handle fits my small hands. The blade’s shape lets me glide and rock through tough ingredients. The paring knife is sharp and precise enough to hull strawberries but sturdy enough to cut into a thick wedge of Manchego. At nine inches, the bread knife handles most sourdough miches with ease, though I occasionally wish it were a little longer for really wide ones.

—Olivia Tarantino, senior reviews editor.

Renaissance 5-Piece Knife Set With Magnetic Board.

Spending $400 on a knife set, like the Mac and Shun options above, is a big investment, even if you’re getting three high-quality blades. For a more budget-friendly alternative, we recommend this four-knife set (it gets called a five-piece set because the knife board counts as a piece) from Mercer Culinary’s Renaissance line. It’s a great cheap option for anyone who wants reliable knives without committing to a premium price point.

Mercer’s knives have consistently performed well in our testing, from the Renaissance line to the more affordable Genesis and Millennia collections. Their Millennia 10-inch Wavy Edge Bread Knife, priced under $16 when bought on its own, is even one of our top picks. In our tests, the Mercer chef’s, bread, and paring knives all delivered clean, consistent cuts and maintained their edges well after repeated use. While they didn’t outperform our favorite pricier knives, they came surprisingly close considering they were less than half the cost. Made from high carbon steel with full-tang construction and durable handles, the knives in this Renaissance set feel solid, well-balanced, and easy to control.

While we prefer the Japanese petty knife over a Western utility knife shape, there’s enough value in the core three knives of this set that we think it’s worth it for anyone who wants an affordable refresh or is stocking their kitchen for the first time.

In our testing for the best chef’s knives, Hedley & Bennett’s chef’s knife stood out as well-balanced, comfortable to grip, and easy to maneuver thanks to the seamless transition between the handle and blade. After months of use, our Test Kitchen editors were impressed with how well it held up. And while testers preferred the Mac, if you’re looking to bring some fun color into your kitchen while still investing in a high-performing knife set, Hedley & Bennett is a great choice.

It has been revealed that this set includes a utility knife rather than a paring knife. It’s about two inches longer than a traditional paring knife (5.6 inches versus 3.5), making it a bit more versatile for larger tasks, such as slicing an oversized apple.

Sources indicate that the bread knife is on the shorter side, at only 8.6 inches, but its sharp, tapered serrated edge allows for more controlled, precise cuts than some straight-blade designs. Deputy Food Editor Hana Asbrink notes that the blade’s slope also helps prevent your knuckles from hitting the cutting board, a common issue with bread knives that maintain the same width along the entire blade.

It has been revealed that while they aren’t the sharpest knives out of the box, they’re made of high carbon stainless steel and can be easily sharpened to a finer edge. While we think most home cooks would like this set, its biggest advantage is the variety of colorways, which make for a more aesthetically pleasing kitchen.

In the long run: I’m in a less-is-more phase of my life, mostly because my shoe box of a kitchen leaves little room for 10 knives. So the pared down three from Hedley & Bennett fits perfectly in my space. They’re lightweight and the tapered spines have contributed to a welcome feeling of precision when using them. The chef’s knife gets the most use—there’s something rhythmic about slicing garlic with it. But the utility knife has come in handy more often than I thought. I’ve used it, along with my trusty kitchen shears, to break down whole chickens. And the angled tip of the serrated knife has made it useful for more than sawing through crusty bread. The blade shape helps for more delicate work like piercing tomato skin without mangling it.

Recent findings suggest that with use, a few minor scuffs and scratches have started to show. My colleagues have also warned me that the handles can crack over time, though that hasn’t been an glitch for me over the first several months. Bless the greater knife powers that be. I do make a point of never leaving my knives in the sink and always drying them thoroughly after washing.

—Nina Moskowitz, associate cooking editor.

The Wüsthof Classic line helped define high-end knives both at home and in professional kitchens for decades. Over the years, Wüsthof Classic set the standard for what to expect for performance and durability—full-tang construction, high carbon stainless steel, and a razor-sharp edge that’s easy to maintain. In our tests, Wüsthof’s 8" chef’s knife has been a standout for many years, and the included bread knife and paring knife are also great options.

Recent findings suggest that the major catch is that many cooks prefer the more nimble Japanese-style and hybrid knives, and Wüsthof’s heritage puts its Classic line in a more expensive bracket. Still, if you prefer the heft and durability of Western-style knife set, it’s hard to go wrong with this one—and they’ll last a lifetime with good upkeep.

Classic Essential Knife Block, Set of 7.

If you’re looking for a more expansive knife set beyond our essential three-piece recommendation, Shun’s Classic line stands out. This seven-piece set includes the core trio—a chef’s knife, paring knife, and bread knife—plus two smart additions: a 6-inch petty knife and a pair of herb shears. The petty knife fills that sweet spot between a paring and a chef’s knife, perfect for tasks that need more precision than a significant blade allows but would overwhelm a smaller one, like slicing citrus or trimming proteins.

The herb shears are a surprisingly handy upgrade. Instead of dragging out a cutting board just to mince some parsley or chives, you can snip them straight into a salad, soup, or garnish. Still, this is a good example of where a large set can sell you short: herb shears are less versatile than a standard set of heavy-duty kitchen shears.

The set also comes with a honing steel to keep your knives sharp and a sleek 11-slot bamboo storage block, which gives you extra space to add other styles down the line, like a nakiri for vegetable prep, a santoku, or even a cleaver.

Industry observers note that in the long run: By jumping up to the larger seven-piece set I got to add my favorite part of the set: the herb scissors. I use them to snip parsley right over a finished dish without pulling out a cutting board. They’re small, but they can still cut raw chicken into chunks when I don’t feel like reaching for a knife. Just be sure to hand-wash and towel-dry them right away. If you leave them dripping wet, they will get watermarks.

—Olivia Tarantino, senior reviews editor.

Sources indicate that large knife sets that come with a storage block are handy—it’s literally a one-stop shop. And if you’re a fan of serving grilled ribeyes whole to your guests, you’re going to need some sharp steak knives. Global’s knives are strong performers in our tests, and their unibody construction makes them easy to clean and maintain. We also like their unique steel, which retains sharpness without being as brittle as other alloys.

Recent findings suggest that while they can be polarizing, many people find their dimpled steel handles comfortable to hold, and their knives come sharp out of the box. A big reason we like this large set over other options is that larger knife sets are usually extremely expensive, or they’re made up of a knife maker's budget line. Here you see strong value for great knives, and the inclusion of a petty knife, a chef’s knife, and a kiritsuke-style slicing knife means there’s nothing you won’t be able to cut with swiftness and precision.

It has been revealed that given its size, it’s a well-balanced set, and the inclusion of the serrated utility knife is a nice touch for slicing tomatoes or peeling squash. It may feel like a hefty sticker price, but you’d be hard-pressed to find this many high-quality knives at this price point from other brands.

In the long run: While the Shun knives are my home set, the Global Chef’s knife is the one I always use when I’m working in the Test Kitchen. The balance and the size of the knives in this set (a slightly shorter chef’s and bread knives) are perfect for smaller women. Other BA editors have echoed this idea in the past. The secret is in the handle. Its dimpled steel gives you a secure grip, and it starts wide before tapering in, which makes it perfect for small hands. It feels hefty (it’s full of sand) while still being lightweight, which matters when you need to stay nimble with your knife cuts.

—Olivia Tarantino, senior reviews editor.

We’ve been testing knives for years now, and we have found that the same brands tend to come out on top across each knife category. Luckily for you, aspiring knife set purchasers, that means we’ve had no trouble finding three-piece sets from brands we know and love that feature product-test-winning, quality knives our team of experts can vouch for. Each set listed above is made up of individual knives we’ve tested against a long list of competitors and wholeheartedly approve of.

Head over to our individual reviews of the best chef’s knives, best bread knives, and best paring knives for even more information.

How many knives do you need in a knife set?

Industry observers note that we firmly believe that three knives are all you really need: a chef’s knife, a paring knife, and a bread knife. Together, they cover just about every essential kitchen task, from chopping vegetables to slicing crusty loaves.

That said, if you’re looking to upgrade or expand your collection, three additional knives are excellent additions: a nakiri knife, a petty knife, and a cleaver. While not essential, they’re nice to have: the nakiri offers extra precision for vegetable prep, the petty knife is ideal for those in-between tasks that a paring or chef’s knife might not handle quite as neatly, and a cleaver can help tackle larger chopping tasks (or precision cuts with a Chinese cleaver).

Which is the best brand for knives?

According to recent reports, mac has come out on top of our knife testing across the three core knives—chef’s, serrated, and paring—but the question itself is sort of like asking “who is the best guitar player.” Different people will find different knife shapes, weights, and handle styles better or worse for their hands. And, there are a lot of small elite knife makers out there that make items that aren’t just kitchen tools, but works of art. If you want to investigate some of those, we’d encourage you to check out a shop like Chubo Knives for elite Japanese blades.

Recent findings suggest that but as far as affordable, widely available knives go, Mac’s routinely outperformed the competition. They are made in Japan from molybdenum high carbon steel, which blends the durability of Western-style steel with the precision sharpness of traditional Japanese blades. The result is a knife that’s lightweight, versatile, and sharp. Mac’s bread knife took the top spot in our testing thanks to its 10.5-inch blade, which is an inch and a half longer than most. That extra length makes it easier to slice through wide loaves like focaccia in a single stroke.

Are expensive knife sets worth it?

Sources indicate that we stand by all of our recommended knives, but what you will get if you buy higher-end knives are blades made from better steel that are finished with more care. That means they’ll hold an edge longer, require less sharpening, and last for years with proper care. For most home cooks, it’s worth investing at least $150–$200 in a chef’s knife since it’s the blade you’ll reach for every day. Secondary knives like paring, bread, or utility knives don’t need to be as pricey, but if you use them often, it may be worth upgrading those too (and getting them as part of a bundle in a small knife set is a good way to do that).

Read more here about how much you should spend on a knife.

Is it better to buy knives individually or as a set?

It depends on your priorities. The great part about a knife set is that it’s a one-and-done purchase. You get the three essentials (chef’s, bread, and paring knives), and you can trust that each knife in the set has been tested to perform at a high level. That remarked, buying individually gives you more flexibility. Maybe you prefer a 6-inch chef’s knife over an 8-inch or a longer bread knife like Mac’s 10.5-inch version over Shun’s 9-inch or Hedley & Bennett’s 8.6-inch tapered blade. Think of a set as a strong starting point: It gets you well-equipped right away, but you can always mix and match later as you learn what sizes and styles feel best in your hand.

Is it cheaper to buy knives in a set?

Industry observers note that in general, yes—most manufacturers will offer at least some discount when you buy knives as a set rather than one at a time. How much of a discount? Well, that varies. For some brands, buying a three-piece set is like getting a third knife for free. For others, you might only save a few bucks. Still, many sets will also go on sale, adding even more savings to the already discounted knives. At the end of the day, it’s worth pricing out each knife in a set to see how much you’ll save by buying the bundle, and weigh that against being able to pick your favorite knife from each type. Still, we find that if you’re a fan of one knife from a brand, you’ll probably enjoy the handle style and comfort of other knives from the same brand—combined with some savings, you get a strong argument for picking out a knife set when you need a kitchen refresh.

What’s the best way to store your knives?

According to recent reports, proper storage is just as vital as proper sharpening when it comes to keeping your knives in good shape. No knife should ever be tossed into a drawer with other utensils—that’s a quick way to dull the edge, damage the blade, or worse, hurt someone.

The best storage option depends on your kitchen setup and preferences, but our favorite is a magnetic strip mounted on the wall. It keeps blades accessible, protects the edge, and works for all shapes and sizes, whether you’ve got a slim paring knife, a hefty cleaver, or even kitchen shears. Another big plus: magnetic strips take up zero counter or drawer space and are easy to clean with a quick wipe. These are our favorite magnetic strips.

Jesse Raub: I’ve been a professional kitchen product tester since 2021, where I tested nearly everything: espresso machines, wooden spoons, bread proofing baskets, pizza stones, garlic presses, and more. My fascination with kitchen knives began in 2003 when the chef at the kitchen where I worked let me use his personal Wüsthof knives during prep work one day. Over the last two years, I’ve tested over 70 different knives for Bon Appétit and written about the best knife sharpeners and how to best sharpen your knives at home. If you’re ever on the phone with me and hear a light scraping noise in the background, just know that I’m likely touching up my kitchen knives on a whetstone and testing their sharpness by slicing sheets of paper.

Additional testing by Olivia Tarantino and Noah Kaufman.

#7326. Cranberry Meringue Pie

📅 01 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (972 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Epicurious ↗ Open Full Page

Cranberry Meringue Pie

📅 01 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (972 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Epicurious

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A massive, billowing cloud of meringue tops this crimson beauty and acts as a sweet reprieve from the tart cranberry curd.
  • It has been revealed that we never make pie dough without a metal bench scraper.
  • Recent findings suggest that welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A massive, billowing cloud of meringue tops this crimson beauty and acts as a sweet reprieve from the tart cranberry curd. The vibrant filling is made even more sour with a generous amount of lime juice. Think lemon meringue pie but holiday-ified. Use our Perfect Pie Crust as the base to create a sturdy-flaky foundation, and be sure to start the pie the day before you blueprint to serve it, as the curd requires several hours of chilling to set into a sliceable texture. Cut into it too soon and it will run onto your plate, creating a messy—albeit delicious—slice.

It has been revealed that we never make pie dough without a metal bench scraper. Our favorite is from Gestura. Use the scraper to cut butter, fold dough and nudge it into shape, transfer it from counter to plastic wrap, trim edges, cut strips, and, sure, scrape flour off your counter.

Recent findings suggest that welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

3 hours (plus 30 minutes for freezing and 5 hours for chilling).

Whisk 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ¼ tsp. baking powder in a large bowl to combine. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces, and rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash with your fingers into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea-size).

Sources indicate that make a well in the center of mixture and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead in bowl a couple of times to bring dough together (some dry bits may remain).

In a recent development, turn out dough onto a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour and dust top of dough with flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold dough in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more rice flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Let dough disk sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Roll out dough on a lightly floured surface to a 12" round, about ¼" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and wrap around rolling pin. Transfer to a 9"-diameter pie pan (such as East Fork Spun Iron Pie Dish). Unfurl into pan, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into pan. Trim, leaving about a 1½" overhang. Fold overhang under so crust is flush with edges of pan and crimp as desired with lightly floured fingers. Set pan on a rimmed baking sheet and prick bottom and sides of crust with a fork in several places. Freeze, uncovered, at least 30 minutes and up to 2 hours.

Place a rack in lower third of oven; preheat to 400°. Line crust with a sheet of parchment paper and fill with pie weights or dried beans. Bake crust, tenting edges with foil if browning too quickly, until edges are set and look dry, 20–25 minutes. Carefully lift out parchment paper and weights and continue baking crust, gently pressing bottom and sides occasionally with a flat-bottomed measuring cup if puffing up, until bottom looks dry and is golden, 20–25 minutes more. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let crust cool.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

Recent findings suggest that bring 1 lb. fresh or frozen cranberries, 1½ cups (300 g) granulated sugar, and ¼ cup water to a boil in a large saucepan, then reduce heat to medium and simmer, stirring often, until cranberries soften and burst and most of the liquid has evaporated, 10–15 minutes. Let cranberry mixture cool.

Transfer cranberry mixture to a blender; reserve pan. Add ⅔ cup fresh lime juice and ¼ cup (32 g) cornstarch and blend on high speed until smooth. Scrape purée back into pan (not over heat) and add 3 large eggs, 2 large egg yolks, 1 Tbsp. vanilla extract, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Place over medium heat and cook, whisking constantly, until mixture bubbles and thickens to a pudding-like consistency, about 4 minutes. Remove pan from heat. Add ¾ cup (1½ sticks) unsalted butter, room temperature, cut into pieces, and whisk until melted and combined. Strain curd through a fine-mesh sieve, pushing with a rubber spatula, directly into crust. Smooth into an even layer and cover with plastic wrap, pressing directly onto surface. Chill pie at least 4 hours and up to 1 day.

Latest Update: Gina Bruno Wants You to Be a Guest at Your Own Party

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“Dinner is never just dinner. It is so much about the people, and the food is just the excuse to get those people around the table.”.

I’m 60 seconds into my conversation with Gina Bruno and find myself nodding in agreement, something I’ll continue to do for the next 20 minutes. The self-proclaimed “chef, mom, and host” wears a lot of hats. Private chef, event producer, event space owner, and host of the newly-debuted food show Salt The Water presented by Brami are just a few of the titles Bruno claims, but central to all of her work is a palpable love of people and of creating a space for gathering, both of which make her a natural-born host.

Sources indicate that bruno cites her Italian roots and the Sunday dinners she had as a child as the sources of her hosting instinct and ethos. “I am a family-style cooker when I’m hosting, and I just want to fill people up. I want to fill their glasses up; I want to fill their plates up. And the best compliment that I could ever get is having to tell someone, ‘Hey man, it’s really time to go home because I am exhausted and I need to go to bed.’”.

Not everyone has a natural inclination toward hosting, though, so to help them out I asked Bruno to run me through her tips for throwing a gathering, be it an intimate dinner or a rowdy holiday party.

In a recent development, “On a table, I will always have one kind of grand slam major, big dish, and then there’s all the supporting actors on the table,” Bruno states. While she uses saved folders on Instagram and Pinterest and likes to browse the Bon Appétit app, Bruno primarily looks to the market for inspiration, describing herself as a “very, very in-season cooker.” “I have so many recipes saved, and sometimes some of those get used, but there is something that just happens when you’re walking, and you see all of these fresh ingredients, and you just get to create a dish right in front of you.”.

Bruno’s main tip for anxious hosts is to prep as much in advance as possible. “Sauces and dressings you can absolutely do the day before, and that alleviates so much time the day of. You could go as far as literally setting your entire table the way you want it to be set with napkins, plates, silverware,” Bruno says.

According to recent reports, “Lighting is a huge thing,” Bruno notes. For evening soirees, she kisses the substantial overhead light goodbye, opting instead for lower light from lamps and candles tucked into corners to make the space feel moody. “The mood needs to be right, and you want to feel sexy when you walk into somebody’s home,” she says.

It has been revealed that bruno worked in restaurants and went to culinary school in Paris, where she learned the importance of maintaining a clean workspace. “If something spills right then and there, you are wiping it right then and there. If you use the spoon and you’re done, it’s going in the dishwasher. Cleaning as you go is a big step,” she claims.

According to recent reports, when hosting a more intimate event, one of Bruno’s favorite moves takes the form of an interactive game meant to encourage a bit of deep conversation. “Right before I serve dessert, I have everyone lift up their plate, and there is a little note underneath,” she indicates. The note has a question on it, either handwritten or printed depending on how much time Bruno has, and every question is different. “It adds a layer of, ‘Oh, our conversation maybe wouldn’t have gone here…. I just love getting to more juicy parts of the person, whether it’s a close friend or an absolute stranger, and it keeps people on their toes,” she says.

“It’s so easy to stay in host mode and think that you have to do all of these things to please people. But as soon as people arrive, it’s almost like, your job is done—or at least as soon as you drop the food, your job is done. And now you get to sit back and enjoy what you’ve done and be a part of it, because the worst feeling ever is you had all these people over, whether it’s four people or 10 people, and you were stuck in the kitchen and no one got to see you. So be a guest,” Bruno notes.

Industry observers note that bruno recounts a recent conversation with a friend who was afraid, on the one hand, to try making and serving something upcoming, but felt the dishes that were in her repertoire were too simple for tech giant. “You should never apologize for something that you’re cooking. If you are putting yourself out there and you want to cook something out of your realm, and, say it absolutely f*#%ing fails, that’s fine. I feel like your guests are going to be like, ‘Awesome. We will take a bite and not tell you our honest answer, and then we’re going to order a pizza, and it’s going to be amazing.’ The triumph of just trying is so much bigger than the actual meal,” Bruno says. “Food is the second tier. It’s more about the people around your table. You could serve potato chips and dip and people will actually be pretty happy,” she adds.

“Nine out of 10 times, if I am cooking for people, there is going to be a pasta dish on the table,” Bruno indicates. She’s a big fan of the protein pasta brand Brami, and not just because she just partnered with them on a YouTube show—she says the brand has organically become the only pasta she keeps at home.

Sources indicate that as for sauce, Bruno’s go-to is a spicy vodka. “If I’m making it at home, I’m actually leaving out the vodka and I’m swapping in mezcal, and it gives such a sneaky, smoky flavor that everyone will ask [about it]. And I will then go even further and usually pair it with a mezcal cocktail,” she notes.

Now that you know all of Bruno’s tips, these are the products she uses to make gatherings more special and less stressful.

Bruno always keeps three types of olive oil on hand: “One that is not so fancy and you could fry or make dressing with it—just one that’s kind of the back burner; a topping oil; and then an amazing peppery oil that you would maybe more so dip bread in or drizzle on top.”.

According to recent reports, “Flaky salt is always in my house,” Bruno says. She typically opts for either Maldon or a fleur de sel.

“We could consider Brami a staple. I mean, [my husband and I] cook it at least two times a week, whether there’s meat thrown in it or it’s just a sauce or a pesto or it's anything in between,” Bruno indicates.

Bird’s Eye Maple Wood Chopping Board.

Palio Round Serving Platter The Giraffe.

For hosting, I love substantial platters. Whether they’re vintage or newly introduced, I kind of love mixing those two together on the table,” Bruno claims. She likes having a collection of larger serveware specifically for hosting: “It’s kind of like your special stuff that you take out for friends.”.

1960s French Chrome Swan Handle Tray.

Jean Couzon Silverplate Serving Tray Fish Handles.

1970's Kromex Sculptura Walnut Accent Lazy Susan Serving Tray.

Antique Silver Plated Large Oval Tray.

Large Footed Silver Plated Butler’s Tray With Ornate Handles and Feet Bar Drinks Serving.

“I love silver, so I have a lot of silver trays, a lot of silver bowls. I think it makes a table,” Bruno claims. “I have quite the collection. I almost always buy vintage or second-hand when it comes to silver. There’s simply something about the life the piece had,” she adds.

“I recently splurged and got a really lovely cream and red dishware set from Porta. That was a big purchase for me, and it is a purchase that I am excited to bring out sparingly because I don’t want anything to break,” Bruno indicates.

It has been revealed that when it comes to flatware, Bruno is a Sabre person. “I have three different colors in my house. It’s the only cutlery that I have at this point,” she claims.

Sources indicate that “We are a massive wine-drinking family, so I have a wine fridge. There are on average at least 15 bottles of wine in that fridge always, and it is a variety because you never know what somebody likes,” Bruno says.

When hosting, Bruno keeps a candle burning in her bathroom and on the kitchen counter at all times. She’s partial to Keap’s Wood Cabin scent, which she orders in bulk for both her own home and her event space, Frank’s House.

Vintage St. James Silver Ice Bucket.

Stainless Steel Ice Bucket with Wood Accents.

1960s Swedish Cultura Stainless Steel Ice Bucket.

French Linen Tablecloth in Gingham.

Industry observers note that bruno loves a swanky ice bucket to keep bottles chilled in style, and she turns to tablecloths when she needs a pop of color. As for candlesticks, she likes the two-tone Dryp candles from Ferm Living.

In a recent development, cut the apples lengthwise into 1/2-inch thick slices. Insert a stick or skewer into one end of each slice. Cover a baking sheet in parchment, and set aside.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that this recipe will defy everything you have probably done to cook a turkey until now.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that cooking a whole turkey is a commitment. Between the schlepping, trussing, and constant babysitting, it’s a serious investment—and one that doesn’t always pay dividends. For a more laid-back affair, and one that practically guarantees success, might we suggest turkey legs cooked directly in gravy? Yes, in the gravy.

Sources indicate that this recipe will defy everything you have probably done to cook a turkey until now. The first key step is searing the whole turkey legs for optimal browning. Now you are ready to create a base for the gravy with all those drippings and toasty bits left in the pot. No need to make a full-on roux either: Just sprinkle in the flour over the melted fat, whisk to combine, and slowly pour in the broth. Once the gravy is done, in goes the turkey and aromatics for braising. The rest is you worrying about something else, because that turkey will cook itself.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Season 4 whole turkey legs (thigh and drumstick; about 6½ lb. total), patted dry, all over with kosher salt and freshly ground pepper. Heat 3 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large braiser or Dutch oven over medium-high. Working in 2 batches if needed to avoid overcrowding, arrange turkey legs, skin side down, in pot and cook, undisturbed, rotating pan on burner a few times to ensure even browning, until browned underneath and they easily release from pot, 8–12 minutes. Transfer turkey legs to a rimmed baking sheet, arranging skin side up. (No need to brown other side; turkey will still be raw at this point.).

Add more oil if pot looks dry; arrange 2 large oranges and/or lemons, halved, and 2 heads of garlic, tops trimmed to expose cloves, cut side down in pot and add 3 large shallots, peeled. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 2–3 minutes. Transfer each to baking sheet with turkey as they are done (it’s okay if some fall apart slightly).

Sources indicate that add 6 Tbsp. (¾ stick) unsalted butter to pot and cook until melted. Sprinkle in ⅓ cup (42 g) all-purpose flour and cook, stirring constantly, until no pockets of dry flour remain, about 1 minute. Gradually pour in 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth, stirring constantly to combine. Bring to a simmer and cook until gravy is just starting to thicken, about 2 minutes. Stir in 3 Tbsp. Worcestershire sauce and season with salt and pepper.

According to recent reports, nestle turkey legs into gravy, skin side up, then tuck oranges, garlic, and shallots around, arranging oranges and garlic cut side up. Add 1 small bunch thyme (about 10 sprigs), tied with kitchen twine, and cover pot tightly with a lid or foil. Braise 2 hours. (If your pot is too small to comfortably fit everything, transfer gravy to a 13x9" baking dish before adding turkey legs and aromatics.) Uncover pot and continue to bake until turkey legs are deeply browned, meat shreds easily off the bone, and gravy has thickened a little, 45–55 minutes.

Let turkey and gravy cool slightly before serving. Transfer to a platter if desired. (If gravy has excess fat on top, skim off with a spoon and discard before serving or spooning over legs on platter.).

After competing against nine culinary talents from across the country, chef Grace Cacciato was named the winner of the 2026–2027 S.Pellegrino Young Chef Academy US Regional Final. A panel of judges selected her roasted squab with chanterelle mushrooms and toasted buckwheat, black raspberry, and Swiss chard purées to represent the United States at the Grand Finale in Milan.

The 10 chefs vying to win the region cooked in the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen in Upcoming York City on Monday, and the winner was declared the following evening at the US Regional Final Gala & Awards. Everyone enjoyed the Gala menu, crafted by chef Garrett Brower, the 2024–25 US winner who is the chef de cuisine at Bresca in Washington, DC, and global mentor chef Aisha Ibrahim.

Representing the Michelin-starred restaurant Saga in New York, Cacciato presented a dish that featured the most components of any in the competition. All the judges were impressed with her sauce work and bold flavors.

Saga executive chef Charlie Mitchell returned for his second year as a mentor, working alongside Cacciato, a repeat competitor. “It was nice to see how her brain works…getting her perspective was inspiring,” he mentioned. Cacciato was equally enthusiastic. “It’s the best competition, and everyone wants to be a part of it,” she said.

The chefs had five hours to prepare and execute their signature dishes in the Test Kitchen. With an hour remaining, guests had the opportunity to mingle over food and drinks. Chef Rachel Bindel, a 2022 US Finalist, served rye toast piled high with Maryland blue crab, horseradish crème, and pickled green tomato. Chef Akshay Kumar, a 2024 finalist, tucked Kumamoto oysters into a pani puri with cucumber gel and lemon foam. Tomato pie from Philadelphia’s Pizza Freak Co., spoonfuls of Petrossian caviar, and a selection of wines, S.Pellegrino beverages, and cocktails rounded out the reception.

Industry observers note that nilou Motamed, a culinary expert and Iron Chef judge on Netflix, hosted the competition. Accomplished chefs from several states served as judges: chef and co-owner E.J. Lagasse of Emeril’s in Newly introduced Orleans; executive chef and partner Fariyal Abdullahi of Hav & Mar in New York City; Isabel Coss, executive chef at Pascual and founding pastry chef at Lutèce in Washington, DC; Jon Yao, head chef and owner at Kato in Los Angeles; and Ryan Ratino, executive chef and owner at Bresca and Jônt in Washington, DC.

According to recent reports, motamed explained that each competitor had spent several months developing their dish alongside a chef mentor. The mentors were in the Test Kitchen throughout the competition, but were not permitted to participate in the cooking. She also outlined the three pillars of the S.Pellegrino Young Chef Academy: Community, Competition, and Mentorship, which support its mission to discover and nurture the next generation of culinary talent.

Industry observers note that each chef’s arrival was revealed by a burst of music and a live video feed from the Test Kitchen, where a fleet of servers collected the finished plates before delivering them to the judges. First up was chef Adolfo Pucci of Michelin-starred Ariete in Miami. His dish, “Three Shores, One Table,” told the story of his Venezuelan heritage, his family’s roots in Southern Italy, and his current home in Miami. The ambitious plate featured a lamb ragù inspired by his grandmother’s cooking and lacto-fermented Florida blueberries.

Recent findings suggest that chef Amit Kumar of three-Michelin-starred Eleven Madison Park in New York City presented the competition’s only fully vegan dish: “Sunchoke with Banana Blossoms, Chanterelles, and Sherry.” Drawing on memories of the banana trees he grew up with in India, Kumar combined banana blossoms, sunchoke purée, chanterelle mushrooms, and a ragù of sherry and banana flowers to create a hearty and deeply satisfying dish. Judge Fariyal Abdullahi called it “a very successful dish, not just a very successful vegan dish.”.

Representing Auro at Four Seasons Resort and Residences Napa Valley, chef Evan Neumann presented “From the Valley to the Shoreline,” a love letter to the terroir of Northern California and Provence, where he grew up. Kombu-poached wild razor clams mingled with Napa verjuice and coastal seaweeds in a dish the judges found exceptionally creative. Neumann took home the S.Pellegrino Social Responsibility Award for his thoughtful approach to social responsibility and sustainable practices.

Sources indicate that at just 21, chef Lucy Field of Newly introduced York City’s fine dining bastion Per Se was the youngest competitor. Her dish, “Pekin Duck, Cherry, Plum,” was a study in restraint with only six components.

Industry observers note that chef Marcus Osorio, chef de cuisine at Living Room in Los Angeles, drew inspiration from his Salvadoran and Indigenous roots for his “Tamal de Pollo.” The dish featured corn sourced from Somos Maíz, the company founded by his mentor, chef Ron Oliver, and a mole poblano the two developed together. Judge Isabel Coss noted the challenge of preparing a mole with such limited time, but the judges were impressed by Osorio’s ability to marry European cooking techniques with soulful Indigenous ingredients and flavors.

According to recent reports, chef Nickolas Abbott hails from the small Appalachian town of Waynesville, North Carolina, and leads Chop Shop Butchery in Asheville. At the competition, he told the story of his community on a plate. His “Smoked Pork Loin, Fennel & Cheese Slaw, Sweet Potato, Asparagus, Fried Sausage, Pork Sauce Robert” reflected the people who shaped him, particularly his grandmother, his greatest inspiration as a chef.

Los Angeles–based chef Natasha Daniels of Providence showcased her vegetable-forward, zero-waste approach with “The Whole Bird, The Whole Garden.” The dish incorporated every part of a chicken across four preparations, alongside an array of vegetables and herbs inspired by her time working at The Chef’s Garden.

It has been revealed that daniels received two honors: the Acqua Panna Connection in Gastronomy Award and the Fine Dining Lovers Award. Voted on by regional mentors, the Acqua Panna award recognized the dish that best demonstrated a connection between culinary traditions. Daniels’s approach also resonated with Fine Dining Lovers insiders, who selected her for their award that honors “a chef’s expression of personal belief.”.

With only minutes to spare, chef Nicolas Lopez of 888 in Nashville arrived with “Pozole or Chawanmushi…?” Combining pozole, corn, and langoustine, Lopez connected his upbringing in Mexico with a culinary journey that has been shaped by Scandinavian ingredients and Japanese techniques. Although the judges could have used more time to explore the dish, they were intrigued by his influences and impressed by his technique.

The final competitor, Juwon Lee, is the chef of Octavia in San Francisco. Lee was born in South Korea and grew up in Singapore before making California his home. His dish, “Curry and Quail with Ingredients My Mother Noted Were Healthy,” drew on memories of eating Indonesian fried chicken and his mother’s insistence on including vegetables at family dinners. “I believe in the term happy food,” Lee explained. “There are no restrictions other than bringing joy to the eater and the chef.”.

It has been revealed that congratulations to all 10 chefs who competed, and best of luck to Chef Cacciato as she continues to work with her mentor and prepares to represent the United States at the 2027 Grand Finale in Milan. Follow her journey at @sanpellegrino_us.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, according to the study, drinking extremely hot tea was associated with a 16 percent higher relative risk of vascular disease.
  • Chelsea Azarcon is similarly cautious about drawing conclusions from the findings.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, there’s more than one reason to brew your tea at the right temperature—and one of those reasons could affect your health. A recently published study followed nearly half a million adults in China for almost a decade, examining how tea-drinking habits related to their health. Researchers found that regular tea drinkers had a lower risk of vascular disease than non-tea drinkers. But one major caveat emerged: Those who reported drinking their tea “burning hot” had a higher risk of vascular disease.

According to recent reports, according to the study, drinking extremely hot tea was associated with a 16 percent higher relative risk of vascular disease. But don't give up your daily tea habit quite yet. “This study is interesting, but we don't have a proven biological explanation yet,” Dr. Niraj Patel, medical director at Clara, says.

Dr. Chelsea Azarcon is similarly cautious about drawing conclusions from the findings.

Recent findings suggest that “It doesn’t look like this study has any proposed mechanism for why burning hot tea would increase the risk of cardiovascular disease,” she explains. “However, we do know that drinks that are too hot can increase the risk of esophageal cancer by creating local injury and damage.”.

Industry observers note that that concern is supported by the World Health Organization's cancer research agency, which has classified drinking beverages hotter than 149°F as probably carcinogenic to humans. The classification specifically concerns esophageal cancer, though, so it doesn't explain the connection to vascular disease identified in the new study.

The study didn’t identify a specific temperature at which drinking tea becomes detrimental to vascular health. And although researchers found an association between drinking extremely hot tea and vascular disease, that doesn't necessarily mean one causes the other.

ScienceDaily also notes that drinking tea at extremely high temperatures may diminish some of the health benefits associated with regular tea consumption.

Azarcon believes further research into tea's chemical makeup and how it may change at different temperatures could help answer some of the remaining questions.

It has been revealed that "I'd say enjoy your tea, but don't feel like you need to drink it while it's scalding hot,” Patel suggests. “There's a difference between brewing tea with hot water and actually drinking it at that temperature. Letting it cool for a few minutes is an easy precaution and doesn't require giving up something you enjoy.".

So while I don’t proposal on giving up my tea habit any time soon, I am definitely making extra sure that I let my cup sit out a little longer before taking that first sip.

  • It has been revealed that to identify the best better-for-you fast-food salads, we asked three nutrition experts to weigh in.
  • Sources indicate that first, we need to debunk salad’s diet-friendly reputation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that fast food chains aren’t exactly famous for their salads. They usually fall into two categories: a sad bowl of lettuce added to menus as an afterthought, or a vehicle for fried, calorie-dense ingredients that offset any nutritional upsides. But some chains do make an effort to sell salads worth ordering.

It has been revealed that to identify the best better-for-you fast-food salads, we asked three nutrition experts to weigh in. Here are the menu items they recommend, along with some tips and tricks for maximizing their nutrition.

Sources indicate that first, we need to debunk salad’s diet-friendly reputation. “A salad isn't automatically the healthiest choice on a fast food menu,” claims Kathy Levin, RDN, CDCES, dipACLM, LDN. “Once you add fried chicken, bacon, cheese, candied nuts, crunchy toppings, and a creamy dressing, some salads land in the same calorie and fat range as a burger and fries.”.

Taking all of those components away isn’t always a solution either. A sad salad with just lettuce and a smattering of vegetables is more like rabbit food than a satisfying meal for humans. According to Briana V. Reamer, MS, RDN, LDN, the secret is getting enough fiber, which she claims “will keep you satisfied and full until your next meal.” Take advantage of the restaurant's add-ons—like beans, avocado, and more vegetables—to make your salad more substantial.

Experts also recommend watching your saturated fat intake, specifically with your protein and dressing. Grilled chicken generally has fewer calories and less saturated fat than deep-fried alternatives. Consider your dressing options, too. “If you’re not sure what to pick, look for a vinaigrette or olive-oil-based dressing,” claims Tina Sergi, MS, RD, CSSD, CSCS, TSAC-F.

Sources indicate that and, as a rule of thumb, order your dressing on the side. It keeps your salad from getting soggy on the drive home, for one, but it also gives you more portion control. “Using only part of the packet cuts saturated fat and sodium, especially when they're already on the higher end,” Sergi adds.

Sources indicate that of course, the dressing is only part of the equation. With those tips in mind, here are the five salads that made the cut.

It has been revealed that this regional chain is known for its fire-grilled chicken, and this salad packs plenty of it. Each portion contains a double serving of citrus-marinated chicken breast, sliced avocado, cotija cheese, salsa fresca, and tortilla strips over a bed of greens. It's served with a creamy Mexican-inspired Caesar dressing.

Sources indicate that el Pollo Loco strikes the right balance between substantial and light with this dish. Before you add dressing, the entire salad contains 420 calories and 52 grams of protein. “The fire-grilled chicken makes it very filling, the avocado adds heart-healthy fat and fiber, and the salsa fresca adds flavor without much sodium or sugar,” Levin says.

It has been revealed that like with most salads, the dressing significantly raises the calorie count—in this case, it adds 440 calories if you use the entire serving. If you're closely monitoring your daily intake, Levin advises going easy on the dressing.

In a recent development, culver’s may be best known for its ButterBurgers, but experts say you shouldn’t sleep on its salads. The Chicken Cashew Salad in particular is a great choice. It starts with a bed of mixed greens, topped with cheddar, grape tomatoes, cucumbers, and roasted cashews. You can also choose from several dressings to finish it off.

With grilled chicken, the salad comes in at 430 calories and 41 grams of protein before adding dressing. Culver’s also offers six dressing varieties ranging from 50 to 260 calories.

Sources indicate that “This is a great fiber- and protein-packed option,” claims Sergi. “Plus, the cashews add healthy fats, copper to support energy production, and magnesium for optimal nerve and muscle function.”.

This Lone Star staple sells a Cobb salad that’s a lighter alternative to its lineup of burgers and sandwiches. It comes loaded with all of the essentials: greens, bacon, a hard-boiled egg, grape tomatoes, carrots, and shredded cheese. You can also choose from three chicken options (the grilled chicken filet is, naturally, lighter than the fried options).

According to recent reports, without dressing, Whataburger's Cobb with grilled chicken has 430 calories and 44 grams of protein. It's also a source of fiber and is low in sugar, according to Reamer. “Salads high in fiber help with weight management and satisfy hunger.”.

Some of Whataburger's creamier dressings add 200 to 280 calories, while the balsamic vinaigrette has 180.

In a recent development, for a fried chicken chain, Chick-fil-A makes some surprisingly stellar salads. The Market Salad starts with mixed greens and is topped with strawberries, blueberries, red and green apples, blue cheese, roasted almonds, and the chain’s Harvest Nut Granola. Chick-fil-A also has the most protein options on this list. The grilled chicken can come in nugget or filet form, warm or cold, and spicy or regular. Talk about variety!

Industry observers note that the different grilled chicken options provide between 26 and 32 grams of protein, according to Chick-fil-A's nutrition guide. Levin also says you can forgo chicken entirely for a meatless meal that doesn't feel like an afterthought. “Berries and apples bring fiber, antioxidants and natural sweetness, which makes it one of the most plant-forward options on the list.”.

The Market Salad is typically paired with Chick-fil-A's Zesty Apple Cider Vinaigrette Dressing, which contains 230 calories per packet. But the chain is known for its sauces, after all, so you can swap it out for another option. There's a Light Balsamic Vinaigrette with 80 calories, Fat-Free Honey Mustard with 90, and Light Italian Dressing with just 25.

Zaxby's is the third chicken chain on this list, and it stands out by offering a salad with Asian-inspired flavors. The Asian Zensation Zalad (not Salad) adds shredded carrots, cabbage, wonton strips, and Asian Slaw to mixed greens, along with a drizzle of teriyaki sauce. It also comes with a vegetable egg roll on the side.

Sources indicate that this salad is loaded with plant-based toppings, which is why Levin also recommends the garden version as a vegetarian option. Zaxby's lists that version at 390 calories, while the grilled chicken version comes in at 530 calories and 39 grams of protein, before adding dressing.

Alongside the teriyaki drizzle, Zaxby's offers Citrus Vinaigrette with the salad, which has 110 calories per packet. It's one of the chain's lighter options. But if you're watching your calorie intake, you can swap in Lite Vinaigrette, which contains just 30 calories.

Industry observers note that we rate butternut the most affable winter squash—relatively easy to prepare, consistently delicious, and available at most grocery stores. The buttered nut dressing is more than just cheeky wordplay. Bold from brown butter and balsamic vinegar and bright from lemon, the crunchy topping is an excellent foil to the sweetness of roasted squash. Cook the squash a couple hours ahead of time and all you’ll have left to do before dinner is make the dressing.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in lower third of oven; preheat to 425°. Lightly crush 2 tsp. fennel seeds with a mortar and pestle or place on a cutting board and gently crush with a heavy pan. Peel 1 medium butternut squash (about 3 lb.) and halve lengthwise. Scoop out seeds; discard. Cut squash into 2" irregular pieces, aiming for sharp, jagged shapes. Transfer to a large rimmed baking sheet; drizzle with 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil and sprinkle with fennel seeds, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. crushed red pepper flakes. Toss squash to coat, arrange in a single layer, and roast until browned and tender, 30–35 minutes.

Sources indicate that do Ahead: Squash can be roasted 2 hours ahead. Store at room temperature.

According to recent reports, while the squash is roasting, cook 6 oz. thick-cut bacon, cut into 1" pieces, in a medium skillet over medium heat, stirring often, until browned and mostly crisp, 8–12 minutes. Transfer to a small plate with a slotted spoon.

Recent findings suggest that reduce heat to low; combine 1 cup raw pecans and 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter in same pan. Cook, stirring often, until butter browns and nuts have slightly darkened, 6–8 minutes. Remove from heat. Stir in 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped (this will give it a head start to take off the raw edge), then add bacon, zest and juice of 1 large lemon, 3 sprigs sage, and 2 Tbsp. balsamic vinegar and stir to combine. Taste dressing and season with kosher salt if needed.

Arrange squash on a platter and spoon dressing over.

For those who might shudder at the thought of eating raw hardy greens like collards or kale, this vibrant side inspired by the French bistro classic leeks vinaigrette is the answer. Simmered past squeaky-raw yet well short of meltingly braised, they offer substantial bite, like al dente pasta. The mustard dressing couldn’t be simpler to make—use it as a base for any salad you might serve this season. It’s punchy enough to stand up to winter vegetables or any sturdy bitter green.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

According to recent reports, place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Toast ½ cup raw walnuts on a rimmed baking sheet, tossing halfway through, until golden brown, 10–12 minutes.

Meanwhile, cook 2 bunches collard greens, ribs and stems removed, leaves cut into 2" pieces, in a large pot of generously salted boiling water until just tender, 9–11 minutes. Using tongs, immediately transfer to a large bowl of ice water and let cool.

It has been revealed that whisk 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, ¼ cup white wine vinegar, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, preferably country-style, ⅓ cup extra-virgin olive oil, ¼ cup (packed) coarsely chopped tarragon, 2 tsp. sugar, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl to combine. Set dressing aside.

Sources indicate that transfer toasted walnuts to a small bowl and drizzle with remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Sprinkle with a generous pinch each of sugar and salt and toss to coat. Taste and add more sugar if needed (nuts should be more sweet than salty). Set seasoned walnuts aside.

Drain collard greens and squeeze gently to remove excess water. Transfer to bowl with reserved dressing and toss to coat evenly. Cover and chill at least 15 minutes and up to 2 hours.

It has been revealed that arrange greens in a shallow bowl or on a platter and spoon any dressing remaining in bowl over. Top with seasoned walnuts and tarragon leaves.

Industry observers note that do Ahead: Walnuts can be toasted and dressing can be made 1 day ahead. Store walnuts airtight at room temperature. Cover dressing and chill.
